messages.subject: ShinyStan 2.2.1 released
messages.subject_clean: ShinyStan 2.2.1 released
messages.body_plain:
Version 2.2.1 of the shinystan R package is now available. This release doesn't introduce any new features but fixes a few important issues resulting from changes to several packages used to generate content for the ShinyStan GUI. Most importantly, prior to this release, updating to the latest version of the DT package would cause errors with ShinyStan's posterior summary statistics table (thanks to GitHub users tjmahr and cvr7 for bringing this to our attention). Release notes for this version and previous versions (the previous release did introduce some new features) can be found here <https://github.com/stan-dev/shinystan/releases>.

You can check if binaries for your platform have been built at cran.r-project.org/package=shinystan <http://cran.r-project.org/package=shinystan>. At this moment it appears that only Windows binaries have been built but Mac binaries should be available shortly. To install from CRAN and verify that you have latest version run

install.packages("shinystan")
packageVersion("shinystan")  #should be 2.2.1

If the binary for your platform hasn't been built then you can install from source by adding the argument type="source" when calling install.packages. Alternatively, for all platforms the latest release can be installed from GitHub (using the devtools package) by running

devtools::install_github("stan-dev/shinystan", build_vignettes = TRUE)

- The Stan Development Team

P.S. Be on the lookout for new features coming this fall (or spring for those of you in the southern hemisphere). To request a feature (or file a bug report) you can use the GitHub issue tracker for ShinyStan at https://github.com/stan-dev/shinystan/issues

No worries, and thanks for responding! I also suspect it has something to do with my RTools installation, but what that might be is mysterious. I've removed and reinstalled RTools with slightly different PATH variables, manually edited the PATH, etc. What's bizarre is that as far as I can tell, the RTools configuration and the relevant lines of the PATH are exactly the same as they were when I was using RStan 2.9 (which worked), and are identical to those on my other machine (where 2.10 and 2.11 have worked).

messages.subject: Categorical contrast not working
messages.subject_clean: Categorical contrast not working
messages.body_plain:
Question about categorical analysis:
I get the same slope values when exchanging categorical variables.  I expect differences (since the data suggest that the UV will have the largest lambda, and trap catch count means were certainly not equal):

unique(d$trap) #BG (default intercept category), EVS, UV, CDC
d$trap.EVS <- ifelse( d$trap=="2" , 1 , 0 ) #"2" used to match cvs file
d$trap.UV <- ifelse( d$trap=="3", 1 , 0)
d$trap.CDC <- ifelse( d$trap=="4" , 1 , 0)
# Got a = 4.49 (mean) using BG as default intercept

#when I redo same calculation using EVS:
d$trap.BG <- ifelse( d$trap=="1" , 1 , 0 ) #EVS now default slope "a"
d$trap.UV <- ifelse( d$trap=="3", 1 , 0)
d$trap.CDC <- ifelse( d$trap=="4" , 1 , 0)
# Got a = 4.49 (mean) using EVS as default inercept

#model follows:
NAM1.0 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt.BG*trap.EVS + bt.UV*trap.UV + bt.CDC*trap.CDC,
    a ~ dnorm(0,10),
    bt.BG ~ dnorm(0,1),
      bt.UV ~ dnorm(0,1),
      bt.CDC ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ),
  data = d)
precis(NAM1.0)

#Results for letting BG = intercept default
> precis(NAM1.0)
        Mean StdDev  5.5% 94.5%
a       4.49   0.04  4.43  4.55
bt.EVS -0.97   0.07 -1.08 -0.85
bt.UV   0.58   0.05  0.51  0.66
bt.CDC  0.10   0.05  0.01  0.18

#Results for letting EVS =  intercept default
> precis(NAM1.0)
        Mean StdDev  5.5% 94.5%
a       4.49   0.04  4.43  4.55
bt.BG  -0.97   0.07 -1.09 -0.86
bt.UV   0.58   0.05  0.50  0.65
bt.CDC  0.09   0.05  0.01  0.17

Please advise.

I posted Max Joseph's rendered case study, Exact Sparse CAR Models in Stan This document details sparse exact conditional autoregressive (CAR) models in Stan as an extension of previous work on approximate sparse CAR models in Stan. messages.subject: Help?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thank you for developing STAN. I am currently doing a PhD and I have been using STAN to fit a multi-state back-calculation model to estimate age-specific HIV incidence.

I wrote and ran the model, but I have occasional divergent transitions warnings and the model runs quite slowly (despite it mixes well), so I was wondering if you could help me with that.

This model is the biggest part of my PhD work, so I am not entirely willing to put it on the mailing list. Would it be too much to ask to contact you, and send the codes, via email?

Many thanks
F.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help?
messages.body_plain:
The first thing to try is to increase adapt_delta to something higher: 0.9 or higher. See the manuals / documentation for the interface you're using to figure out how to set that parameter. It will force the stepsize used in HMC to be smaller, which will hopefully be able to simulate the Hamiltonian trajectory accurately enough to avoid the divergences.

The next thing to do is try to reparameterize. For that, see the manual and look for the section on non-centered parameterization.

Want to try those two things first?

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel and Bob,

Many thanks for your quick replies.

To Daniel: I have been playing a lot with re-parametrizations of the model. For example I have a multivariate normal prior (with known covariance matrix) on some of my parameters: I started by using the covariance matrix formulation but I had a lot of divergent transitions and in that case increasing adapt_delta (to 0.99) did not solve the problem. I then found that parametrizing in terms of the precision (rather than the covariance matrix) leads to very little divergent transitions (0/1/2 depending on the seed), in this case I have not tried increasing adapt_delta but I guess it would help even though it would also make the model even slower (it takes approximately 6h for 2000 iterations now). Concerning non-centered re-parametrization I have read the manual, however my observations are Poisson distributed so I do not know how to re-parametrize in such case.

To Bob: I understand your point and I understand that private questions are not a priority. However, after discussion with my advisor, we concluded that it is not a good idea to make the model public yet. If we get the model to work and the issues I encounter can help other people, we are very happy to make it public later. I have a commented version of the code along with some modeling notes that I wrote to clarify what the codes do that I could share if you can help me.

Thank you
Fran

For example I have a multivariate normal prior (with known covariance matrix) on some of my parameters: I started by using the covariance matrix formulation but I had a lot of divergent transitions and in that case increasing adapt_delta (to 0.99) did not solve the problem. I then found that parametrizing in terms of the precision (rather than the covariance matrix) leads to very little divergent transitions (0/1/2 depending on the seed), in this case I have not tried increasing adapt_delta but I guess it would help even though it would also make the model even slower (it takes approximately 6h for 2000 iterations now). Concerning non-centered re-parametrization I have read the manual, however my observations are Poisson distributed so I do not know how to re-parametrize in such case.

Hard to tell without seeing the model.  But it's the parameters
that get non-centered, not the observations.  It'll work for
any GLM-type model (basically any hierarchical parameters with
location-scale parameterizations).

We very strongly recommend parameterizing in terms of Cholesky
factors for correlation matrices and scaling them (see the manual).
It will be much much faster and much much more stable arithmetically.

You also may not need 2000 iterations.  And whatever you do,
run multiple chains so you can diagnose non-convergence issues.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Just to play bad cop a bit — I think everyone on the Stan team
came to their current positions because they want to help
scientists to better science, but it’s _really_ hard to do that
without seeing the models and the data.  There’s just too
much that can go wrong, so if the generic advice in the manual
hasn’t been helpful then there’s not too much more that we can
do.

We are sympathetic to the sensitivity of the results, but honestly
private consulting is very time consuming and without proper
collaboration (including input on the model and co-authorship)
it’s hard to motivate such help when we could be helping so many
more people with open problems.

Given the constraints I think that your most promising approach
right now is to try to identifying parts of the model that might be
causing issues, and abstract those away to examples that you
can share publicly.  It is so much easier to answer specific questions
with example models.

Chuck

I'd like to echo Chuck's appreciation.  This forum was a huge help during my dissertation, and I still glance through the topics a few times each week to read threads related to the issues I use Stan for.  The plurality of expertise among the contributors (some with pragmatic programming tricks, some (particularly Michael!) with great conceptual explanations of the underlying math that would otherwise make my head explode, some with decades of "field" experience, etc.) makes these email threads useful just to peruse and bookmark for later use.  Thanks so much to everyone here!

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

us while working in an online advertising shop after finishing a Ph.D.
in physics.

messages.body_plain:
> On Sep 3, 2016, at 8:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <christopher...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This is question is probably more about statistics than Stan specifically.
>
> I'm interested in modeling some data where each group's standard deviation is allowed to differ, but assumed to share some common information. Essentially, I'm looking for a prior that shrinks the group level variance towards the overall variance.  I've read a number of papers on hierarchical shrinkage priors (e.g., the horseshoe prior), which allow a few parameters to have a large standard deviation while shrinking most of the others to zero, but these don't really have the behavior for which I'm looking.
>
> I've considered a possible candidate, but I'm unsure as to if it actually makes any sort of sense.
>
> y[i,j]    ~ Normal(mu[j], sigma[j])
> sigma[j]  = lambda[j] * tau
> tau       ~ half-t(nu_tau, 0, s_tau)
> lambda[j] ~ log_normal(0, epsilon)
> epsilon   ~ half-t(nu_epsilon, 0, s_epsilon)
> mu[j]     ~ ... However you wish to model the means
>
> The s and nu variables are fixed hyperparameters, and j represents a group. The idea is that as epsilon -> 0, lambda[j] -> 1 and sigma[j] -> tau.

epsilon won't go to 0 as the scale and d.o.f. of tau is fixed.

Whether this makes sense as model for your scales sigma[j] depends
on the application area.  This isn't a one-size-fits-all kind of
problem any more than other aspects of regressions.

> I've run a few simulations (attached). The estimates for tau and epsilon are vague and have an effective sample size that's usually around 10% of of the number of retained iterations; lambda and raw_log_lambda have an n_eff in the same range.  Despite this, it does a very good job at estimating sigma, with n_eff equal to the number of iterations. PP checks also appear to be performing well.  There don't appear to be any convergence issues.
>
> Could anyone here with a better statistical understanding than I have comment as to whether this seems like a reasonable prior?  I'm also somewhat confused as to how sigma can have such a high effective sample size when its components (tau, epsilon, lambda) do not.

This is an identifiability issue.  If there are many ways parameters
theta1 and theta2 can lead to the same theta3 = f(theta1, theta2),
you can get theta3 with high n_eff even if theta1 and theta2 have
low n_eff.

Because sigma[j] = lambda[j] * tau,
you can multiply lambda by a constant C and divide tau by C and get the
same answer for sigma.  You're controlling this non-identifiability by
centering the lambdas, but Lognormal and Student-t are not going to
be particularly strong, especially as you allow the scale of lambda
to vary as epsilon.  This isn't wrong but can lead to low effective
sample sizes and you should see banana-like pair plots between lambda[j] and
tau and also high correlation among the lambda[j] (the funnel problem you
get with any hierarchical model).

> Does anyone have any suggestions for reparameterizing the model to deal with these issues?

It can help to use the non-centered parameterization for lambda to
deal with the funnel-like issue.  It's just the usual one on the log scale.

It might also help to add an intercept term to the sigma[j] instead of
modeling them purely multiplicatively, though that can sometimes lead
to more identifiability problems.

- Bob

messages.subject: discrete lower-bound truncation bug
messages.subject_clean: discrete lower-bound truncation bug
messages.body_plain:
There's a serious bug in the way the contribution to
the log density of the normalization term induced by
the truncation for discrete distribution lower bounds.

Instead of treating the bound L as inclusive in
T[L, U]  and T[L, ], it is being normalized in such
a way that L is exclusive and U is inclusive.

Upper bounds for discrete distributions are OK and
all bounds for continuous distributions are OK.

This will be fixed for 2.12.

This will affect sampling and optimization for cases
where a discrete distribution has a parameter that's
declared as a parameter in the Stan model, e.g.,

  parameters {
    real<lower=0> lambda;

  model {
    y ~ poisson(lambda) T[4, ];  // *** BAD NORMALIZATION ***

There is no problem for upper bounds or continuous distributions.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Stan assumes the models are programmed on the log scale.
So you want to code the log likelihood, not the likelihood.

So when you apply log() and then use log_sum_exp on the additive
terms, you'll wind up needing the log-scale CDFs.

Not that our log-scale CDFs are particularly robust.  They're
pretty much coded up as the log of the CDF pending help from
a numerical analyst who can write good log CDF and derivatives
for us!

- Bob

> On Aug 29, 2016, at 8:13 AM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Just for your information, I re-ran with exactly the same parameters and model as in the second run above (i.e. with extended bounds on parameters), but with 15,000 samples rather than 5000, to see if that made the estimates better. It seems to consolidate the separation between the expected results and those that the model gets:
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>
>

> On Monday, 29 August 2016 11:44:06 UTC+8, Steven and Jeanette Murray wrote:
> Thanks for your fast response Bob.
>
>
> On Saturday, 27 August 2016 03:12:18 UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Why have a lower=0 bound on the log scale?
>
> You're right, I've removed that now, not that it should make much difference.
>
> And we don't genrally recommend bounds like (-2, 0)
> unless the parameter is physically constrained to (-2, 0).
>
> What do you suggest then? I wanted to (at least initially) use a uniform prior, but of course it's improper to use an unbounded uniform prior. I know alpha is ~-1.87 and should have a very tight constraint. It will never be greater than -1.5 and there's reason to expect it to be constrained above -2 (though technically it could be lower). Typically I find that it's -1.87 +- 0.02 or so. Given that kind of range, would these bounds still be a source of bias? I've run it again (see below) with more generous bounds to check for myself.
>
> Otherwise, you can bias the posterior means considerably by
> truncating non-negligible probability mass.
>
> In general, you just code the generative model directly
> in Stan and Stan does the inversion---you shouldn't try
> to code the inversion directly unless you have analytical
> steps (which can save time and make the statistical mixing
> more efficient).
>
>
> Sorry, yes I used the generative model directly. I mean, I generate the data by choosing the parameters, sampling from the truncated_logGGD with those parameters to get log_mtrue, then sampling from a normal to get log_m_meas. That's directly what I have in my model.
>
> The MLE is not the iteration with the highest log density.
> Often the MLE isn't in the typical set at all, so you won't
> get anywhere near it (e.g., try sampling from a 20-dimensional
> unit normal exactly and see how close you get to zero, the MLE).
> What you want to be doing is checking posterior interval
> calibration (coverage, say, of the 50% intervals).
>
>
> Okay, fair enough. So, are you saying that even though the expected solution had a lower likelihood than another region in my chains, that it's possible that the chain would centre around the expected solution anyway?
>
> Also, just measuring by the log density won't tell you much.
>
>
> In a couple of re-runs below I show the parameter intervals instead. Is this better?
>
> I'm afraid I don't understand this truncated density---maybe
> someone else could help?
>
>
> That's fine. I'm confident that the truncated density is doing what it's supposed to.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> So, I ran again with the following model (note I just took out some of the bounds on log parameters):
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N;                // number of halos
>     vector[N] log_m_meas; // measured halo masses
>     vector<lower=0>[N] sd_dex;     // uncertainty in halo masses (dex)
>     real<lower=0> V;               // Volume of the survey
>
>     // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
>     vector[2] hs_bounds;             // Bounds of logHs
>     vector[2] alpha_bounds;          // Bounds of alpha
>     vector<lower=0>[2] beta_bounds;  // Bounds of beta
>     vector[2] mmin_bounds;           // Bounds of log_mmin
>     vector[2] mtrue_bounds;          // Bounds of log_mtrue
>     vector[2] lnA_bounds;            // Bounds of lnA
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real<lower=hs_bounds[1],upper=hs_bounds[2]> logHs;               // Characteristic halo mass
>     real<lower=alpha_bounds[1],upper=alpha_bounds[2]> alpha;         // Power-law slope
>     real<lower=beta_bounds[1],upper=beta_bounds[2]> beta;            // Cut-off parameter
>     real<lower=mmin_bounds[1],upper=mmin_bounds[2]> log_mmin;        // Truncation mass
>     vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_bounds[2]>[N] log_mtrue;       // True mass estimates
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>     real lnA;
>     real raw_lnA;
>     real gzx;
>
>     gzx <- gammainc((alpha+1)/beta,exp(log10()*(log_mmin-logHs)*beta));
>     raw_lnA <- log(N) - log10()*logHs - log(gzx);
>     lnA <- raw_lnA - log(V);
> }
>
> model {
>     vector[N] y;
>     y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
>     y ~ truncated_logGGD(logHs, alpha, beta, raw_lnA, gzx);
>     log_m_meas ~ normal(log_mtrue,sd_dex);
> }
>
>
> I first ran with the following data [this is the same as I used in my results for the last post] (note I constrain alpha, i.e. the power-law slope of the function to (-1.99,-1.7)):
>
> {'N': 5078,
>  'V': 1190658.039618655,
>  'alpha_bounds': (-1.99, -1.7),
>  'beta_bounds': (0.4, 1.2),
>  'hs_bounds': (13, 15.5),
>  'lnA_bounds': (-48, -37),
>  'log_m_meas': array([ 13.35251163, 11.78469724, 12.01253925, ..., 12.72611462, 14.18542692, 12.40310497]),
>  'mmin_bounds': (10, 14),
>  'mtrue_bounds': (10, 17.0),  # Note: only the upper bound here is actually used.
>  'sd_dex': array([ 0.63660784, 0.79483786, 0.79483786, ..., 0.7411142 , 0.7411142 , 0.7411142 ])}
>
> The Stan summary is
>
>                   mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
> logHs            14.61    0.02   0.27  14.15  14.42  14.59  14.77  15.21  280.0   1.01
> alpha             -1.8  4.7e-3   0.06  -1.92  -1.84   -1.8  -1.75  -1.71  156.0   1.03
> beta              0.87  8.4e-3   0.21   0.44   0.71    0.9   1.05   1.19  646.0    1.0
> log_mmin         12.03  2.1e-3   0.02  11.98  12.01  12.03  12.04  12.07  126.0   1.03
>
>
> and the input values were
>
> {'alpha': -1.8682714014860426,  ## outside 50% coverage
>  'beta': 0.6999588565297955,    ## outside 50% coverage
>  'logHs': 14.312105251983247    ## outside 50% coverage
>
>  'log_mmin': 12.04004004        ## just outside 50% coverage
> }
>
> The traceplot looks like:
>
>
>
>
>

> I then ran it again, with the following data (note the relaxation of several bounds):
>
> {'N': 5046,
>  'V': 1190658.039618655,
>  'alpha_bounds': (-3, -1),
>  'beta_bounds': (0.2, 2.0),
>  'hs_bounds': (12, 15.05),
>  'lnA_bounds': (-48, -37),
>  'log_m_meas': array([ 12.64310298,  11.64157076,  12.23913006, ...,  12.24778487,
>          11.71975052,  13.23577041]),
>  'mmin_bounds': (10, 14),
>  'mtrue_bounds': (10, 17.0),
>  'sd_dex': array([ 0.8705571 ,  0.7411142 ,  0.79483786, ...,  0.79483786,
>          0.79483786,  0.66539496])}
>
>
> and get the following results:
>
>                   mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
> logHs            14.27    0.03   0.49  12.63  14.23  14.45  14.56  14.64  278.0    1.0
> alpha            -1.74  7.1e-3    0.1  -1.88  -1.81  -1.76  -1.69  -1.48  209.0   1.01
> beta              1.04    0.02   0.51   0.26   0.58    1.0   1.48   1.95  449.0    1.0
> log_mmin         12.02  1.9e-3   0.03  11.97   12.0  12.02  12.03  12.06  190.0   1.01
>
>
>
> Now logHs is within range, and so is beta (on account of its range being very large). But alpha is way off.  While running these, I noticed one interesting thing: if logHs is larger than max(log_mtrue), its effect plateau's in terms of its correlation with beta. That is, if the scale where the exponential cut-off happens is outside the range of masses, then it doesn't matter what beta is at all. That's why I've kept logHs bounded to ~15.
>
> I ran the same model but setting the log_mtrue to the actual intrinsic masses (so no hierarchical model) and as a comparison I get the following plot (blue is the constrained model):
>
>

> You can see the offset of alpha clearly. Do you think I'm doing everything right but perhaps there's just not enough data?
>
> Thanks again,
> Steven

     vector[N] log_lik;

        if ( cens[i] ==0 ) {

            log_lik[i] = log(pre[i])-log(sigma) -log(sqrt(2*pi())) -(diff[i])^2 + log(a0^2 + 2*a0*a1*diff[i] + a1^2*(diff[i])^2);}

     }
}

messages.body_plain:
I didn't see a discussion already posted for this, and I hope this is the best way to collect little quality improvements like this.

Reference manual for v2.11.0 in section 45.3 says that the exponent of $y$ in the pdf of {/sf InvChiSquare} is $-(\nu/2 - 1)$, but I think it should be $-(\nu/2 + 1)$. (All using LaTeX notation.) Note that it is correct in section 45.4 for the {\sf ScaledInvChiSquare} distribution.

It is a small matter, but I can tell the developers care about quality and just want to help out.

Gary

messages.subject: Hierarchical shrinkage prior
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical shrinkage prior
messages.body_plain:
Dear experts,

I'm just a beginner in Bayesian statistics but really likes Stan and the nice discussions on this mailing list. I'm trying to implement a hierarchical shrinkage prior with fat tails in Stan. This leads to many divergent transitions. I use a non-centered parametrization for the normal distribution in the model but this didn't solve all the divergent transitions. I'm currently in doubt what I should do next to prevent divergent transitions. From the manual and discussion on this mailing list I learnt that alternative parameterizations might prevent divergent transitions. From the manual I understood that there are possibilities to use a non-centered parameterization of the Dirichlet distribution (but I had troubles to implement this) and from discussions on this mailing list I understood that there might be alternative parameterizations of the gamma distribution. Or should I go another way?

On the other hand, although there are many divergent transitions, estimates were pretty good in simulated data. From posts of Michael Betancourt I know however, that I shouldn't trust outcomes if there are any divergent transitions so I hope that anyone can help me solving these divergent transitions. I included R code to simulate data and a stan file including the model.

Any help would be greatly appreciated!
D

messages.subject: hierarchical model with divergent transitions after warm-up.
messages.subject_clean: hierarchical model with divergent transitions after warm-up.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan developers and users:

I posted similar questions on the forum before and I have taken some of your suggestions to use NCP hierarchical model however I still experience the problem of having divergent transitions after warm up.

A quick recap of my model, my data are intervals and thus I transform it to be a bivariate vector y_ij==(m_ij=midpoints of the intervals,  r_ij=log(range) of the intervals)  where J is the number of groups and i is the observation per group.

This bivariate vector is fitted a bivariate normal distribution, N_2(beta_j, Sigma_j)
I have some hard constraints on beta_j as all midpoints should be greater than 0, ie: beta_j1>0 and the lower bounds of the interval should also be greater than 0 which translates to a constraint on beta_j2<log(2*beta_j1)

I adopt univariate NCP on beta_j1=mu_j1+alpha_j1*sigma_j1
Declaring mu_j1, alpha_j1, sigma_j1 in the parameter block with constraints on mu_j1> -alpha_j1*sigma_j1 to ensure that beta_j1 is non-negative;
Also declaring beta_j2 to be real with constraints on its upper bound to be log(2*(mu_j1+alpha_j1*sigma_j1))

And in the transformed parameter block,
declaring beta_j1=mu_j1+alpha_j1*sigma_j1

Furthermore, I assign mu_j1~N(0,10000);
sigma_j1~cauchy(0,2.5)
alpha_j1~normal(0,1)

Also the prior on variance and covariance matrix Sigma_j is parameterised as diag(scale_j)*Omega*diag(scale_j) and follows the instructions per Rstan manual to use LKJ_corr_cholesky prior and half-Cauchy prior on scale_j.

When I run this model( 4 chains, 4000 iterations per chain), there are some numerical problems saying that the location is -inf, but it should be. 0. However, the count is small.
I think the more serious problem is that there are divergent transitions after warm up even when I increase adapt_acceptance to be 0.9999.
I have already use non-centered parameterisation and setting adapt_acceptance rate to be nearly 1, how can I fix model divergent problem in this case?
Weirdly, when I look at posterior summary, n_eff=1 for nearly all of the parameters in my model, in this case, I do not think I can trust the posterior results given divergent behaviours after warm up right?

Can someone please provide some ideas or suggestions for me to explore and fix my model?

Thanks in advance,
Jaslene

messages.subject: Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.subject_clean: Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Users,

Thanks for the great software and documentation!

I was hoping someone could give me some advice with the following problem. First a caveat; I am an astrophysicist by training, not a statistician so I might use incorrect terminology and/or be making an obvious mistake!

I am trying to model a situation where I have noisy observed data points sampled from some underlying distribution, and my data are truncated such that points with low observed values are excluded. I would like to recover the parameters of the underlying distribution.

I have tried modelling the truncation as described in 9.3 of the reference manual. However, when I include the extra level of scatter in the data, the modelling returns biased parameters.

Here is a simplified model to generate some toy data in R

## start with 1000 data points
J <- 1000

## the underlying distribution of values is normal
mu <- 0
sigma <- 1
## generate a rate for each data point
x <- rnorm(J,mu,sigma)

## I observe a noisy version y of these data with known amount of
## noise, ysig
ysig <- 1
y <- rnorm(J,x,ysig)

## but I only include those above some threshold
ymin <- 0
x <- x[y>ymin]
y <- y[y>ymin]
J <- length(y)

Now I write my model in Stan:

data {
  int<lower=0> J; // number of observed points
  real ymin; // minimum allowed observed value
  real<lower=0> ysig; // known amount of noise
  real<lower=ymin> y[J]; // observed values
}

parameters {
  real mu; // mean of underlying normal
  real<lower=0> sigma; // sd of underlying normal
  real x[J]; // "true" values of each data point
}

model {

  x ~ normal(mu, sigma); // points are normally distributed

  for (i in 1:J){
    y[i] ~ normal(x[i],ysig) T[ymin,]; // with truncated normal noise
  }

}

and then run Stan

## make list for stan
sim_dat <- list(J = J,
                y = y,
                ymin = ymin,
                ysig = ysig
                )

## initial values
inits <- list(list(mu=mu,sigma=sigma,x=x))

## fit
niter <- 5000
fit <- stan(file = "my-model.stan", data = sim_dat, iter = niter, chains = 1, seed=666, init = inits)

## examine results
fit_summary <- summary(fit, pars = c("mu","sigma"), probs = c(0.025,0.5,0.975))$summary
print(fit_summary)

When I run this, I recover a biased values of mu and sigma for e.g. for ymin=0:

       mean     se_mean         sd      2.5%       50%     97.5%    n_eff
mu    0.5434274 0.003793941 0.08376895 0.3653829 0.5473229 0.7010205 487.5117
sigma 0.8635829 0.008732197 0.11146207 0.6399063 0.8624748 1.0797541 162.9323
      Rhat
mu    1.000211
sigma 1.001197

If I set ymin to be very low so there is effectively no truncation (e.g. ymin=-10), the parameters are not biased, as expected. The bias increases as I raise ymin.

Can anyone suggest what I might be doing wrong here?

Cheers,

 Ben

Hi Bob:

Sorry, I meant Rhat=1 for most of the parameters. I did generate some fake data and for some situations, the posterior distributions contain the true value but for some other situations they do not.

I have attached the model and the simulated dataset. Thanks so much for looking into them.

A quick note of my model (estimating species abundance) , I have bottom 7 categories (2 observed and 5 unobserved) that directly determine top 5 categories' midpoints and log(range).

say category 12 is the highest level in my model,

its midpoints= category 11's midpoints + category 5's mipoints

its log(range)=log(2*(category 12's midpoints-category 11's midpoints-category 5's midpoints)+exp(category 11's log(range))+exp(category 5's log(range))).

In reality, I do not observe or have data on those 5 unobserved other categories, these categories are just created to absorb the differences between categories' midpoints and log(range). Hence, my first simulation is that when there is no difference between bottom and top categories then the model should estimate those 5 unobserved categories' midpoints to be very small and essentially zero range, in other words, these categories are non-existent even though I fit them in the model. This simulation, it appears that my model can recover the "true" parameters that I set.

The second simulation is where there are differences between bottom and top level's midpoints and log(range). However, in this case, the model can recover all midpoints "true" parameters but fail to estimate other unobserved categories' log(range),ie, they are still estimated to be very small and essentially zero, which means that the model estimate these categories to be single points rather than intervals.

Along with estimation problems, the model have divergent transitions after warm up and some numerical problems in chains.

Thanks again for your advice,
Jaslene

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Difference between mu and a posteriori estimates
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difference between mu and a posteriori estimates
messages.body_plain:
Stan's samplers report the posterior mean for parameters,
whereas max a posteriori reports the posterior mode.  These
are often not the same and the mean often exists when the mode
doesn't.  The posterior mean minimizes expected square error of
the estimate---posterior mode doesn't have the same interpretability
as an expectation.

But if you want to do Bayesian posterior predictive inference,
you need to average over the posterior, which you can do in
generated quantities to compute the relevant integral.  This
is the measure that gives you the correct uncertainty calibration
relative to your model.  Look at the section titled "Prediction"
in the Stan manual chapter on regression;  there's an explanation
of the integral being computed in the chapter on Bayesian Data
Analysis.

- Bob

There are various ways to parameterize distributions;  for instance,
the normal can use scale (sigma), variance (sigma^2), or precision (1 / sigma^2).
negative_binomial has many parameterizations as does the gamma;  check
out the Wikipedia articles.

Using _lpdf functions with sampling notation won't work until Stan 2.12,
which is due out any day now (it's already been tagged and is just
winding through the interfaces).  Until then, you'd have to use the old
_log syntax (see the deprecated functions section of the manual) if
you want to use ~.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

The issue is that the Stan program you've written doesn't match the data generating process, so the mu that you're fitting with Stan won't match the true mu. If you add a generated quantities block, you'll see that the posterior predictive ys line up with the data. Try adding this to your Stan program and comparing y_rep to the data y.

generated quantities {
  real<lower = ymin> y_rep[J];
  y_rep = rep_array(ymin - 1, J);
  for (j in 1:J) {
    while (y_rep[j] < ymin) {
      y_rep[j] = normal_rng(x[j], ysig);
    }
  }
}

So first, the Stan program is working as you've written, but what you've written isn't what you really want. In your program, mu is being estimated as the marginal mean of the xs (with that much data).

Here's a Stan program that will work:
data {
  int<lower = 0> J;
  real ymin;
  real<lower = 0> ysig;
  real<lower = ymin> y[J];
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower = 0> sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower = 0> sigma_combined;
  sigma_combined = sqrt(square(sigma) + square(ysig));
}
model {
  for (j in 1:J)
    y[j] ~ normal(mu, sigma_combined) T[ymin, ];
}

This will correctly estimate mu and sigma. I'll let you add in a generated quantities block.

I haven't broken it down into an x component and an error term, but I'm sure it could be parameterized that way. Here, I'm assuming your data generating process where you first generate xs then the error terms as normal(0, ysig). Independent variances add, so sigma_combined is just the square root of the combined variance.

Hopefully that makes sense. If you're able to explain it clearer than what I've written out, please send a better explanation out to the list. It's a bit early and I need more coffee before being much more lucid.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Simplest thing to do is just fix one of the parameters to
a constant and see if that works.  It always helps to develop
code if you start with simple models that work and build up to
more complex models.  Then you can see when the problems get
introduced.

Otherwise, a tighter prior than exponential(0.5) would help.

Or reformulating in a way that has a direct representation rather
than something multiplicatively scaled.

- Bob

messages.subject: CmdStan v2.12.0 released!
messages.subject_clean: CmdStan v2.12.0 released!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

CmdStan v2.12.0 is now available! For the full release notes, see:
CmdStan: https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/tag/v2.12.0
Stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.12.0
Math: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/releases/tag/v2.12.0
Some notable changes:
Some bugs were squashed in the language that prevented well-formed Stan programs from compiling. Please see the Stan release notes for more details.
We've added these functions to the language since v2.11: mdivide_left_spd(), mdivide_right_spd(), cov_exp_quad(), append_row(), and append_col()
We've added a new core team member, Charles Margossian!
There's one outstanding bug that we know about and it's existed in older versions of Stan. There should be a fix by the next version of Stan. If you're using lower truncation with a probability mass function, the normalizing constant isn't computed correctly. This only applies to discrete distributions when truncating with a only lower bound and the workaround is to write the truncated distribution by hand. See https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2054 for more details.

Thanks,

Stan Development Team

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.body_plain:
Daniel's right.  Your model doesn't match your generating
process.  In the generating process, you censor out
items where y <= ymin.

If you don't record how many get censored and account for
that in the model, you won't be able to accurately estimate
the parameters.

Here's a simple example:

> y <- rnorm(100, 0, 1)
> mean(y)
[1] 0.0642081

> y <- y[y > 0]
> mean(y)
[1] 0.8642496

Check out the section on Censored Data in the Truncated or
Censored Data chapter. You just have a lower truncation instead
of an upper truncation.  So you'd use the normal_lcdf instead
of the normal_lccdf if you want to marginalize out the censored
values.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical shrinkage prior
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical shrinkage prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks a lot for your advice and patience! I tried to follow your advice as good as possible:
1. Fixing one of the parameters. The only parameter that was possible to fix was ksi. I changed omega ~ gamma(a, ksi) to omega ~ gamma(a, 0.1). a is a constant, in this example 1. This did improve number of divergent transitions but there were still 171 divergent transition with adapt_delta=0.99. Additionally, number of effect samples sharply decreased to <10 for many variables.

2. Starting with a simple model. I'm always trying to do this but for hierarchical shrinkage priors this is difficult. I performed a test by omitting omega, thus changing beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * omega * (psi .* phi)) to beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * (psi .* phi)). This did not improve number of divergent transitions but effective number of samples and estimates looked good. I also removed psi from the model (instead of psi), thus beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * omega * phi), but this did also not improve number of divergent transitions.

3. Tighten the exponential(0.5) prior. I changed this prior to exponential(10) but this did unfortunately not improve the number of divergent transitions and because of the multiplication in the model omega increased largely. I therefore additionally fixed omega to omega ~ gamma(1, 0.1) but this also did not change number of divergent transitions (but estimates looked good).

4. Reformulate in something not multiplicatively scaled. With the values of a_pi I'm using, the model is in fact equivalent to:
ksi ~ gamma(b, 1);

messages.subject: Inverse-lengthscale parameterized cov_exp_quad()?
messages.subject_clean: Inverse-lengthscale parameterized cov_exp_quad()?
messages.body_plain:
Great to see the new cov_exp_quad() function in v2.12.0, but I see that it's been parameterized with a lengthscale argument, whereas I think a good argument could be made for inverse-lengthscale (see section on Gaussian Processes at bottom of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations).

Obviously users preferring inverse-lengthscale can transform before using cov_exp_quad() as is, but that's an extra operation. Indeed, where the formula in the cov_exp_quad() description involves 1/(2*lengthscale^2), parameterization with inverse-lengthscale should actually eliminate one operation. Admittedly, I don't know enough to assert whether there'd be a real-world performance difference between these cases, but thought it worth raising the point.

Thoughts?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

Ok, pretty embarrassed to have asserted that there's an extra computation with the lengthscale parameterization : P Obviously cov_exp_quad() doesn't compute 1/(2*lengthscale^2) then multiply by the squared euclidian distance term, but instead just divides the latter value by 2*lengthscale^2.

Still, those of us that actively want to assert priors on inverse-lengthscale (though maybe just me?) will have to compute lengthscale=1/inverse_lengthscale before using cov_exp_quad() as is.

While I'm being compute stingy, is there any reason for the parameterization as dx/2l^2 rather than dx/z? The squaring then doubling of the lengthscale parameters aren't really necessary computationally, just in terms of interpretation after the fact. Or possibly I'm missing a nuanced reason for it being easier to imagine a prior for l rather than z (let alone 1/z)?

--

Dalhousie University

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Inverse-lengthscale parameterized cov_exp_quad()?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Keep asking questions! Hopefully you'll make use of this function. Our plan is to roll out more covariance kernels. I also don't speak for the whole development team -- I'm just answering them from my own perspective.

Regarding parameterization: we went with the Rasmusen and Williams parametrization from "Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning." I've seen a handful of implementations, including GPStuff, and other mathematical descriptions like wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process) and the kernel cookbook (http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~duvenaud/cookbook/index.html) and they all parameterize it by length scale. It's a non-trivial amount of developer work to have multiple parameterizations. It also makes it more difficult on the user when they have choices to make regarding parameterization. There are a few cases where the demand has been high enough to warrant a second parameterization (I'm thinking negative binomial), but honestly, it's been more trouble than it's worth with user error, buggy code, and just giving users choice. For the version after v2.12.0, we'll have a faster version of the function for what we're thinking is a going to be a more common use of the function. Rob's gone and analytically computed the gradients for the function instead of using autodiff, but not for every use of the function. We've just introduced this function. I'm more interested in adding additional kernels rather than adding a reparameterization. In terms of work, they're on the same order of effort. Hopefully you feel the same. And... if you're into computation, we'll take help!

Regarding being compute stingy: this is a low order concern. When you're computing distances of two arrays of vectors, a divide isn't going to hurt. What's going to be useful is parameterizing the problem correctly. Rob's got some tricks up his sleeve that you might be interested in. I didn't look at the math, but it sounds like there's a modeling trick where a product is identifiable, but most people parameterize by the two factors. I think it's along those lines, but I could be wrong. Anyway, I know how the cov_exp_quad() function is built and a single divide isn't going to make a dent in the computation time.

More inline.

On Wed, Sep 7, 2016 at 9:45 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Ok, pretty embarrassed to have asserted that there's an extra computation with the lengthscale parameterization : P Obviously cov_exp_quad() doesn't compute 1/(2*lengthscale^2) then multiply by the squared euclidian distance term, but instead just divides the latter value by 2*lengthscale^2.
>
> Still, those of us that actively want to assert priors on inverse-lengthscale (though maybe just me?) will have to compute lengthscale=1/inverse_lengthscale before using cov_exp_quad() as is.

Yup. And that's easy!

>
> While I'm being compute stingy, is there any reason for the parameterization as dx/2l^2 rather than dx/z? The squaring then doubling of the lengthscale parameters aren't really necessary computationally, just in terms of interpretation after the fact. Or possibly I'm missing a nuanced reason for it being easier to imagine a prior for l rather than z (let alone 1/z)?
>
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence
> Graduate Student
> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> Dalhousie University
>
> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
>
> On Wed, Sep 7, 2016 at 10:28 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Great to see the new cov_exp_quad() function in v2.12.0, but I see that it's been parameterized with a lengthscale argument, whereas I think a good argument could be made for inverse-lengthscale (see section on Gaussian Processes at bottom of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations).
> >
> > Obviously users preferring inverse-lengthscale can transform before using cov_exp_quad() as is, but that's an extra operation. Indeed, where the formula in the cov_exp_quad() description involves 1/(2*lengthscale^2), parameterization with inverse-lengthscale should actually eliminate one operation. Admittedly, I don't know enough to assert whether there'd be a real-world performance difference between these cases, but thought it worth raising the point.

I think there's a bigger point to be made here. Speeding up the computation of a Stan program by a small percent isn't really that useful. You'll be a little faster, but you probably could have saved the effort and let the program run for just that much longer. The results will be identical, you'll have the same estimates for effective samples, etc. Where you're going to make big jumps are when you think about the parameterization of the Stan program in relation to the data you have. Although the Stan language is designed to be agnostic to the inference algorithms, when you start talking efficiency, you'll need to take into account the algorithm that's being run. If you're running with defaults, it's NUTS and you'll need to think about the joint lpdf of the data and the parameters on the unconstrained scale. But... if you're able to parameterize the problem correctly, you could get massive jumps in efficiency (orders of magnitude / correct vs incorrect). If you're looking to do thinks more efficiently, that's where I would turn; not shaving a handful of operations.

I think most of the devs would agree that shaving a few operations isn't how we'd go about making a Stan program go fast. Of course, I understand the desire to do that. It's easy (almost every program can be written just a little bit faster) and the alternative isn't always clear. In this case, I'd just forget about the cost of a divide.

Whenever the interface you're using catches up to 2.12, just for kicks, could you try using the length scale parameter in one program and in another try inverting twice -- so parameter l, transformed parameters inv_l = 1 / l and l2 = 1 / inv_l. Use inv_l in the cov_exp_quad() function. Set seeds and see if there's any noticeable time difference. (you could even put it in the model block if you want it to be run every leapfrog step.)

> >
> > Thoughts?

That's it for now. Maybe someone else will chime in, but back to your original question -- I don't think we'll be adding a second parameterization soon. If you wanted to do it, we'd welcome it.

Daniel

messages.subject: How to improve mixing for a multilevel model
messages.subject_clean: How to improve mixing for a multilevel model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Users,

I have a multilevel model (attached) describing binary choices data between 2 monetary rewards at different delays. Choices for each individual in the experiment are modeled using 3 parameters (logK, c, and tao) that have normally distributed hyper-parameters. C and tao are constrained to be > 0.

For the majority of individuals i, c[i], tao[i] and logK[i] mix well and appear to converge. But for a few individuals, mixing is really poor (see trace plots attached) and rhat >>1 with very low n_eff despite long chains (ran 4 chains, iter = 10,000). How can I try to improve mixing?

I think it’s possible that some individuals responded in the experimental task in a way that makes their c, tao, and logK poorly identifiable. What I am really interested in are the hyper-parameters defining the normal distributions of c’s, tao’s and logK’s and later adding in some predictors for these hyper-parameters. If Stan samples for the hyper-parameters mix well and converge (e.g. mu_logK & sigma_logK), but some of the associated lower parameters do not (e.g. logK[61]), can the hyper-parameter estimates still be used for inference or are they invalidated by any lack of convergence for parameters in the model?

I've attached the model, some example trace plots for parameters with good and bad mixing, and the output file which shows a few numerical problems during sampling but no divergence warnings.

Thank you for your help,

Erin

*I posted recently (8/26) about a similar model, but different question, so I hope it is ok to have started a different thread*

Dear Bob,

Thanks for your comments.

>     If you don't record how many get censored and account for
>     that in the model, you won't be able to accurately estimate
>     the parameters.

Maybe I'm using the wrong terminology (and maybe it isn't important)
but although in my toy model I know the number of missing data points
that fell below ymin, in my real data I do not. For this reason I was
following the model for truncated data rather than censored data in
the "Truncated or censored data chapter". In my Stan model above I
used

    y[i] ~ normal(x[i],ysig) T[ymin,]; // with truncated normal noise

to model the effect of truncation on the observed y values, while my
"intrinsic/true" (not sure what the correct term is) x values are not
truncated. I'm still unclear why this does not match the data
generation, and this seems to be an important gap in my understanding.

Following from your comment I tried applying the approach for censored data:

  data {
    int<lower=0> N_obs; // number of observed points
    int<lower=0> N_cen; // known number of missing points

    real<lower=0> ysig; // known amount of noise

    real y[N_obs]; // observed values
    real<upper=min(y)> ymin; // known minimum allowed observed value

  }

  parameters {
    real mu; // mean of underlying normal
    real<lower=0> sigma; // sd of underlying normal

        mean se_mean   sd 2.5% 97.5%  n_eff Rhat

On Thu, Sep 8, 2016 at 1:56 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Hi Mike,
>
> Keep asking questions! Hopefully you'll make use of this function. Our plan is to roll out more covariance kernels. I also don't speak for the whole development team -- I'm just answering them from my own perspective.
>
> Regarding parameterization: we went with the Rasmusen and Williams parametrization from "Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning." I've seen a handful of implementations, including GPStuff, and other mathematical descriptions like wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process) and the kernel cookbook (http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~duvenaud/cookbook/index.html) and they all parameterize it by length scale. It's a non-trivial amount of developer work to have multiple parameterizations. It also makes it more difficult on the user when they have choices to make regarding parameterization. There are a few cases where the demand has been high enough to warrant a second parameterization (I'm thinking negative binomial), but honestly, it's been more trouble than it's worth with user error, buggy code, and just giving users choice. For the version after v2.12.0, we'll have a faster version of the function for what we're thinking is a going to be a more common use of the function. Rob's gone and analytically computed the gradients for the function instead of using autodiff, but not for every use of the function. We've just introduced this function. I'm more interested in adding additional kernels rather than adding a reparameterization. In terms of work, they're on the same order of effort. Hopefully you feel the same. And... if you're into computation, we'll take help!
>
> Regarding being compute stingy: this is a low order concern. When you're computing distances of two arrays of vectors, a divide isn't going to hurt. What's going to be useful is parameterizing the problem correctly. Rob's got some tricks up his sleeve that you might be interested in. I didn't look at the math, but it sounds like there's a modeling trick where a product is identifiable, but most people parameterize by the two factors. I think it's along those lines, but I could be wrong. Anyway, I know how the cov_exp_quad() function is built and a single divide isn't going to make a dent in the computation time.
>
> More inline.
>
> On Wed, Sep 7, 2016 at 9:45 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Ok, pretty embarrassed to have asserted that there's an extra computation with the lengthscale parameterization : P Obviously cov_exp_quad() doesn't compute 1/(2*lengthscale^2) then multiply by the squared euclidian distance term, but instead just divides the latter value by 2*lengthscale^2.
> >
> > Still, those of us that actively want to assert priors on inverse-lengthscale (though maybe just me?) will have to compute lengthscale=1/inverse_lengthscale before using cov_exp_quad() as is.
>
> Yup. And that's easy!
>
> >
> > While I'm being compute stingy, is there any reason for the parameterization as dx/2l^2 rather than dx/z? The squaring then doubling of the lengthscale parameters aren't really necessary computationally, just in terms of interpretation after the fact. Or possibly I'm missing a nuanced reason for it being easier to imagine a prior for l rather than z (let alone 1/z)?
> >
> >
> > --
> > Mike Lawrence
> > Graduate Student
> > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > Dalhousie University
> >
> > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> >
> > On Wed, Sep 7, 2016 at 10:28 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Great to see the new cov_exp_quad() function in v2.12.0, but I see that it's been parameterized with a lengthscale argument, whereas I think a good argument could be made for inverse-lengthscale (see section on Gaussian Processes at bottom of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations).
> > >
> > > Obviously users preferring inverse-lengthscale can transform before using cov_exp_quad() as is, but that's an extra operation. Indeed, where the formula in the cov_exp_quad() description involves 1/(2*lengthscale^2), parameterization with inverse-lengthscale should actually eliminate one operation. Admittedly, I don't know enough to assert whether there'd be a real-world performance difference between these cases, but thought it worth raising the point.
>
> I think there's a bigger point to be made here. Speeding up the computation of a Stan program by a small percent isn't really that useful. You'll be a little faster, but you probably could have saved the effort and let the program run for just that much longer. The results will be identical, you'll have the same estimates for effective samples, etc. Where you're going to make big jumps are when you think about the parameterization of the Stan program in relation to the data you have. Although the Stan language is designed to be agnostic to the inference algorithms, when you start talking efficiency, you'll need to take into account the algorithm that's being run. If you're running with defaults, it's NUTS and you'll need to think about the joint lpdf of the data and the parameters on the unconstrained scale. But... if you're able to parameterize the problem correctly, you could get massive jumps in efficiency (orders of magnitude / correct vs incorrect). If you're looking to do thinks more efficiently, that's where I would turn; not shaving a handful of operations.
>
> I think most of the devs would agree that shaving a few operations isn't how we'd go about making a Stan program go fast. Of course, I understand the desire to do that. It's easy (almost every program can be written just a little bit faster) and the alternative isn't always clear. In this case, I'd just forget about the cost of a divide.
>
> Whenever the interface you're using catches up to 2.12, just for kicks, could you try using the length scale parameter in one program and in another try inverting twice -- so parameter l, transformed parameters inv_l = 1 / l and l2 = 1 / inv_l. Use inv_l in the cov_exp_quad() function. Set seeds and see if there's any noticeable time difference. (you could even put it in the model block if you want it to be run every leapfrog step.)
>
>
> > >
> > > Thoughts?
>
> That's it for now. Maybe someone else will chime in, but back to your original question -- I don't think we'll be adding a second parameterization soon. If you wanted to do it, we'd welcome it.
>
>
>
> Daniel

You'll see that it generates the exact same code other than
that which saves the parameters.  If there are a lot of
transformed parameters, saving them each iteration imposes
some overhead, especially if you're using something like
distributed disks on a cluster.  We should probably allow
some blocking/buffering of output---it all just streams
by default (in CmdStan anyway), which is probably not the right
behavior for a cluster.

Your data generating process is not truncated, though, it's
censored.

> In my Stan model above I
> used
>
>     y[i] ~ normal(x[i],ysig) T[ymin,]; // with truncated normal noise
>

That's not what this does.

> while my
> "intrinsic/true" (not sure what the correct term is) x values are not

> generation, and this seems to be an important gap in my understanding.

You want to think in terms of the density function and the generative
model.  With the truncation above, you get the following contribution:

  PROD_i normal(y[i] | x[i], ysig) / (1 - normal_cdf(y_min | x[i], ysig))

trying to apply what looks like a measurement error model (there's
another chapter in the manual for those), whereas what you really have
is censoring (you remove data points below ymin).

Dear Bob,

Thanks for the continuing help. I think I am being quite obtuse here, but your distinction between truncation and censoring is unclear to me. I should start by saying that I am sure you are right, since I can see for myself that my truncated model doesn't work!

My understanding from the manual and elsewhere was that the only difference between censorship and truncation is that in the case of censorship you know the number of missing points, while for truncation you do not. If that is correct, then can I just pretend that I did not know how many points I generated before rejecting those below ymin? I could also ask a colleague to generate the data in the same way and not tell me how many points they started with. In that case, have I not generated a truncated rather than censored dataset, and shouldn't the truncation model work?

In my actual data, I am looking at a class of astrophysical object (active galactic nuclei or AGN) that has a distribution of X-ray emission rates (let's say it is lognormal, and that I want to know the mean and variance). I observe the sky with a photon counting detector which measures the number of X-ray photons in some length of time (i.e. sampling a Poisson distribution), and I detect an AGN if I receive more than some minimum number of photons in a pixel of the detector (say, 4 photons). I am trying to use the observations of photon counts for a large number of such AGN to infer the parameters of the distribution of rates, but I don't know how many AGN are out there that did not meet the detection threshold. My toy model was an attempt to replicate this in the simplest useful way, with x representing the rates, y representing the detected counts and ymin the detection threshold. I believe this is a truncated dataset rather than censored - is that the case, and if so would you maintain that there is no way to recover the parameters I am interested in?

The way I would try to replicate the data described above would be something like

x <- rlnorm(1000,log(mu),sigma)
y <- rpois(1000,x)

y <- y[y>ymin]

but does this somehow fall into the trap of generating censored rather than truncated data and therefore not reproducing my experiment (even if I pretend I don't know that I started with 1000 points)? If so, I'd be really grateful for any suggestion of how to generate data correctly.

(N.B. I started by generating and modelling data along the lines above - lognormal and poisson - to more closely match my observations, but after failing with that I boiled it down to the toy model with two normal distributions in my original question as I thought that would be the simplest case to understand!)

Thanks for your patience!

 Ben

> Dear Bob,

>

If that is correct, then can I just pretend that I did not know how many points I generated before rejecting those below ymin? I could also ask a colleague to generate the data in the same way and not tell me how many points they started with. In that case, have I not generated a truncated rather than censored dataset, and shouldn't the truncation model work?

Simplistically, perhaps, censoring means you know that there is an observation outside the zone but you don't know what it is. Truncation means you don't know anything outside the zone. For example, in actuarial work, if a loss hits a policy limit, it is censored from above. We know it exists, and it is at least X, but we don't know how much larger. Losses that fail to breach a deductible are truncated from below—no one knows that they exist, even though NEXT TIME, that event may cause a large-enough loss to register.

Hope that helps,

Avi

messages.body_plain:
Firstly and somewhat tangentially, no you did not measure any measurement
noise ysig.  Physicists make this mistake all the time because they’re used
to Poisson asymptotic estimators of the form lambda = N +/- \sqrt{N}.  But
if your noise is Poisson then model it generatively as

y ~ poisson(lambda);

or if there are measurement affects that corrupt the simple Poissonian variation

y ~ neg_binomial2(lambda, phi);

etc, etc.  Or make a normal approximation as

y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

and _fit_ sigma as a parameter.

Anyways, unless you have some other measurements sensitive to how many
observations that you are missing then you cannot infer how many you missed
as there is literally no information about that (i.e. you can’t compute an efficiency
if you don’t have counts before and after some process!).

BUT you can do something even better if you think generatively.  Really what
you have here is a generative model with two components: a latent population
of AGN and a measurement model for those AGN with sufficient magnitude.
If you fit both of those together then you can infer the shape of the AGN population
distribution even with the truncation, and then you can recover the overall rate
of the observations you missed by integrating the tail of that distribution from
the truncation.

Very, very prototypically, something like

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  real y[N];
}

parameters {
  real agn_mu; // AGN population log mean
  real<lower=0> agn_sigma; // AGN population deviation

  real y_latent[N]; // Latent AGN magnitudes

  real thresh; // measurement threshold
  real<lower=0> sigma; // heteroskedastic measurement deviation
}

model {
  // priors on everything!  No uniform distributions!

  // AGN population model
  for (n in 1:N)
    y_latent[n] ~ normal(agn_mu, agh_sigma) T[thresh,];

  // Measurement model
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(y_latent[n], sigma);
}

generated quantities {
  real true_rate;
  real missing_rate;

  true_rate = N / normal_ccdf(thresh, agn_mu, agh_sigma);
  missing_rate = true_rate - N;
}

In practice you’ll want to vectorize everything and probably switch
to a non-centered parameterization for the y_latent.

Generative models — they are the best!

messages.body_plain:
What your R code is doing is censoring.

To generate truncated data with y > ymin, you could
build a simple rejection sampler

  y <- normal_rng(mu, sigma);
  while (y <= ymin)
    y <- normal_rng(mu, sigma);

or you can invert a CDF:

  z <- uniform_rng(normal_cdf(ymin, mu, sigma), 1)
  y <- normal_inverse_cdf(z, mu, sigma);

(I don't know the R calls to do this.)

But this isn't your generative process, so just having
truncation won't get you the right answer.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks for this. If I understand your model correctly, it models the case where I might measure a y value to be below thresh even though its y_latent must be above thresh. However, I have the opposite case; my data may have any value of y_latent, but the measured y must be above thresh. In the above model, the probability that would be assigned to (y_latent<thresh & y>thresh) is zero, but this is perfectly possible in nature.

Specifically, an AGN might have a low magnitude that makes it unlikely to be detected, but in a particular observation the Poisson fluctuations in photon counts might just get over the detection threshold. In that case y_latent < thresh but y > thresh. This is what I tried to set up with my toy model by using the truncated normal for my measured y, but this did not work.

Am I misunderstanding your model?

Cheers,
 Ben

On Thursday, September 8, 2016 at 10:28:29 PM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Firstly and somewhat tangentially, no you did not measure any measurement
> noise ysig.  Physicists make this mistake all the time because they’re used
> to Poisson asymptotic estimators of the form lambda = N +/- \sqrt{N}.  But
> if your noise is Poisson then model it generatively as
>
> y ~ poisson(lambda);
>
> or if there are measurement affects that corrupt the simple Poissonian variation
>
> y ~ neg_binomial2(lambda, phi);
>
> etc, etc.  Or make a normal approximation as
>
> y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> and _fit_ sigma as a parameter.
>
> Anyways, unless you have some other measurements sensitive to how many
> observations that you are missing then you cannot infer how many you missed
> as there is literally no information about that (i.e. you can’t compute an efficiency
> if you don’t have counts before and after some process!).
>
> BUT you can do something even better if you think generatively.  Really what
> you have here is a generative model with two components: a latent population
> of AGN and a measurement model for those AGN with sufficient magnitude.
> If you fit both of those together then you can infer the shape of the AGN population
> distribution even with the truncation, and then you can recover the overall rate
> of the observations you missed by integrating the tail of that distribution from
> the truncation.
>

>   int<lower=1> N;
>   real y[N];
> }
>
> parameters {

>
>   real y_latent[N]; // Latent AGN magnitudes
>
>   real thresh; // measurement threshold
>   real<lower=0> sigma; // heteroskedastic measurement deviation
> }

>   // AGN population model

>
>   // Measurement model

> }
>
> generated quantities {
>   real true_rate;
>   real missing_rate;
>
>   true_rate = N / normal_ccdf(thresh, agn_mu, agh_sigma);
>   missing_rate = true_rate - N;
> }
>
> In practice you’ll want to vectorize everything and probably switch
> to a non-centered parameterization for the y_latent.
>
> Generative models — they are the best!

messages.body_plain:
As Bob and Dan very clearly explained, your original results
were invalid because you weren’t simulating data correctly.
You simulated data assuming that you knew the total number
of trials, but such truncation models assume that you only
know the number of measured trials.  Hence you have to
do rejection sampling or, in the Gaussian case, inverse
CDF transform sampling to generate appropriate simulation
data.

Even once you do that, however, you can only infer the
latent rate of missingness (or the latent true rate).  This is
actually more informative than the actual number of missing
events as it isn’t corrupted by measurement noise.

messages.body_plain:
The paper Andrew linked has a clear explanation of
what's going on in section 2.1:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/parameterization.pdf

I was wrong in saying you couldn't infer the parameters,
though.  And now that I think about it, you could probably infer
the amount of missingness from the CDFs given the parameters,
because you know the mass < ymin and the mass > ymin, which
gives you the expected ratio of missing to observed, and then
it's just binomial stuff after that to do inference on number
of missing items.  At least I think that's right.  I love
having my work checked on this list!

- Bob

> On Sep 9, 2016, at 8:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> As Bob and Dan very clearly explained, your original results
> were invalid because you weren’t simulating data correctly.
> You simulated data assuming that you knew the total number
> of trials, but such truncation models assume that you only
> know the number of measured trials.  Hence you have to
> do rejection sampling or, in the Gaussian case, inverse
> CDF transform sampling to generate appropriate simulation
> data.
>
> Even once you do that, however, you can only infer the
> latent rate of missingness (or the latent true rate).  This is
> actually more informative than the actual number of missing
> events as it isn’t corrupted by measurement noise.
>
> On Sep 9, 2016, at 12:02 PM, Ben Maughan <benma...@gmail.com> wrote:

>>
>> That is precisely what I did in my initial model (see first post, x is the latent population, ymin is thresh):

>>   }

>>

>>  Ben
>>
>> On Friday, September 9, 2016 at 10:05:52 AM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Then move the truncation to the measurement model for the y.
>> The point is that you can’t infer anything about the missing
>> measurements unless you model the latent population distribution
>> exactly.

>>> Hi,

However, I have the opposite case; my data may have any value of y_latent, but the measured y must be above thresh. In the above model, the probability that would be assigned to (y_latent<thresh & y>thresh) is zero, but this is perfectly possible in nature.
>>>
>>> Specifically, an AGN might have a low magnitude that makes it unlikely to be detected, but in a particular observation the Poisson fluctuations in photon counts might just get over the detection threshold. In that case y_latent < thresh but y > thresh. This is what I tried to set up with my toy model by using the truncated normal for my measured y, but this did not work.
>>>

>>>

>>>  Ben
>>>

>>> Firstly and somewhat tangentially, no you did not measure any measurement

>>> distribution even with the truncation, and then you can recover the overall rate
>>> of the observations you missed by integrating the tail of that distribution from

>>>
>>> Very, very prototypically, something like

>>>   missing_rate = true_rate - N;
>>> }
>>>
>>> In practice you’ll want to vectorize everything and probably switch
>>> to a non-centered parameterization for the y_latent.
>>>
>>> Generative models — they are the best!
>>>

Ok, I've tested this on a PC running linux and a Mac, in addition to the Linux VM running on Google's compute engine. All have lots of RAM (min 16GB) and fast CPUs, and all are running Stan v2.11 via RStan. For a given machine, I computed all models while the machine was doing relatively little else, using single chain single core sampling (i.e. no parallel chains), and interleaving multiple sampling runs of the models.

The results are weird.

Here's a gist of the code for my experimentation:
https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/96d14bac6264b5f4eff4f3d7001acec9

The R file is what generates data and samples the models (using the same seed when comparing the different models).

"tp0.stan" is a version that uses transformed parameters, "tp1.stan" is a version that uses a local block at the very top of the model block, and "tp2.stan" is what I use to look at the consequence of putting the local block in the model block at different places. Why would I put it at different places? - tp2 local block @ end: initialization errors, model can't sample

Presumably this is not expected behaviour?

The only real way to debug is with print statements,
perhaps embedded in conditionals.

If you're running out of memory, you can always cut down on
the number of operations.  But if the model won't fit even
on a small set of simulated data, then there may be
something else going on.

Just this expression recalculates 1/profundidad_cap several
times per loop iteration:

  w[i]=(1/(profundidad_capa * exp(lbeta(eta * ((1/profundidad_capa) * y[i]) + 1,eta - eta * ((1/profundidad_capa) * y[i])+ 1)))) * (z[i] ^ (eta * ((1/profundidad_capa) * y[i]))) * ((1 - z[i]) ^ (eta-eta * ((1/profundidad_capa) * y[i])));

Better to calculate it on the outside of the loop and reuse it.  Same
with eta * (1 / profundidad_capa).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Variables declared in model block not saved?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Variables declared in model block not saved?
messages.body_plain:
Remember that everything in the transformed parameters block is computed one extra time per sample vs. quantities that are put in the model block. When the transformations are computationally expensive, like building a covariance matrix and doing a cholesky decomposition on that matrix, you'll notice that a model that uses a transformed parameters block will be a bit slower than a model that puts the computation in the model block.

Rob

On Fri, Sep 9, 2016 at 8:12 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Results should match when setting seeds on the same platform with the same compiler. I wouldn't expect results to match across different OSes.
>
>
> On Fri, Sep 9, 2016 at 8:09 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > You can't put the local block past the use of f, because
> > the local block defines f.
> >
> > Did tp0 and tp1 also always got the same answers?
> >
> > I'd expect the same answers as long as the block defining
> > f was before the use of f.  If we're not getting that, I'm
> > not sure what would be causing it.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Sep 9, 2016, at 5:44 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Ok, I've tested this on a PC running linux and a Mac, in addition to the Linux VM running on Google's compute engine. All have lots of RAM (min 16GB) and fast CPUs, and all are running Stan v2.11 via RStan. For a given machine, I computed all models while the machine was doing relatively little else, using single chain single core sampling (i.e. no parallel chains), and interleaving multiple sampling runs of the models.
> > >
> > > The results are weird.
> > >
> > > Here's a gist of the code for my experimentation:
> > > https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/96d14bac6264b5f4eff4f3d7001acec9
> > >
> > > The R file is what generates data and samples the models (using the same seed when comparing the different models).
> > >
> > > "tp0.stan" is a version that uses transformed parameters, "tp1.stan" is a version that uses a local block at the very top of the model block, and "tp2.stan" is what I use to look at the consequence of putting the local block in the model block at different places. Why would I put it at different places? Because I discovered that, regardless of machine, when the local block is at the top of the model block, as in tp1 I get identical performance & samples as I get with tp0". However, if I move the location of that local block around within the model block, I get different timing and samples from tp0. As a summary:
> > >
> > > Machine: Linux VM on Google
> > > - tp2 local block @ beginning: same samples and timing as tp0
> > > - tp2 local block @ end: initialization errors, model can't sample
> > > - tp2 local block anywhere in middle: different samples from tp0, slower by 30% *if* placed right before the last line (this happened to be the position that I used earlier, hence my report of the 30% timing difference), else same timing as tp0
> > >
> > > Machine: Linux PC & Mac OS X (same story on both)
> > > - tp2 local block @ beginning: same samples and timing as tp0
> > > - tp2 local block @ end: initialization errors, model can't sample
> > > - tp2 local block anywhere in middle: different samples from tp0, same timing as tp0
> > >
> > > So, the previously reported timing difference only occurs with the Linux VM on Google compute engine, and only when the local block is placed at a very specific location in the model block. > > >

> > > >
> > > >         mean se_mean   sd 2.5% 97.5%  n_eff Rhat
> > > >   noise 1.03       0 0.02 0.99  1.08 100000    1
> > > >   eta   1.23       0 0.37 0.64  2.06  48137    1

> > > >   [1] 29.12736

> > > >   [1] 0.3682616

No, I'm talking about the call to write_array  that reruns the transformed parameters block with doubles once per iteration. I only figured this out because I wanted to make sure my rev specialization of cov_exp_quad was getting called during sampling so I put cout calls in both rev and prim versions and found that the prim version got called once per post-warmup sample (I assume because I hadn't elected to save warmup samples).

Rob

>> Remember that everything in the transformed parameters block is computed one extra time per sample vs. quantities that are put in the model block. When the transformations are computationally expensive, like building a covariance matrix and doing a cholesky decomposition on that matrix, you'll notice that a model that uses a transformed parameters block will be a bit slower than a model that puts the computation in the model block.

>>>

>>>

Why would I put it at different places? Because I discovered that, regardless of machine, when the local block is at the top of the model block, as in tp1 I get identical performance & samples as I get with tp0". However, if I move the location of that local block around within the model block, I get different timing and samples from tp0. As a summary:
>>>

>>> - tp2 local block @ beginning: same samples and timing as tp0
>>> - tp2 local block @ end: initialization errors, model can't sample

Presumably this is not expected behaviour?
>>>

>>> Mike
>>>
>>>
