messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan,

      I am working on the implementation of Neatest Neighborhood Gaussian Process (NNGP) in Stan. I wrote a test folder and here is the share link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/0ByIcksYvjph9aS1GajdzY2dCWGc?usp=sharing.
The folder exceeds the limits for this group so I put it in the google driver. Please let me know if it is not accessible. It contains the synthetic data and codes for four different models. For more information, please check "readme" and "summary.pdf". Since it hasn't been completed yet, the summary report is still in editing. Welcome for suggestions for improving my code. I also posted two questions in the end of this topic. Thank you very much!

The following is file "Readme.txt" which gives a brief introduction of this folder:

# Introduction:

This is a test folder for implementing Full Gaussian process and Nearest
Neighborhood Gaussian Process on spatial data in Stan. For more details
about synthetic data, models, and simulation results, please refer to
“summary.pdf”.

# How to run the program:

The language interface to perform the analysis is Rstan. All the executable files
are in subfolder “projects” and Stan codes are saved in subfolder “src”. To run
the analysis, open R program in “projects” and set the working directory to be
the path of this folder. R code in subfolder “projects” will load data and link
Stan codes with a relative path.

# Folder Structure:

data:  Synthetic data and parameters for priors

projects:          Rstan codes for two models.

results:          Simulation results

src:          Stan codes

The following are two questions I met, more information can be found in "summary.pdf":

1. In model1, the performance of FullGP highly depends on initial values. NNGP did not have such a high number of divergent transitions with the same initials and number of iterations as follows. What's more, it converged. I want to compare FullGP and NNGP with initial values far from the true value, but the results from FullGP didn't even converge.

Initial value: beta = c(0, 0), sigmasq = 6, tausq = 1, phi= 10;

With 400 iterations, I got Warning messages:
1: There were 199 divergent transitions after warm up. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.8 may help.
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems

2. The Full Gaussian Process in model 2 takes a very long time to run. I got 1200 out of 2000 iterations over 10 hours and then my computer stopped running. Hope someone could give me some suggestions on the coding.

Best Wishes,

Lu Zhang

Regarding your question #2, on improving the efficiency of the fullGP models:

First, in your custom function "get_w_L" you should take advantage of the fact that the covariance matrix is symmetric by doing:

    for (j in 1:(N-1)){
        for (k in j:N){
            temp_dist[j, k] = sigmasq * exp(- phi * dist[j, k]) ;
            temp_dist[k, j] = temp_dist[j, k] ;
        }
    }
  for(i in 1:N){
  temp_dist[i,i] = sigmasq + tausq ;
  }

You might also be getting into trouble with your priors; for GPs, I follow the guidelines posted at the bottom of the wiki: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

messages.body_plain:
And for model fullGP_w.stan, I would rewrite the parameters/model block like follows:
...
parameters {
    vector[2] beta;
    real<lower = 0> sigmasq;
    real<lower = 0> tausq;
    real<lower = ap, upper = bp> phi;
    vector[N] eta;
}
model {
    vector[N] w;
    matrix[N, N] L_cov;
    L_cov = get_w_L(sigmasq, tausq, phi, dist, N);
    sigmasq ~ inv_gamma(as, bs);
    tausq ~ inv_gamma(at, bt);
    eta ~ normal(0, 1);
    w = mu_w + L_cov * eta;
    for (i in 1:N){
        Y[i] ~ normal((X[i,] * beta + w[i]), tausq);
    }
}

Rob

messages.body_plain:
OK, we're talking about the same thing.  That call to write_array()
is what writes out the parameters, transformed parameters, and generated
quantities values for the iteration.  It has to transform the parameters
from the unconstrained space, then run the transformed parameters block
and then the model block.

We should make sure the transformed parameter block in this eval doesn't
calculate the Jacobian because we don't need it.

- Bob

> On Sep 9, 2016, at 9:58 PM, Robert Trangucci <robert.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> No, I'm talking about the call to write_array  that reruns the transformed parameters block with doubles once per iteration. I only figured this out because I wanted to make sure my rev specialization of cov_exp_quad was getting called during sampling so I put cout calls in both rev and prim versions and found that the prim version got called once per post-warmup sample (I assume because I hadn't elected to save warmup samples).
>
> Rob
>
>> On Sep 9, 2016, at 9:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> The sampling shouldn't vary as long as everything is defined
>> before it used.
>>

>> generated quantities?  The generated quantities will be
>> evaluated once per iteration (per warmup iteration or per
>> draw post-warmup) with double values only.  But that could

>>> Remember that everything in the transformed parameters block is computed one extra time per sample vs. quantities that are put in the model block. When the transformations are computationally expensive, like building a covariance matrix and doing a cholesky decomposition on that matrix, you'll notice that a model that uses a transformed parameters block will be a bit slower than a model that puts the computation in the model block.
>>>
>>> Rob
>>>
>>> On Fri, Sep 9, 2016 at 8:12 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>>> Results should match when setting seeds on the same platform with the same compiler. I wouldn't expect results to match across different OSes.
>>>
>>>
>>> On Fri, Sep 9, 2016 at 8:09 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>> You can't put the local block past the use of f, because
>>> the local block defines f.
>>>
>>> Did tp0 and tp1 also always got the same answers?
>>>
>>> I'd expect the same answers as long as the block defining
>>> f was before the use of f.  If we're not getting that, I'm
>>> not sure what would be causing it.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> On Sep 9, 2016, at 5:44 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Ok, I've tested this on a PC running linux and a Mac, in addition to the Linux VM running on Google's compute engine. All have lots of RAM (min 16GB) and fast CPUs, and all are running Stan v2.11 via RStan. For a given machine, I computed all models while the machine was doing relatively little else, using single chain single core sampling (i.e. no parallel chains), and interleaving multiple sampling runs of the models.
>>>>
>>>> The results are weird.
>>>>
>>>> Here's a gist of the code for my experimentation:
>>>> https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/96d14bac6264b5f4eff4f3d7001acec9
>>>>
>>>> The R file is what generates data and samples the models (using the same seed when comparing the different models).
>>>>
>>>> "tp0.stan" is a version that uses transformed parameters, "tp1.stan" is a version that uses a local block at the very top of the model block, and "tp2.stan" is what I use to look at the consequence of putting the local block in the model block at different places. Why would I put it at different places? Because I discovered that, regardless of machine, when the local block is at the top of the model block, as in tp1 I get identical performance & samples as I get with tp0". However, if I move the location of that local block around within the model block, I get different timing and samples from tp0. As a summary:
>>>>
>>>> Machine: Linux VM on Google
>>>> - tp2 local block @ beginning: same samples and timing as tp0
>>>> - tp2 local block @ end: initialization errors, model can't sample
>>>> - tp2 local block anywhere in middle: different samples from tp0, slower by 30% *if* placed right before the last line (this happened to be the position that I used earlier, hence my report of the 30% timing difference), else same timing as tp0
>>>>
>>>> Machine: Linux PC & Mac OS X (same story on both)
>>>> - tp2 local block @ beginning: same samples and timing as tp0
>>>> - tp2 local block @ end: initialization errors, model can't sample
>>>> - tp2 local block anywhere in middle: different samples from tp0, same timing as tp0
>>>>
>>>> So, the previously reported timing difference only occurs with the Linux VM on Google compute engine, and only when the local block is placed at a very specific location in the model block. Leaving that mystery as probably too hardware involved to bother with, a remaining mystery is that, for all platforms, placement of the local block at anywhere but the beginning of the model block yields different samples from the version that uses the transformed parameters section, and placement of the local block at the end of the model block yields initialization errors that prevent sampling. Presumably this is not expected behaviour?
>>>>
>>>> Other weirdness: despite setting the random seed both in R when generating fake data and in the calls to rstan::sampling(), I seem to be getting different samples from machine to machine. Is my expectation that I should be getting the same samples naive?
>>>>
>>>> Mike
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> On Thu, Sep 8, 2016 at 2:59 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>> You'll see that it generates the exact same code other than
>>>> that which saves the parameters.  If there are a lot of
>>>> transformed parameters, saving them each iteration imposes
>>>> some overhead, especially if you're using something like
>>>> distributed disks on a cluster.  We should probably allow
>>>> some blocking/buffering of output---it all just streams
>>>> by default (in CmdStan anyway), which is probably not the right
>>>> behavior for a cluster.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>

>>>>> I just scanned it -- it's a bit too long. But if it's just moving a variable declared in the model block over to the transformed parameters block, then you shouldn't see a difference in ESS. > I have a problem where I want to sample from a distribution that is loosely speaking a "two-sided Gaussian" -- it is composed of the left half of a gaussian of width sigma2 and the right half of a gaussian of width sigma 1. The right half is to be scaled so that its peak is the same as that of the left. So the distribution looks like a Gaussian that is asymmetric about its peak.
>
> I think a way to do this is to use a mixture of two truncated Gaussians with mixture fractions equal to sigma1/(sigma1+sigma2) and sigma2/(sigma1+sigma2)
>

> The distribution for the right side is y ~ normal(mu,sigma2) T[mu,], so that it has support only on the right side of the peak
>
> I implemented the mixture by drawing a uniform random variable called mixingParam; if it's less than sigma1/(sigma1+sigma2), I draw from the first distribution and otherwise I draw from the second.

Hi Joe,

Sorry -- I missed the relevant error message from the original post:

RuntimeError: Rejecting initial value:
  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity.
  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value.
Rejecting initial value:

The first thing I'd do is remove the initialization. I haven't really needed to provide initial values for Stan when sampling. And, it'll help diagnose problems with multiple chains if you allow random initialization.

You might also want to check that there is support (probability > 0) for the parameter values. If not, then you might need constraints on your parameters.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
The error "gnu_lto_v1" relates to link-time optimization. By removing "-flto" from Makevars you are no longer asking GCC to perform LTO, so the problem should go away. On Windows, the current gcc is 4.9.3 whose LTO is existent but not a flawless as later versions of GCC and it tends to cause R-related packages to fail.

Avi

messages.body_plain:
Yes flat prior will probably increase computing time
relative to a weakly informative or informative prior.

The advantage of putting a prior on the scale (std dev) rather
than squared scale (variance) is that the scale parameter has the
same units as the mean, making it easier and more natural to work
with.  A perhaps bigger issue is the behavior of the prior as the
scale approaches zero and how much mass it spreads out into
the tail.

- Bob

messages.subject: Random Neighbor GPs?
messages.subject_clean: Random Neighbor GPs?
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

In a recent thread here at stan-users, Lu Zhang posted an implementation of a Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Process, and while I am not entirely sure how it works, my impression is that it avoids computing the full NxN multivariate normal by instead cutting up the domain of the GP into pieces and a GP for each using the same kernel parameters. I'm not sure how the size/number of these pieces are chosen, and whether there is overlap between pieces; from what I can tell these choices are made outside Stan and submitted as data to Stan.

This reminded me of a possibly silly idea I had a while ago to speed up GPs, and I'd like to know whether it makes sense and could be implemented in Stan.

Specifically, and taking the example of a 1-dimensional GP, if the data reflect N locations on the dimension, a full GP requires computation of an NxN covariance matrix and then use of this matrix as input to a multivariate normal. My alternative idea is to, for every iteration, select a random subset of size M of the N locations, where M is much smaller than N. The selection of the value of M itself could also be set to be random (uniform from 2 to N) if one wanted to avoid making the choice fixed.

I *think* this won't cause any bias in the estimation of the GP parameters, as the distribution of pairwise distances of a random subset of locations should approximate that of the full set of locations (n.b. unlike alternatives that subsample the full space with equally-spaced knots, which yields undersampling of the smaller distances). But I'm not sure whether this alters the conceptual meaning of the resulting posterior, or whether it's even possible to code it in Stan.

On the latter, I think possibly not since the *_rng functions are only usable in the generated quantities section and presumably one can't create a model block that refers to variables defined in the generated quantities block. Another idea is to have the random sampling achieved by stepping through a matrix provided as data, but this would require the model block have access to the current iteration number, which I presume is not a feature of the language.

Thoughts?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
messages.body_plain:
There’s a general theme with random subsampling algorithms
of this flavor.  When you subsample the data your posterior almost
never looks anything close to the full-data posterior and any samples
you generate will not be close to the typical set of the full-data
posterior, either inducing large biases when no correction is made,
or resulting in vanishing acceptance probabilities if a correction is
made.

Perhaps more intuitively, as you aggregate more and more data
your typical set concentrates, but wiggles as it does so because
each bit of data is extremely informative and significantly impacts
the shape of the typical set.  So the various iterations of the typical
set intersect only in a few neighborhoods of very small probability.
This intuition helps explain why subsampling algorithms are so
extremely fragile in practice.

Ten American dollars that try to subsample the input data in a GP
model will scale really poorly and we can track to back to this
intuition.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have two data: One from the mothers (evolution of AB over time) and one from their offsprings (also evolution of AB over time).
We believe that the measurement of AB in mothers at delivery certainly affect the estimate of AB in infants over time.
And we want to put everything together, in one model.
So we want to have a non-linear mixed effect model for data of mothers, and use the prediction values from the last measurements of these mothers to be a covariate in the
non-linaer mixed effect model in infants.
It means we have two data, two likelihood and they are related to each other by the previous condition. We want to put all together.

Is it possible to do something like that in Stan?
I have read many threats in this Stan users mailing list but there seem to have no really good information for this question.
If yes, could you provide a link for a reference (if it is available) for at least give a general direction (if it is not a demanding request).

Thank you.

It's hard to say for certain given your description, but I strongly suspect that what you'd be looking for is a multivariate model with the measurement of the mother and measurement of the offspring as paired outcomes. If there are multiple offspring per mother, you'd still have a single "offspring mean" measurement paired with the mother measurement as multivariate outcome, then model the offspring as random deviates from this intercept.

Though possibly you're saying that you have data where you have many generations, with each offspring generation later becoming mothers, in which case I'd have to think further on how to do it.

Merci.

On Sunday, 11 September 2016 23:07:27 UTC+2, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> It's hard to say for certain given your description, but I strongly suspect that what you'd be looking for is a multivariate model with the measurement of the mother and measurement of the offspring as paired outcomes. If there are multiple offspring per mother, you'd still have a single "offspring mean" measurement paired with the mother measurement as multivariate outcome, then model the offspring as random deviates from this intercept.
>
> Though possibly you're saying that you have data where you have many generations, with each offspring generation later becoming mothers, in which case I'd have to think further on how to do it.

> > We believe that the measurement of AB in mothers at delivery certainly affect the estimate of AB in infants over time.
> > And we want to put everything together, in one model.
> > So we want to have a non-linear mixed effect model for data of mothers, and use the prediction values from the last measurements of these mothers to be a covariate in the
> > non-linaer mixed effect model in infants.
> > It means we have two data, two likelihood and they are related to each other by the previous condition. We want to put all together.

Op donderdag 8 september 2016 02:33:39 UTC+2 schreef David West:

> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks a lot for your advice and patience! I tried to follow your advice as good as possible:
> 1. Fixing one of the parameters. The only parameter that was possible to fix was ksi. I changed omega ~ gamma(a, ksi) to omega ~ gamma(a, 0.1). a is a constant, in this example 1. This did improve number of divergent transitions but there were still 171 divergent transition with adapt_delta=0.99. Additionally, number of effect samples sharply decreased to <10 for many variables.
>
> 2. Starting with a simple model. I'm always trying to do this but for hierarchical shrinkage priors this is difficult. I performed a test by omitting omega, thus changing beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * omega * (psi .* phi)) to beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * (psi .* phi)). This did not improve number of divergent transitions but effective number of samples and estimates looked good. I also removed psi from the model (instead of psi), thus beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * omega * phi), but this did also not improve number of divergent transitions.
>
> 3. Tighten the exponential(0.5) prior. I changed this prior to exponential(10) but this did unfortunately not improve the number of divergent transitions and because of the multiplication in the model omega increased largely. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
messages.body_plain:
1) I think the simplest thing to try for scaling up the generic situations you're talking about is inducing points. (I typically work on spatiotemporal settings where Kronecker tricks are more helpful than inducing points...but combining the two is a pretty good idea!)

I can't remember--has anyone coded inducing points up in Stan yet? The nice thing would be that you could always start with just a few inducing points as you're building/testing the model and then add some more points to see how much difference it makes. Ultimately if you can afford it at the end you could switch to a bunch of inducing points or the full thing. (Note that learning the locations of the inducing points might be hard with HMC...?)

2) I'm not as pessimistic as Mike B about subsampling working in practice. Here's a recent paper <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.05427.pdf> by Filippone and Engler in which they were able to get Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to work. The main caveat from my experience with similar stuff is that tuning the parameters in stochastic gradient MCMC methods (and especially SGLD) is pretty tricky at this point. Not to mention Mike's valid concerns.

3) And finally, I just sent a simple implementation of a random Fourier features approach [Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximating GP regression to Stan-users. This uses randomization in a totally different way, and hopefully some minor improvements (see my question in that email) will make it ready for the birthday problem!

Seth
P.S. Mike B: I'll bet you one of the new plastic fivers we have here now instead.

On Sun, Sep 11, 2016 at 5:09 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> There’s a general theme with random subsampling algorithms
> of this flavor.  When you subsample the data your posterior almost
> never looks anything close to the full-data posterior and any samples
> you generate will not be close to the typical set of the full-data
> posterior, either inducing large biases when no correction is made,
> or resulting in vanishing acceptance probabilities if a correction is
> made.
>
> Perhaps more intuitively, as you aggregate more and more data
> your typical set concentrates, but wiggles as it does so because
> each bit of data is extremely informative and significantly impacts
> the shape of the typical set.  So the various iterations of the typical
> set intersect only in a few neighborhoods of very small probability.
> This intuition helps explain why subsampling algorithms are so
> extremely fragile in practice.
>
> Ten American dollars that try to subsample the input data in a GP
> model will scale really poorly and we can track to back to this
> intuition.
>

> > Hi folks,

> > In a recent thread here at stan-users, Lu Zhang posted an implementation of a Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Process, and while I am not entirely sure how it works, my impression is that it avoids computing the full NxN multivariate normal by instead cutting up the domain of the GP into pieces and a GP for each using the same kernel parameters. I'm not sure how the size/number of these pieces are chosen, and whether there is overlap between pieces; from what I can tell these choices are made outside Stan and submitted as data to Stan.
> >
> > This reminded me of a possibly silly idea I had a while ago to speed up GPs, and I'd like to know whether it makes sense and could be implemented in Stan.
> >
> > Specifically, and taking the example of a 1-dimensional GP, if the data reflect N locations on the dimension, a full GP requires computation of an NxN covariance matrix and then use of this matrix as input to a multivariate normal. My alternative idea is to, for every iteration, select a random subset of size M of the N locations, where M is much smaller than N. The selection of the value of M itself could also be set to be random (uniform from 2 to N) if one wanted to avoid making the choice fixed.
> >
> > I *think* this won't cause any bias in the estimation of the GP parameters, as the distribution of pairwise distances of a random subset of locations should approximate that of the full set of locations (n.b. unlike alternatives that subsample the full space with equally-spaced knots, which yields undersampling of the smaller distances). Another idea is to have the random sampling achieved by stepping through a matrix provided as data, but this would require the model block have access to the current iteration number, which I presume is not a feature of the language.

messages.subject: random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
messages.subject_clean: random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.

Attached are two examples of using random Fourier features
[Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximate Gaussian process regression.
The idea is that the covariance matrix is approximated by an explicit
randomized feature expansion of the kernel. With an explicit feature
space expansion, there's no costly multivariate matrix algebra--it
just becomes Bayesian linear regression on the new features.

In rff1.stan, I don't learn the lengthscale and it's very fast for
1000 data points. In rff2.stan, I do learn the lengthscale and it's
pretty slow (10 minutes), though it can still handle 1000 data points
with a small number of features. (Note that in the attached I only
have 10 features, but in real applications people often use 10K-100K
features!)

Anyone have thoughts on speeding up rff2.stan? My guess is that
there'd be a big speedup from a vectorized sin/cos, with analytic
gradients. If that sounds right, I'll file a feature request and
hopefully Rob and I can tackle this (+ anyone else who wants to help).

Seth

messages.body_plain:
We'll have all the unary functions vectorized soon, but there
won't be any speedup over loops because there are no shared
computations.  We might be able to get fancier with the implementation
and cut down some virtual function calls, but that's minor compared
to shared computations.

But you can speed up this loop:

  for(i in 1:n)
    for(j in 1:k) {
      cosfeatures[i,j] = scale * cos(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
      sinfeatures[i,j] = scale * sin(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
    }

Define the I x J matrix of omega * x, then multpily it by bw,
then use it to define cosfeatures and sinfeatures without the
scale, then multiply through by the scale.

The target+= forms of the densities are slower than the
~ forms because they don't drop constant terms (yes, yes, versions
that do drop constants are on my to-do list buried somewhere I
might get to them next year if I'm lucky).

With transformed data now, different RNGs get used per chain.
I'm going to fix that for the next release.

It'll also be faster if you only save fhat as a transformed parameter
and use that in the last normal_lpdf --- less I/O per iteration (reduces
n x k to n) and also saves some redundant calculations in generated
quantities.

sqrt(2.0 / n) rather than sqrt(2 / (1.0 * n)) just for clarity.

- Bob

Here's a recent paper by Filippone and Engler in which they were able to get Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to work. Not to mention Mike's valid concerns.

I'm not sure what you're saying about "pretty tricky at this point"
but "not as pessimistic as Mike B".   The latter statement's
almost vacuous in these contexts!  Even I'm not as pessimistic
as Michael and I'm pretty darn pessimistic about these algorithms
working well in general without a huge effort spent tuning them
and then validating that the tuned model works.

I'm not sure why you aren't pessimistic when you say "Pretty
tricky at this point".  I think that's what Michael's saying.

There's a strong publication bias and no reproducibility measured
in papers.  Everyone's stochastic algorithms work in their own papers.
I haven't looked at this particular paper, but most of the SGD papers
drive me crazy because they compare a well-tuned set of learning rates
with some other algorithm.  And they work on problems where they know
the right answer.  One of the difficult issues with these things is
knowing when the answer you got is right.  If you go the machine learning
route, that's not such a big deal, as you can concentrate on predictive
accuracy and nobody cares if you actually find the penalized MLE
or have approximated predictive uncertainty well.

My own experience has been that SGD is hard to tune even for penalized
max likelihood for logistic regression.  That's why we like L-BFGS.
It tends to be much more robust.

On that point, Marcus brought up other issues of false termination
in many of the SGD algorithms when they hit a flat patch of the posterior.
This often doesn't matter if you measure held out predictions (it can even
be a good thing as it can be seen as more regularization), but
can mean that you don't actually find the optimum of the function (the penalized
MLE or ELBO optimal point or whatever).  That may also be acceptable in your
applications, but be careful with it and compare to something that does
find the "right" answer if you want to claim fast general optimization.

> 3) And finally, I just sent a simple implementation of a random Fourier features approach [Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximating GP regression to Stan-users. This uses randomization in a totally different way, and hopefully some minor improvements (see my question in that email) will make it ready for the birthday problem!

Neat.

messages.body_plain:
These are all very good points about SGD and the related ML work on
it. What I understand Mike to be saying is that the situation is
hopeless when it comes to stochastic HMC approaches. But what I'm
predicting is that we'll eventually have ways of automatically tuning
some of these stochastic MCMC algorithms. For example, Gorham and
Mackey [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.03039v4.pdf] were able to choose an
appropriate step size for SGLD using Stein discrepancy.

Seth

On Mon, Sep 12, 2016 at 3:27 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> On Sep 12, 2016, at 8:39 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> 1) I think the simplest thing to try for scaling up the generic situations you're talking about is inducing points. (I typically work on spatiotemporal settings where Kronecker tricks are more helpful than inducing points...but combining the two is a pretty good idea!)
>>
>> I can't remember--has anyone coded inducing points up in Stan yet? The nice thing would be that you could always start with just a few inducing points as you're building/testing the model and then add some more points to see how much difference it makes. Ultimately if you can afford it at the end you could switch to a bunch of inducing points or the full thing. (Note that learning the locations of the inducing points might be hard with HMC...?)
>>
>> 2) I'm not as pessimistic as Mike B about subsampling working in practice. Here's a recent paper by Filippone and Engler in which they were able to get Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to work. The main caveat from my experience with similar stuff is that tuning the parameters in stochastic gradient MCMC methods (and especially SGLD) is pretty tricky at this point. Not to mention Mike's valid concerns.
>
> I'm not sure what you're saying about "pretty tricky at this point"
> but "not as pessimistic as Mike B".   The latter statement's
> almost vacuous in these contexts!  Even I'm not as pessimistic
> as Michael and I'm pretty darn pessimistic about these algorithms
> working well in general without a huge effort spent tuning them
> and then validating that the tuned model works.
>
> I'm not sure why you aren't pessimistic when you say "Pretty
> tricky at this point".  I think that's what Michael's saying.
>
> There's a strong publication bias and no reproducibility measured
> in papers.  Everyone's stochastic algorithms work in their own papers.
> I haven't looked at this particular paper, but most of the SGD papers
> drive me crazy because they compare a well-tuned set of learning rates
> with some other algorithm.  And they work on problems where they know
> the right answer.  One of the difficult issues with these things is
> knowing when the answer you got is right.  If you go the machine learning
> route, that's not such a big deal, as you can concentrate on predictive
> accuracy and nobody cares if you actually find the penalized MLE
> or have approximated predictive uncertainty well.
>
> My own experience has been that SGD is hard to tune even for penalized
> max likelihood for logistic regression.  That's why we like L-BFGS.
> It tends to be much more robust.
>
> On that point, Marcus brought up other issues of false termination
> in many of the SGD algorithms when they hit a flat patch of the posterior.
> This often doesn't matter if you measure held out predictions (it can even
> be a good thing as it can be seen as more regularization), but
> can mean that you don't actually find the optimum of the function (the penalized
> MLE or ELBO optimal point or whatever).  That may also be acceptable in your
> applications, but be careful with it and compare to something that does
> find the "right" answer if you want to claim fast general optimization.
>
>> 3) And finally, I just sent a simple implementation of a random Fourier features approach [Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximating GP regression to Stan-users. This uses randomization in a totally different way, and hopefully some minor improvements (see my question in that email) will make it ready for the birthday problem!
>
> Neat.
>
> - Bob

Thanks for all the suggestions! (Down to 8 minutes, and more than
twice as many effective samples.) Updated versions attached.

1) Moving the random number generation to R instead of transformed
data is important as there's now much better convergence of the
different chains, which makes sense since they're actually using the
same features now. But before you go and fix this, might be worth
seeing what other people use it for...I could imagine the current
behavior of different seeds for transformed data making sense in some
cases.

2) OK, good to hear about unary function vectorization. I guess I was
hoping that analytic gradients would make a big difference in terms of
the shared computations you're talking about. Consider n = 1 so we
have a real x, a parameter bw we want to learn, and omega is a vector
of size k. If sin(.) was vectorized, then we'd have:

sinfeatures = sin(omega * bw * x);

and the gradient with respect to x would be:

(omega * bw) .* cos(omega * bw * x)

i.e. elementwise product of two vectors. (For n > 1 it's elementwise
product of two matrices.) Won't that be faster since omega * bw will
only need to be calculated once?

Seth

On Mon, Sep 12, 2016 at 3:17 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> We'll have all the unary functions vectorized soon, but there
> won't be any speedup over loops because there are no shared
> computations.  We might be able to get fancier with the implementation
> and cut down some virtual function calls, but that's minor compared
> to shared computations.
>
> But you can speed up this loop:
>
>   for(i in 1:n)
>     for(j in 1:k) {
>       cosfeatures[i,j] = scale * cos(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
>       sinfeatures[i,j] = scale * sin(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
>     }
>
> Define the I x J matrix of omega * x, then multpily it by bw,
> then use it to define cosfeatures and sinfeatures without the
> scale, then multiply through by the scale.
>
> The target+= forms of the densities are slower than the
> ~ forms because they don't drop constant terms (yes, yes, versions
> that do drop constants are on my to-do list buried somewhere I
> might get to them next year if I'm lucky).
>
> With transformed data now, different RNGs get used per chain.
> I'm going to fix that for the next release.
>
> It'll also be faster if you only save fhat as a transformed parameter
> and use that in the last normal_lpdf --- less I/O per iteration (reduces
> n x k to n) and also saves some redundant calculations in generated
> quantities.
>
> sqrt(2.0 / n) rather than sqrt(2 / (1.0 * n)) just for clarity.
>
> - Bob

Lester’s work is awesome, but they are able to tune the algorithm only
under a certain set of assumptions.  Even then it’s just getting the best
performance of SGLD, which we know doesn’t scale well with dimension
and target complexity, i.e. bias that depends on the _fourth_-order
derivatives of the target density.  Nasty stuff.

Certainly if you want to use stochastic methods you should use their
best possible implementations.  I’m just saying that that upper floor
is pretty terrible in the kinds of problems of applied interest.  As Seth
alluded, I can show this formally for HMC but the intuition carries
over to any computational algorithm.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
messages.body_plain:
Bochner's theorem says any stationary kernel has a spectral
representation that's a probability measure--the kernel is the Fourier
transform of the spectral measure. So the idea is to approximate the
kernel, which is an integral, you use Monte Carlo samples from the
spectral measure. For a Gaussian kernel, the corresponding spectral
representation is also a Gaussian, so you sample the Fourier
frequencies (hence the sin/cos) from a Gaussian distribution. Once you
have the features, you can learn the coefficients for them, i.e.
Bayesian linear regression. People have generalized it to
non-stationary kernels, have shown how to get lower variance with
quasi-Monte Carlo, and have computational tricks for when you need
100K features for large n datasets.

A related idea is Sparse Spectrum GPs [Lázaro-Gredilla et al 2010], in
which instead of fixing the frequencies you optimize them (but fix the
coefficients) and thus learn a new kernel. I'm not aware of anyone
trying to learn a posterior over the frequencies by putting a prior on
them and sampling, but that might be a nice way of getting a Bayesian
non-parametric kernel. Or it might be very unidentifiable...

...but I'm not sure what a KL expansion of the GP would be...maybe
there's a connection?
Seth

It would be, but you're talking about an analytic gradient
for a compound expression.

> On Sep 12, 2016, at 11:19 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for all the suggestions! (Down to 8 minutes, and more than
> twice as many effective samples.) Updated versions attached.
>
> 1) Moving the random number generation to R instead of transformed
> data is important as there's now much better convergence of the
> different chains, which makes sense since they're actually using the
> same features now. But before you go and fix this, might be worth
> seeing what other people use it for...I could imagine the current
> behavior of different seeds for transformed data making sense in some
> cases.

I am going to fix it.  We decided a couple meetings ago.

There are two arguments, seed and chain ID.  Seed will control
how transformed data goes and chain ID how the rest goes.  So you
will still be able to get different results by changing the seed.

> 2) OK, good to hear about unary function vectorization. I guess I was
> hoping that analytic gradients would make a big difference in terms of
> the shared computations you're talking about. Consider n = 1 so we
> have a real x, a parameter bw we want to learn, and omega is a vector
> of size k. If sin(.) was vectorized, then we'd have:
>
> sinfeatures = sin(omega * bw * x);
>
> and the gradient with respect to x would be:
>
> (omega * bw) .* cos(omega * bw * x)
>
> i.e. elementwise product of two vectors. (For n > 1 it's elementwise
> product of two matrices.) Won't that be faster since omega * bw will
> only need to be calculated once?

That'd be faster if we could somehow be this clever on the algebra.
But that's not how autodiff works.  It just blindly plugs the
chain rule through element by element.

We'll eventually figure out a way to get user-defined analytic gradients,
or when there are reusable special functions, we can plumb analytic
gradients through.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

Thanks a lot for your help.

D

Op maandag 12 september 2016 16:39:40 UTC+2 schreef Bob Carpenter:

>
> > On Sep 7, 2016, at 8:33 PM, David West <davidw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > Thanks a lot for your advice and patience! I tried to follow your advice as good as possible:
> > 1. Fixing one of the parameters. The only parameter that was possible to fix was ksi. I changed omega ~ gamma(a, ksi) to omega ~ gamma(a, 0.1). a is a constant, in this example 1. This did improve number of divergent transitions but there were still 171 divergent transition with adapt_delta=0.99. Additionally, number of effect samples sharply decreased to <10 for many variables.
>
> Can you put a more informative prior on omega than gamma(1, 0.1)?
>
> > 2. Starting with a simple model. I'm always trying to do this but for hierarchical shrinkage priors this is difficult. I performed a test by omitting omega, thus changing beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * omega * (psi .* phi)) to beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * (psi .* phi)). This did not improve number of divergent transitions but effective number of samples and estimates looked good. I also removed psi from the model (instead of psi), thus beta = beta_raw .* (0.5 * omega * phi), but this did also not improve number of divergent transitions.
> >
> > 3. Tighten the exponential(0.5) prior. I changed this prior to exponential(10) but this did unfortunately not improve the number of divergent transitions and because of the multiplication in the model omega increased largely. I therefore additionally fixed omega to omega ~ gamma(1, 0.1) but this also did not change number of divergent transitions (but estimates looked good).
> >
> > 4. Reformulate in something not multiplicatively scaled. With the values of a_pi I'm using, the model is in fact equivalent to:
> > ksi ~ gamma(b, 1);
> > lambda ~ gamma(a_pi, ksi);
> > beta ~ double_exponential(0, sqrt_vec(lambda * 0.5)); //sqrt_vec is square root of a vector
> > This model needs less multiplication but unfortunately did not improve the number of divergent transitions. Additionally, it is hard to make hierarchical shrinkage priors without multiplication of the scale (the horseshoe prior needs also multiplication of the scale for example). The model I would like to implement in Stan can be found in formula 8 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.00046v1.pdf. This paper also shows how to implement a Gibbs sampler but because I understood that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is more reliable I would really like to implement this in Stan. Do you think this is possible?
>
> No idea and I don't really have time for another research
> project right now.  Gibbs can work well when there's a lot of
> scale variation because it's completely scale invariate when
> conjugate.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Thank you for your prompt response.

Please see the attachments the model for mothers and infants coded separately in Stan.
I actually have left-censoring observations in both data set and have longitudinal profile over time for both.
- In model in mothers: Assume a curve where the antibodies first increase, and after some time point h, it start falling with decade alpha_mum.
- In model in infants: Assume a curve where the antibodies first decrease with decay rate beta, after 2 months, it increase and then after h, decreases again.
In this model, antibodies of mothers at delivery (currently I am using the observed data, those values less than 5 are replaced by the predicted value obtained from the model of mothers) is considered as a covariate.
- In general, I want to combine the two data sets, and put the prediction of the antibodies of mothers at delivery as a covariate in the model of infants.

It is clear that it would involve in pairing the results, ID of mother and ID of infants.
I would like to have a sense whether we could combine the two data into one analysis like that.
Merci.

> If I've misunderstood, then probably best to send us a pair of models, one reflecting what you want to do with the mother measurements as outcomes, and one reflecting what you want to do with offspring measurements as outcomes (the latter presumably including the mother data as a predictor). > > >

>>
>> Thanks for all the suggestions! (Down to 8 minutes, and more than
>> twice as many effective samples.) Updated versions attached.
>>
>> 1) Moving the random number generation to R instead of transformed
>> data is important as there's now much better convergence of the
>> different chains, which makes sense since they're actually using the
>> same features now. But before you go and fix this, might be worth
>> seeing what other people use it for...I could imagine the current
>> behavior of different seeds for transformed data making sense in some
>> cases.
>>
>> 2) OK, good to hear about unary function vectorization. I guess I was
>> hoping that analytic gradients would make a big difference in terms of
>> the shared computations you're talking about. Consider n = 1 so we
>> have a real x, a parameter bw we want to learn, and omega is a vector
>> of size k. If sin(.) was vectorized, then we'd have:
>>
>> sinfeatures = sin(omega * bw * x);
>>
>> and the gradient with respect to x would be:
>>
>> (omega * bw) .* cos(omega * bw * x)
>>
>> i.e. elementwise product of two vectors. (For n > 1 it's elementwise
>> product of two matrices.) Won't that be faster since omega * bw will
>> only need to be calculated once?
>>
>> Seth
>>
>> On Mon, Sep 12, 2016 at 3:17 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>> > We'll have all the unary functions vectorized soon, but there
>> > won't be any speedup over loops because there are no shared
>> > computations.  We might be able to get fancier with the implementation
>> > and cut down some virtual function calls, but that's minor compared
>> > to shared computations.
>> >
>> > But you can speed up this loop:
>> >
>> >   for(i in 1:n)
>> >     for(j in 1:k) {
>> >       cosfeatures[i,j] = scale * cos(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
>> >       sinfeatures[i,j] = scale * sin(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
>> >     }
>> >
>> > Define the I x J matrix of omega * x, then multpily it by bw,
>> > then use it to define cosfeatures and sinfeatures without the
>> > scale, then multiply through by the scale.
>> >
>> > The target+= forms of the densities are slower than the
>> > ~ forms because they don't drop constant terms (yes, yes, versions
>> > that do drop constants are on my to-do list buried somewhere I
>> > might get to them next year if I'm lucky).
>> >
>> > With transformed data now, different RNGs get used per chain.
>> > I'm going to fix that for the next release.
>> >
>> > It'll also be faster if you only save fhat as a transformed parameter
>> > and use that in the last normal_lpdf --- less I/O per iteration (reduces
>> > n x k to n) and also saves some redundant calculations in generated
>> > quantities.
>> >
>> > sqrt(2.0 / n) rather than sqrt(2 / (1.0 * n)) just for clarity.
>> >
>> > - Bob
>> >
>> >> On Sep 12, 2016, at 8:39 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> >>
>> >> Anyone have thoughts on speeding up rff2.stan? My guess is that

>> >> gradients. If that sounds right, I'll file a feature request and
>> >> hopefully Rob and I can tackle this (+ anyone else who wants to help).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Guidance on interpreting loo's elpd
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Guidance on interpreting loo's elpd
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

Sorry for the late reply.

I'm afraid I didn't state much more than what is written at the bottom of p. 20 of Aki et al's paper (v5):

"Comparing the models on PSIS-LOO reveals an estimated difference in elpd of 10.2 (with a standard error of 5.1) in favor of Model A. "

So in my application I basically state that one model is preferred according to the LOO elpd estimate. Given that I'm comparing one model with and one model without an interaction term, and there's a pretty obvious interaction just from plotting the data, I think the model comparison results for my application are uncontroversial.

More generally though, I think it would be of great practical value if Aki and co-authors could include an example of converting elpd to a more intuitive scale for some given application (as stated in Aki's second reply, above).

On Friday, August 19, 2016 at 12:51:17 PM UTC+2, Daniel Emaasit wrote:
> @Tom Wallis, How did you finally interprete the results? I still did not quite understand Micheal & Aki's responses. (FYI, I am also one of those non-mathematicians)
>
> Thanks,
> -- Daniel
>
> On Friday, March 18, 2016 at 12:30:20 PM UTC+3, Tom Wallis wrote:
> > Great, thanks for the guidance all.
> >
> > So if I take Michael's last sentence, it's basically not appropriate to treat any of these comparators as distance metrics. They only provide ordinal information about the relative model performance, but do not quantify *how* much better one model is than another.
> >
> > On Thu, Mar 17, 2016 at 7:33 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Remember that LOO, cross-valiadtion, WAIC and all of the like
> > > are just estimators of some number that quantifies the _relative_
> > > compatibility of the model with the data.
> > >
> > > That number is tricky to interpret as information gain or loss because
> > > it’s really a difference of two different Kullback-Leibler divergences.
> > > And it’s definitely not a probability so shouldn’t be interpreted as
> > > such.
> > >
> > > Really this is just a way to rank models relative to each other.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mar 17, 2016, at 5:48 PM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
> > >
> > > > On Thursday, March 17, 2016 at 11:46:08 AM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> > > > > I'm looking for guidance on legitimate interpretations of the elpd. Briefly: can the elpd difference between two models be interpreted as the log odds ratio of the posterior model probabilities?
> > > > >
> > > > > Example:
> > > > >
> > > > > Model 1 elpd_loo = -50
> > > > > Model 2 elpd_loo = -48
> > > > >
> > > > > abs difference: 2
> > > > >
> > > > > From these results, could one state that Model 2 "describes the data" (in the sense of expected prediction error) about 7 times better than model 1 (i.e. exp(2)), on average? Similarly, if one converted the elpd difference to base 2 (2 / log(2) = 2.89), could one say that the average expected information gain of Model 2 relative to Model 1 is 2.89 bits?
> > > >
> > > > You could state like this, but then you are ignoring the uncertainty in the estimates. This approach has been proposed informally as pseudo Bayes factor, but there are no papers showing formally or experimentally that this would be a good way to report results. I recommend using the approach described in section 5.2 of "Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC" http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544, which is also implemented in compare function in loo package.
> > > >
> > > > Aki
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I am seeking ways to describe the results of loo such that they could be more easily understood or communicated to non-mathematical audiences. Apologies if my interpretations are way off base (I am a member of that non-mathematical audience).
> > > >

Our other interfaces are using standard GPL, not the Affero version (AGPL),
which is even more restrictively copyleft:

https://www.gnu.org/licenses/why-affero-gpl.html

There's also the issue of what's compatible with Mathematica---I have
no idea what the standard is there for licensing and what options
Mathematica provides for licensing versions as a back-end for products.

It's very confusing to me where the GPL boundaries are with respect
to what constitutes a derivative work.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan/Bayesian (alternative to) Scott-Knott (mean grouping) test?
messages.subject_clean: Stan/Bayesian (alternative to) Scott-Knott (mean grouping) test?
messages.body_plain:
I wonder if there is something similar to a Bayesian variant of a Scott-Knott test (which can be used to group treatments based on differences between their means rather than doing multiple pair-wise comparisons, e.g. http://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S2179-84512014000100002 ) and if someone has used it in Stan?

I have ~20 treatments with 100+ measurements from each and they seem to be roughly log-normal distributed (measurements cannot be below 0) and I want to group the treatments in groups within which it is hard to tell a difference between treatments while the between-group differences are larger/significant. The Scott-Knott does not seem a good alternative here since the mean is not robust to a few outliers. I guess I can log-transform and then apply Scott-Knott but a bayesian treatment seems more useful.

Pointers/helpers appreciated, thanks.

Regards,

Robert Feldt

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 8:36:23 AM UTC-4, Tom Wallis wrote:
> Hi Daniel,
>
> Sorry for the late reply.
>
> I'm afraid I didn't state much more than what is written at the bottom of p. 20 of Aki et al's paper (v5):
>
> "Comparing the models on PSIS-LOO reveals an estimated difference in elpd of 10.2 (with a standard error of 5.1) in favor of Model A. "
>
>
> So in my application I basically state that one model is preferred according to the LOO elpd estimate. Given that I'm comparing one model with and one model without an interaction term, and there's a pretty obvious interaction just from plotting the data, I think the model comparison results for my application are uncontroversial.
>
>
> More generally though, I think it would be of great practical value if Aki and co-authors could include an example of converting elpd to a more intuitive scale for some given application (as stated in Aki's second reply, above).

If you've multiplied by -2 and are on the deviance scale, you can probably use Burnham & Anderson's (2002, §2.6) AIC rules of thumb as does Spieghalter et al.(2002, §9.2.4) for DIC, as they are all estimates of the expected log pointwisepredictive density penalized for bias, I believe. Take the difference between any model's WAIC or elpd-loo on deviance scale from the model with the minimal value. B&A's heuristics are:

Difference between 0 - 2: Substantial evidence for second model as well
Difference between 4 - 7: Considerably less evidence for second model with respect to first
Difference greater than 10: Essentially no evidence for second model

Remember it is the difference that is important, the absolute magnitude is more a function of the number of data points than anything else.

Avi

References:
Burnham, K. P. & Anderson, D. R., Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach, Springer Science+Business Media, Inc., 2002
Spiegelhalter, D. J.; Best, N. G.; Carlin, B. P. & Van Der Linde, A., Bayesian measures of model complexity and fit, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), Blackwell Publishers, 2002, 64, 583-639 http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9868.00353/abstract;jsessionid=22CC7D20205F4D694F6F506D70B60834.f01t02

messages.body_plain:
Greetings.  Are there existing public stan implementations of the following?  I'd be grateful for any pointers.
Model a set of observation counts, {{n_00, n_01, ...}, {n_10, n_11, ...}, ...}, as generated by multinomials {m_0, m_1, ...} sampled from a Dirichlet D, and use NUTS to sample from the posterior on D's pseudocounts given some hyperprior.
Model a set of sets of continuous observations {{x_00, ...}, {x_10, ...}, ...}, as generated by normal distributions {N(μ_0, 𝜎_0), ...} sampled from some conjugate distribution, say a Normal-Inverse-χ², and use NUTS to sample from the posterior on the hyper-parameters μ, ϰ, ν, 𝜎 given some hyperprior.
Best regards,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan models for posterior hyperparameter sampling using NUTS
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan models for posterior hyperparameter sampling using NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Yes, see the manual.  But we tend not to do inference
on the Dirichlet parameters because it's such a weak prior.
You get a generalization to logistic multivariate normal
in the correlated topic model.  But you can also do the
Dirichlet by simple generalizations of the beta-binomial, which
we do describe, including suggestions for hyperpriors.

For the second problem, look at linear regression in the manual.
We don't usually use conjugate priors, though, as they're too
restrictive.  But there's nothing stopping you from using conjugate
priors.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan/Bayesian (alternative to) Scott-Knott (mean grouping) test?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan/Bayesian (alternative to) Scott-Knott (mean grouping) test?
messages.body_plain:
Andrew may want to weigh in on this one, but you can start here:

http://andrewgelman.com/2013/08/20/correcting-for-multiple-comparisons-in-a-bayesian-regression-model/

We discuss K-means and LDA clustering in the manual, if you're more
concerned with the clustering than with hypothesis testing.  But
the clustering analyses are typically very unstable in high dimensions.

- Bob

> On Sep 13, 2016, at 10:30 AM, Robert Feldt <robert...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I wonder if there is something similar to a Bayesian variant of a Scott-Knott test (which can be used to group treatments based on differences between their means rather than doing multiple pair-wise comparisons, e.g. http://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S2179-84512014000100002 ) and if someone has used it in Stan?
>
> I have ~20 treatments with 100+ measurements from each and they seem to be roughly log-normal distributed (measurements cannot be below 0) and I want to group the treatments in groups within which it is hard to tell a difference between treatments while the between-group differences are larger/significant. The Scott-Knott does not seem a good alternative here since the mean is not robust to a few outliers. I guess I can log-transform and then apply Scott-Knott but a bayesian treatment seems more useful.
>
> Pointers/helpers appreciated, thanks.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan models for posterior hyperparameter sampling using NUTS
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan models for posterior hyperparameter sampling using NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Look at the priors for coefficients and scales section
of the regression chapter.

Look for the correlated topic model, page 163 for
the more general prior case.

I'm not sure what you're calling the pseudocount.
In Dirichleta(alpha), the quantity sum(alpha) is
such that alpha - 1 is the prior count (elementwise
subtraction of 1) for each of K outcomes.  At least
if you start with uniform and add for counts observed.

You can also check out the beta-binomial case here,
which is trivial to generalize to Dirichlet:

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

Here's what it looks like in K dimensions:

parameters {
  real<lower=0.1> kappa;  // prior count minus K
  simplex[K] theta;       // prior mean
  simplex[K] phi[J];      // parameters

model {
  ... phi is a K-simplex, either parameters or data ...
  for (j in 1:J)
    phi[j] ~ dirichlet(theta * kappa);  // hierarchical prior on phi[k]
  kappa ~ pareto(0.1, 1.5);  // hyperprior on prior count
  theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // alpha is hyperprior

It decomposes the Dirichlet into mean theta and prior count (minus K)
kappa.  You can just skip the dirichlet prior on theta in which
case it defaults to uniform over simplexes.

I should put this in the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2051#issuecomment-246742910

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan,

Thanks for a really useful set of code.

One quick comment - I think you have your lags back to front

You have the following code line:
mus[t] <- mus[t] + B[p] * Y[t+p-1]

Assume you have P=4 lags.

If t is 10, then t in the original data is t+P = 14.

So then:
p = 1 means you are referencing 10+1-1 = 10 in the original time step
p = 2 means you are referencing 10+2-1 = 11 in the original time step
p = 3 means you are referencing 10+3-1 = 12 in the original time step
p = 4 means you are referencing 10+4-1 = 13 in the original time step.

Would it not make more sense to use t+P-p instead of t+p-1, so that B[1] corresponds to the first lag?

Julian

> I'm not sure what you're calling the pseudocount.
> In Dirichleta(alpha), the quantity sum(alpha) is
> such that alpha - 1 is the prior count (elementwise
> subtraction of 1) for each of K outcomes.  At least
> if you start with uniform and add for counts observed.
>
> You can also check out the beta-binomial case here,
> which is trivial to generalize to Dirichlet:
>

>
> Here's what it looks like in K dimensions:
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0.1> kappa;  // prior count minus K
>   simplex[K] theta;       // prior mean
>   simplex[K] phi[J];      // parameters
>
>
> model {
>   ... phi is a K-simplex, either parameters or data ...
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     phi[j] ~ dirichlet(theta * kappa);  // hierarchical prior on phi[k]
>   kappa ~ pareto(0.1, 1.5);  // hyperprior on prior count
>   theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // alpha is hyperprior
>
> It decomposes the Dirichlet into mean theta and prior count (minus K)
> kappa.  You can just skip the dirichlet prior on theta in which
> case it defaults to uniform over simplexes.

messages.subject_clean: data types and variable declarations
messages.body_plain:
Hi stan users,

I'm just starting to learn stan and am working my way through the stan reference manual trying to understand data types and declaring/assigning variables. To me, it seems that there are some inconsistencies in the manual and to better understand how the program works I would like to ask three questions (I apologize if these questions are stupid and the result of me not reading the manual properly):

1) In the manual (page 268) there is as an example the following declarations:

vector[5] a[4, 3];
vector[5] b[4];

and then it is stated that the following assignment is legal:
b = a[1];

As I understand it a is declared as an array with two dimensions (4 rows and 3 columns) where each "element" is a vector of length 5 and b is declared as an one-dimensional array of length 4 with elements being vectors of length 5. Further, on the top of page 268 it is described how subarrays can be accessed with less than the full number of indexes. Judging from that description I conclude that a[1] would be a one-dimensional array of length 3 (a has three columns and the elements are 5 element vectors). My questons is then how one can assign a[1] (a one-dimensional array of length 3) to b (which is declared to be a one-dimensional array of length 4)? To me it seems as if the sizes mismatch and hence the assignment should not work.

If it is possible to make such an assignment, what happens to b? Is it turned into a one-dimensional array of 3 or is is still an array of length 4 but with an "empty "element (and which of the elements is then empty?), or what?

2)  I'm having trouble understanding the differences between dimensionality and size/length in the description of arrays.

On page 267 it is said that an array is declared by enclosing its dimensions in square brackets following its name, like in these examples:
int n[5]; // giving an array of 5 integers (I take it this is an one-dimensional array of length 5)
real a[3, 4]; //  giving a two-dimensional array of real values with three rows and four columns i.e two dimensions where the first dimension has size 3 and the second size 4
real <lower=0> z[5, 4, 2]; // three dimensions of sizes 5 by 4 by 2

but then it is said that
vector[7] mu[3]; //gives a three-dimensional array of 7-vectors! -> to me this is an one-dimensional array that has 3 elements (length 3) where each element is a 7 element vector
matrix[7, 2] mu[15, 12] // gives a 15x12-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices -> to me this is a two-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices, it has 15*12 elements arranged in 15 rows and 12 columns where each element is a 7 by 2 matrix

Related to this I have seen examples in the manual where a vector is declared as:
vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;
 Why not use matrix<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;?
Is there any difference? Is corr in the first example a column vector (and how many elements does it have) or a matrix?

Do I misunderstand all of this or is it not very thourougly (or correctly) described in the manual?

3) As mentoined arrays are declared using square brackets after its name. But, for example, on page 270 one can find the following referred to as a vector:
vector b[4];
To me, this seems to be an array of vectors (of unknown length!). If it is a vector, why is it declared in this way instead of vector[4] b;? Is it OK to declare vectors and matrices where sizes are set using square brackets on their names rather than on the types? Does it make any difference?

I am grateful for any hints on this.

Sincerely
Martin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling from a lookup table
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sampling from a lookup table
messages.body_plain:
If you define your functions with suffix _lpdf (real outcome)
or _lpmf (discrete outcome), then you can use sampling notation.
See the manual chapter on user-defined functions for details
and examples.

The reason we don't have the real to int conversion built in is
that it breaks derivatives so you have to be very careful
that the result of whatever you do is still continuously
differentiable or Stan's HMC will have a hard time
sampling through the discontinuity.

- Bob

> On Sep 14, 2016, at 2:20 PM, Daniel Rosenbloom <daniel.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I'm not sure... I've never given it a try. I've always just used increment_log_prob (or now, the new target+=).
>
> I am glad that someone else can make use of our rather absurd typecasting-by-binary-search trick!
>
> On Wed, Sep 14, 2016 at 1:32 PM, Joseph Catanzarite <jcat...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you for taking the trouble to answer my question, Daniel!
>
> Question: once I build the function (say I call it error_distribution),
>
> can I then treat it as one of Stan's canned distribution functions and sample from it via a statement such as
>
> y ~ error_distribution
>
>
> Cheers,
> Joe
>
> On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 7:16:09 PM UTC-7, Daniel Rosenbloom wrote:
> Hi Joseph,
>
> So it ain't pretty, but here's what we had to do. First, you need to build a function that typecasts floats to ints, since doing so is not native to the Stan language. This function does so quickly, by binary search:
>
>     int as_integer_bsearch(real i_this, int size_max) {
>         // Outputs int(floor(i_this)), assuming that i_this is non-negative
>         int right_bound;
>         int left_bound;
>         int mid;
>
>         right_bound <- size_max;
>         left_bound  <- 0;
>         mid <- (right_bound + left_bound)/ 2; // int division intentional
>
>         // special case
>         if(i_this == right_bound) {
>             return right_bound;
>         }
>         if(i_this == left_bound) {
>             return left_bound;
>         }
>
>         while(mid != left_bound && mid != right_bound) {
>             if( i_this < mid ) {
>                 right_bound <- mid;
>             }
>             else {
>                 left_bound <- mid;
>             }
>             mid <- (right_bound + left_bound)/ 2;
>         }
>         return mid;
>     }
>
>
> Then here is the function that does the interpolation. The lookup_tbl has to be provided as data. For our particular problem, we had one regime where linear interpolation made the most sense, and another for logarithmic. Note that we are also coding in the left and right tail behaviors for the function (log-pdf of the Landau distribution):
>
>
>     real landau_logp(real[] lookup_tbl,
>                                 int nrow_lkup_tbl,
>                                 real x_lo,
>                                 real x_hi,
>                                 real x_linstep,
>                                 real x_breakpt,
>                                 int idx_breakpt,
>                                 real x_log10step,
>                                 real x_this) {
>         // Outputs Landau logpdf, using linear interpolation (to left of breakpoint), log interpolation
>         // (to right of breakpoint), or tail behavior.
>         // lookup_tbl: Provided as data
>         // nrow_lkup_tbl: # rows in lookup_tbl
>         // x_lo, x_hi: Outside these bounds, use analytic formulas for tail behavior
>         // x_breakpt: Below this value, lookup table is given in linear steps; above it is logarithmic
>         // idx_breakpt: Index of the breakpoint in the table
>         // x_linstep: Linear step size
>         // x_log10step: Log10 step size
>         // x_this: The value to compute
>
>         real log10_x_this;
>         real x_a; // x-value to left of x_this in table
>         int idx_a; // index of x_a in table
>         real f_a; // log-prob of x_a
>         real f_b; // log-prob of x_b (value to right of x_this in table)
>         real perc; // Used in interpolation
>
>         if( x_this < -365) {
>             return negative_infinity(); // at -365, log-prob is -5e306
>         }
>         if( x_this < x_lo ) {
>             return -exp( pow(-x_this,1.20591) / 1.741504 ); // left tail behavior, determined numerically
>         }
>         if (x_this > x_hi) {
>             return  -2 * log(x_this); // right tail behavior
>         }
>
>         if(x_this > x_breakpt) {
>             // Logarithmic interpolation (i.e., linear interpolation on log(x))
>             log10_x_this <- log10(x_this);
>             idx_a <- idx_breakpt + as_integer_bsearch((log10_x_this - log10(x_breakpt))/x_log10step, nrow_lkup_tbl);
>             x_a <- x_breakpt * pow(10, x_log10step * (idx_a - idx_breakpt));
>             perc <- (log10_x_this - log10(x_a)) / x_log10step;
>         } else {
>             // Linear interpolation
>             idx_a <- 1 + as_integer_bsearch( (x_this - x_lo)/x_linstep, nrow_lkup_tbl);
>             x_a   <- x_lo + x_linstep * (idx_a - 1);
>             perc <- (x_this - x_a)/x_linstep;
>         }
>
>         f_a <- lookup_tbl[idx_a];
>         f_b <- lookup_tbl[idx_a+1];
>
>         return f_a  + (f_b - f_a) * perc;
>     }
>
>
> Hope this helps!
>
> Best,

On Wednesday, September 14, 2016 at 5:20:21 PM UTC-4, ralphe...@gmail.com wrote:

Well, you could do the exponentiation once in the transformed data block and that would help a lot. However, raw polynomials tend not to work well in Stan because a and b are highly dependent with different scales. Orthogonal polynomials work much better.

> > On Sep 14, 2016, at 2:20 PM, Daniel Rosenbloom <daniel.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm not sure... I've never given it a try. I've always just used increment_log_prob (or now, the new target+=).
> >
> > I am glad that someone else can make use of our rather absurd typecasting-by-binary-search trick!
> >
> > On Wed, Sep 14, 2016 at 1:32 PM, Joseph Catanzarite <jcat...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you for taking the trouble to answer my question, Daniel!
> >
> > Question: once I build the function (say I call it error_distribution),
> >
> > can I then treat it as one of Stan's canned distribution functions and sample from it via a statement such as
> >
> > y ~ error_distribution
> >
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Joe
> >
> > On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 7:16:09 PM UTC-7, Daniel Rosenbloom wrote:
> > Hi Joseph,
> >
> > So it ain't pretty, but here's what we had to do. First, you need to build a function that typecasts floats to ints, since doing so is not native to the Stan language. This function does so quickly, by binary search:
> >
> >     int as_integer_bsearch(real i_this, int size_max) {
> >         // Outputs int(floor(i_this)), assuming that i_this is non-negative
> >         int right_bound;
> >         int left_bound;
> >         int mid;
> >
> >         right_bound <- size_max;
> >         left_bound  <- 0;
> >         mid <- (right_bound + left_bound)/ 2; // int division intentional
> >
> >         // special case
> >         if(i_this == right_bound) {
> >             return right_bound;
> >         }
> >         if(i_this == left_bound) {
> >             return left_bound;
> >         }
> >
> >         while(mid != left_bound && mid != right_bound) {
> >             if( i_this < mid ) {
> >                 right_bound <- mid;
> >             }
> >             else {
> >                 left_bound <- mid;
> >             }
> >             mid <- (right_bound + left_bound)/ 2;
> >         }
> >         return mid;
> >     }
> >
> >
> > Then here is the function that does the interpolation. The lookup_tbl has to be provided as data. For our particular problem, we had one regime where linear interpolation made the most sense, and another for logarithmic. Note that we are also coding in the left and right tail behaviors for the function (log-pdf of the Landau distribution):
> >
> >
> >     real landau_logp(real[] lookup_tbl,
> >                                 int nrow_lkup_tbl,
> >                                 real x_lo,
> >                                 real x_hi,
> >                                 real x_linstep,
> >                                 real x_breakpt,
> >                                 int idx_breakpt,
> >                                 real x_log10step,
> >                                 real x_this) {
> >         // Outputs Landau logpdf, using linear interpolation (to left of breakpoint), log interpolation
> >         // (to right of breakpoint), or tail behavior.
> >         // lookup_tbl: Provided as data
> >         // nrow_lkup_tbl: # rows in lookup_tbl
> >         // x_lo, x_hi: Outside these bounds, use analytic formulas for tail behavior
> >         // x_breakpt: Below this value, lookup table is given in linear steps; above it is logarithmic
> >         // idx_breakpt: Index of the breakpoint in the table
> >         // x_linstep: Linear step size
> >         // x_log10step: Log10 step size
> >         // x_this: The value to compute
> >
> >         real log10_x_this;
> >         real x_a; // x-value to left of x_this in table
> >         int idx_a; // index of x_a in table
> >         real f_a; // log-prob of x_a
> >         real f_b; // log-prob of x_b (value to right of x_this in table)
> >         real perc; // Used in interpolation
> >
> >         if( x_this < -365) {
> >             return negative_infinity(); // at -365, log-prob is -5e306
> >         }
> >         if( x_this < x_lo ) {
> >             return -exp( pow(-x_this,1.20591) / 1.741504 ); // left tail behavior, determined numerically
> >         }
> >         if (x_this > x_hi) {
> >             return  -2 * log(x_this); // right tail behavior
> >         }
> >
> >         if(x_this > x_breakpt) {
> >             // Logarithmic interpolation (i.e., linear interpolation on log(x))
> >             log10_x_this <- log10(x_this);
> >             idx_a <- idx_breakpt + as_integer_bsearch((log10_x_this - log10(x_breakpt))/x_log10step, nrow_lkup_tbl);
> >             x_a <- x_breakpt * pow(10, x_log10step * (idx_a - idx_breakpt));
> >             perc <- (log10_x_this - log10(x_a)) / x_log10step;
> >         } else {
> >             // Linear interpolation
> >             idx_a <- 1 + as_integer_bsearch( (x_this - x_lo)/x_linstep, nrow_lkup_tbl);
> >             x_a   <- x_lo + x_linstep * (idx_a - 1);
> >             perc <- (x_this - x_a)/x_linstep;
> >         }
> >
> >         f_a <- lookup_tbl[idx_a];
> >         f_b <- lookup_tbl[idx_a+1];
> >
> >         return f_a  + (f_b - f_a) * perc;
> >     }
> >
> >
> > Hope this helps!
> >
> > Best,
> > Daniel

messages.subject: Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
messages.subject_clean: Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to reproduce Random Fatigue-Limit model (Pascual & Meeker 1999, Ryan 2003 doi: 10.1198/1061860032012) using pystan. I get the model (attached .py code) to run without errors but the traces (attached picture) look like it didn't converge.

The model describes specimen lifetime as function of stress level. There is thought to be a fatigue limit which is stochastic variable that defines whether the component will have finite lifetime or not. The joint distribution of (log(lifetime) w, fatigue limit) ~ N(b0 + b1*log(stress - fatigue_limit), sigma), and log(fatigue_limit) = v ~ N(mu_v, sigma_v). Ryan states: "When collecting fatigue data, it is possible to observe a Žfinite value of W exactly or to observe an interval that contains W. But V is not observable. Thus, for purposes of estimating \theta via methods involving a likelihood, it is necessary to obtain the marginal distribution of W. This distribution has both a continuous and a discrete component.". And because of this there is integration performed on the joint distribution to get the marginal distribution of the log(lifetime) w.

Right-censorship is needed because in practice one can't wait forever for the specimen to break. These interrupted tests, called run-outs, form the discrete component of the marginal distribution of W.

Is this model possible to be modeled in stan? My code (137 lines, including test-data) is attached. I have used the functions block to describe the puzzle pieces for the custom likelihood and numerical (trapezoidal) integration of the marginal distribution.

Thank you!
Joona

messages.body_plain:
> The reason we don't have the real to int conversion built in is
> that it breaks derivatives so you have to be very careful
> that the result of whatever you do is still continuously
> differentiable or Stan's HMC will have a hard time
> sampling through the discontinuity.

In particular, the discontinuities at the interpolation points
will prevent the discrete trajectories used in HMC from
following the true trajectories that are needed for scalable
sampling.  The acceptance probability will suffer from this
inaccuracy and you will not really be taking advantage of
the potential performance of Stan.

Aside from a few (important) exceptions, interpolation
is evil.  Evil evil evil.
