messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Biased parameters for truncated, noisy data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks to everyone for the comments. I have been pondering this for
the last few days and believe I understand the nature of my problem
now. As several of you said, the issue was that my data generation was
not consistent with my Stan model.

I'll summarise my understanding in the hope that (a) it is correct and
(b) it is of some use to others.

In my examples, I have some latent quantity x sampled from a
distribution of known form, with parameters θ_x, and then some
observed quantity sampled from a known distribution centred on x, with
parameters θ_y. The data are only collected if y is greater than
some threshold y_min.

I'll denote the pdf of x as P_x, and the pdf of y as P_y. In my first
toy model, P_x and P_y were both normal while in my semi-realistic
model, P_x was lognormal and P_y was Poissonian.

I generated my data using something like

x = rnorm(N_tot,mu,sigma_x)
y = rnorm(N_tot,x,sigma_y)

and applied my detection threshold with

y = y[y>ymin]
N_obs = length(y)

Now consider the likelihood for y. First, neglecting the truncation at
y_min, the likelihood of a particular pair of x and y is

P_1(y,x|θ_x,θ_y) = P_x(x|θ_x) * P_y(y|x,θ_y)

and we can marginalise out x to get

P_2(y|θ_x,θ_y) = \int dx P_x(x|θ_x) * P_y(y|x,θ_y)

Now, taking the truncation into account, we set P_2(y|θ_x,θ_y)=0 for y<=y_min and
renormalise the distribution to give

P_trunc(y|θ_x,θ_y,y_min) = P_2(y|θ_x,θ_y) / \int_y_min^inf dy P_2(y|θ_x,θ_y)

[equation 1]

The problem I had was that my Stan model for truncated data had the form

    x ~ normal(mu,sigma_x);
    for (i in 1:N_obs)
      y[i] ~ normal(x[i], sigma_y) T[ymin,];

but this does not correspond to the likelihood above. Instead, this
corresponds to

P_trunc(y|θ_x,θ_y,y_min) = \int dx P_x(x|θ_x) * P_y(y|x,θ_y) / \int_y_min^∞ dy P_y(y|x,θ_y)

i.e. in this case it is only the distribution of y that is truncated,
while for the first case [equation 1], the x-marginalised distribution
of y is truncated, as in my generated data.

In the simple case of P_x and P_y being normal, then P_trunc
simplifies to a single normal with the variances added to give
sigma_tot^2 (as pointed out earlier in the thread), and you can just
write

y[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma_tot) T[ymin,]

For the general case where P_x and P_y are not both normal, I don't
know a way of writing a model corresponding to [equation 1] concisely
in Stan, (i.e. keeping the x's as latent parameters rather than
integrating them out). An inelegant version in which I compute the
integrals numerically in user-defined functions, correctly recovers the
parameters in my lognormal-poisson generated data.

Any thoughts on whether it is possible to write the general case in
Stan would be gratefully received!

Thanks for all of your time and input!

Ben

On Friday, September 9, 2016 at 3:42:24 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The paper Andrew linked has a clear explanation of
> what's going on in section 2.1:
>
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/parameterization.pdf
>
> I was wrong in saying you couldn't infer the parameters,
> though.  And now that I think about it, you could probably infer
> the amount of missingness from the CDFs given the parameters,
> because you know the mass < ymin and the mass > ymin, which
> gives you the expected ratio of missing to observed, and then
> it's just binomial stuff after that to do inference on number
> of missing items.  At least I think that's right.  I love
> having my work checked on this list!
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Sep 9, 2016, at 8:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > As Bob and Dan very clearly explained, your original results
> > were invalid because you weren’t simulating data correctly.
> > You simulated data assuming that you knew the total number
> > of trials, but such truncation models assume that you only
> > know the number of measured trials.  Hence you have to
> > do rejection sampling or, in the Gaussian case, inverse
> > CDF transform sampling to generate appropriate simulation
> > data.
> >
> > Even once you do that, however, you can only infer the
> > latent rate of missingness (or the latent true rate).  This is
> > actually more informative than the actual number of missing
> > events as it isn’t corrupted by measurement noise.
> >
> > On Sep 9, 2016, at 12:02 PM, Ben Maughan <benma...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Hi Michael,
> >>
> >> That is precisely what I did in my initial model (see first post, x is the latent population, ymin is thresh):
> >>
> >>   x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> >>
> >>   for (i in 1:J){
> >>     y[i] ~ normal(x[i],ysig) T[ymin,];
> >>   }
> >>
> >> and this didn't work - or are you suggesting something different from my first model?
> >>
> >> Cheers,
> >>  Ben
> >>
> >> On Friday, September 9, 2016 at 10:05:52 AM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >> Then move the truncation to the measurement model for the y.
> >> The point is that you can’t infer anything about the missing
> >> measurements unless you model the latent population distribution
> >> exactly.
> >>
> >> On Sep 9, 2016, at 9:11 AM, Ben Maughan <benma...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >>> Hi,
> >>>
> >>> Thanks for this. If I understand your model correctly, it models the case where I might measure a y value to be below thresh even though its y_latent must be above thresh. However, I have the opposite case; my data may have any value of y_latent, but the measured y must be above thresh. In the above model, the probability that would be assigned to (y_latent<thresh & y>thresh) is zero, but this is perfectly possible in nature.
> >>>
> >>> Specifically, an AGN might have a low magnitude that makes it unlikely to be detected, but in a particular observation the Poisson fluctuations in photon counts might just get over the detection threshold. In that case y_latent < thresh but y > thresh. This is what I tried to set up with my toy model by using the truncated normal for my measured y, but this did not work.
> >>>
> >>> Am I misunderstanding your model?
> >>>
> >>> Cheers,
> >>>  Ben
> >>>
> >>> On Thursday, September 8, 2016 at 10:28:29 PM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >>> Firstly and somewhat tangentially, no you did not measure any measurement
> >>> noise ysig.  Physicists make this mistake all the time because they’re used
> >>> to Poisson asymptotic estimators of the form lambda = N +/- \sqrt{N}.  But
> >>> if your noise is Poisson then model it generatively as
> >>>
> >>> y ~ poisson(lambda);
> >>>
> >>> or if there are measurement affects that corrupt the simple Poissonian variation
> >>>
> >>> y ~ neg_binomial2(lambda, phi);
> >>>
> >>> etc, etc.  Or make a normal approximation as
> >>>
> >>> y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> >>>
> >>> and _fit_ sigma as a parameter.
> >>>
> >>> Anyways, unless you have some other measurements sensitive to how many
> >>> observations that you are missing then you cannot infer how many you missed
> >>> as there is literally no information about that (i.e. you can’t compute an efficiency
> >>> if you don’t have counts before and after some process!).
> >>>
> >>> BUT you can do something even better if you think generatively.  Really what
> >>> you have here is a generative model with two components: a latent population
> >>> of AGN and a measurement model for those AGN with sufficient magnitude.
> >>> If you fit both of those together then you can infer the shape of the AGN population
> >>> distribution even with the truncation, and then you can recover the overall rate
> >>> of the observations you missed by integrating the tail of that distribution from
> >>> the truncation.
> >>>
> >>> Very, very prototypically, something like
> >>>
> >>> data {
> >>>   int<lower=1> N;
> >>>   real y[N];
> >>> }
> >>>
> >>> parameters {
> >>>   real agn_mu; // AGN population log mean
> >>>   real<lower=0> agn_sigma; // AGN population deviation
> >>>
> >>>   real y_latent[N]; // Latent AGN magnitudes
> >>>
> >>>   real thresh; // measurement threshold
> >>>   real<lower=0> sigma; // heteroskedastic measurement deviation
> >>> }
> >>>
> >>> model {
> >>>   // priors on everything!  No uniform distributions!
> >>>
> >>>   // AGN population model
> >>>   for (n in 1:N)
> >>>     y_latent[n] ~ normal(agn_mu, agh_sigma) T[thresh,];
> >>>
> >>>   // Measurement model
> >>>   for (n in 1:N)
> >>>     y[n] ~ normal(y_latent[n], sigma);
> >>> }
> >>>
> >>> generated quantities {
> >>>   real true_rate;
> >>>   real missing_rate;
> >>>
> >>>   true_rate = N / normal_ccdf(thresh, agn_mu, agh_sigma);
> >>>   missing_rate = true_rate - N;
> >>> }
> >>>
> >>> In practice you’ll want to vectorize everything and probably switch
> >>> to a non-centered parameterization for the y_latent.
> >>>
> >>> Generative models — they are the best!
> >>>
> >>> On Sep 8, 2016, at 9:49 PM, Ben Maughan <benma...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>>> Dear Bob,
> >>>>

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I ran the same model in Monolix and R software (using rstan) and apprarently they produced different -2loglikelihood.
I have a model based on ODEs which could be stated like:
If t <=2:            dA/dt = -beta*A.
If t>2 and t<=h: dA/dt = gamma*A.
If t>h:               dA/dt = -alpha*A.
Since this system of ODE is quite simple, I can get the analytical form of A (antibody on log10 scale) and formulate the model in rstan where the antibody on log10 scale at time point t has the predicted value of:
If t <=2:                   log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*time)]
If t >2 and t<=h:       log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*2 + gamma*(time-2))]
If t >h:                     log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*2 + gamma*(h-2) -alpha*(time-h))]
(We use log10 transformation for this typical type of data and have seen its good performance).

I have longitudinal profiles so I fixed non-linear mixed effect model in Monolix with 4 random effects of A0, beta, gamma, alpha. The individual parameters of all four parameters are assumed to have log-normal distribution.
The convergence of this model is well-achieved and we got -2loglikelihood of 462.75.
I fit the same model in Stan where individual parameters of A0 is assumed to have a normal distribution, but for beta, gamma, alpha, it is assumed to have normal distribution (I tried to let these individual parameters to have log-normal distributions as well but the model did not give the good estimate (some parameter estimates are approximately 5.6e207)). However, the -2loglikelihood is -494.114 (I use the mean of the -2loglikelihood).

So one obtained from Monolix is positive and one from Stan is negative.
Does any one have the same problem?
How can we explain for that? Or what am I doing wrong?

I attach the program in the attachment for easy following.
Thank you.

messages.body_plain:
I thought I would chime in on this older thread. I have recently been trying to refine my intuition about what affects model speed across different platforms because I recently discovered that my intuition was quite wrong.

Background:

I ran the same model, same data, same random seed on two computers using cmdstan-2.12. The model uses hierarchical shrinkage priors, and matrix operations over 30k data. Both computers were running the same OS (Arch linux), compilers (gcc 6.2), etc. The biggest difference between the two is hardware:

Computer 1 (desktop):
i7-3770 @ 3.7 GHz
24 Gb RAM - DDR3 1033

Computer 2 (laptop):
i5-6200U @ 2.7 GHz
20 Gb RAM - DDR4 2400

Expectation: The large clock-speed advantage of the desktop would give it an advantage. At worse, I expected the clock-speed advantage to outweigh the older architecture and slower RAM and would make the two about equal.

Results: The laptop was 4x faster than the desktop.

I know there are likely some architecture-specific optimizations happening from gcc, but I am curious how large of a difference the memory is making. I have also run this model on a cloud compute server using Haswell chips running at 2.6Ghz, and experienced model speeds between the two above cases. I am very surprised that of all the hardware I have access to, the laptop is the fastest by a large margin.

I would be curious if anyone else has experienced this.

Matt

There's lots of info in the "Transformations of Constrained Variables"

I don't know anything about Monolix...maybe it has default priors? Or
maybe it also drops constants?

Seth

The g function includes both a decay ( x'(i) = x(i) + lamba * x'(-1) )  and a saturation function which can be a power of less than 1 or a neg-exponential or logistic... The only assumptions we make are

1.  that the program defines a proper density up to
an additive constant (i.e., the exp() of the log density
has a finite integral), and

2.  the density is continuously differentiable.

Stan can run into sampling problems with too-fat tails, too-thin tails, or
extreme position-dependent curvature in the posterior.

Time series can have strong dependencies among the parameters,
which can sometimes be tackled by reparameterizing.

E.g., rather than

  theta[t+1] ~ normal(theta[t], sigma);

you can use a non-centered parameterization with a parameter
theta_raw and transformed parameter theta, with

  theta[t + 1] = theta[t] + sigma * theta_raw[t+1];

  theta_raw[t + 1] ~ normal(0, 1);

The sampling will happen over the theta_raw, but you'll still
recover your theta.

- Bob

Yes, memory's a huge deal.   It takes the equivalent of many
CPU arithmetic instructions to move data from RAM into the CPU's
registers (how many depends on relative CPU, cache, memory, and
bus [if any] speed).

If the desktop doesn't have modern CPU architecture
and is still using a frontside bus instead of the adjacent memory,
that adds even more latency.

The other thing to keep in mind is that the clock speed isn't the
only measure of compute throughput.  Better prefetch and memory
dispatch are huge as well as the size of the memory cache, and
then there's the matter of floating point performance and parallel
capacity.  So you might want to look at benchmarks of those CPUs.

Although the i7 looks to be much faster at arithmetic, your
i5 has higher memory bandwidth (aside from the faster memory).

It will also depend on how much you parallelize.  Looks like the i7
has four cores and the i5 only two.

- Bob

> On Sep 14, 2016, at 11:00 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi stan users,
>
> I'm just starting to learn stan and am working my way through the stan reference manual trying to understand data types and declaring/assigning variables. To me, it seems that there are some inconsistencies in the manual and to better understand how the program works I would like to ask three questions (I apologize if these questions are stupid and the result of me not reading the manual properly):
>
> 1) In the manual (page 268) there is as an example the following declarations:
>
> vector[5] a[4, 3];
> vector[5] b[4];
>
> and then it is stated that the following assignment is legal:
> b = a[1];

> As I understand it a is declared as an array with two dimensions (4 rows and 3 columns) where each "element" is a vector of length 5 and b is declared as an one-dimensional array of length 4 with elements being vectors of length 5. Further, on the top of page 268 it is described how subarrays can be accessed with less than the full number of indexes. Judging from that description I conclude that a[1] would be a one-dimensional array of length 3 (a has three columns and the elements are 5 element vectors). My questons is then how one can assign a[1] (a one-dimensional array of length 3) to b (which is declared to be a one-dimensional array of length 4)? To me it seems as if the sizes mismatch and hence the assignment should not work.

Thanks.  It's legal in the language and the program
will compile, but you'd get a runtime error because the
sizes don't match.  I'll change for the next release to
declare a as:

  vector[5] a[3, 4];

>
> If it is possible to make such an assignment, what happens to b? Is it turned into a one-dimensional array of 3 or is is still an array of length 4 but with an "empty "element (and which of the elements is then empty?), or what?
>
> 2)  I'm having trouble understanding the differences between dimensionality and size/length in the description of arrays.
>
> On page 267 it is said that an array is declared by enclosing its dimensions in square brackets following its name, like in these examples:
> int n[5]; // giving an array of 5 integers (I take it this is an one-dimensional array of length 5)
> real a[3, 4]; //  giving a two-dimensional array of real values with three rows and four columns i.e two dimensions where the first dimension has size 3 and the second size 4
> real <lower=0> z[5, 4, 2]; // three dimensions of sizes 5 by 4 by 2
>
> but then it is said that
> vector[7] mu[3]; //gives a three-dimensional array of 7-vectors! -> to me this is an one-dimensional array that has 3 elements (length 3) where each element is a 7 element vector
> matrix[7, 2] mu[15, 12] // gives a 15x12-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices -> to me this is a two-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices, it has 15*12 elements arranged in 15 rows and 12 columns where each element is a 7 by 2 matrix

The terminology for these things is a mess.  Often
a vector with one dimension of size three will be called
3-dimensional because it represents a point in 3-dimensional
space.  I'll try to make this more consistent by saying

> vector[7] mu[3];

is a one-dimensional array of size three holding vectors of size
7.

I tried to stick to "size" rather than "length" (what R uses)
because length is confusable with vector length (e.g., Euclidean).

> Related to this I have seen examples in the manual where a vector is declared as:
> vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;

That's a syntax error.  It should be matrix.

>  Why not use matrix<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;?
> Is there any difference? Is corr in the first example a column vector (and how many elements does it have) or a matrix?

There's a chapter in the manual on the various efficiency
tradeoffs of arrays vs. vectors/matrices.  Some of the older
examples used arrays where I would've

>
> Do I misunderstand all of this or is it not very thourougly (or correctly) described in the manual?
>
> 3) As mentoined arrays are declared using square brackets after its name. But, for example, on page 270 one can find the following referred to as a vector:
> vector b[4];

> To me, this seems to be an array of vectors (of unknown length!).

If that's what it is, it's illegal.  It should be vector[4] b; if it's
a vector or real b[4]; if it's an array.  That may have been introduced
when I changed some of the array examples to vectors.

> If it is a vector, why is it declared in this way instead of vector[4] b;? Is it OK to declare vectors and matrices where sizes are set using square brackets on their names rather than on the types? Does it make any difference?

No, only in functions.  There's a separate syntax for functions.

>
> I am grateful for any hints on this.

Thanks for reporting.  here's the issue which I'll address for the next
release:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2051#issuecomment-247464379

You can report issues directly on GitHub in the currently open
"next manual" issue.  Or submit pull requests to fix them.  Or just
send to our list like this and I'll transfer them over---we really
appreciate corrections like this.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
messages.body_plain:
I don't know the specific model, but I'm familiar with
the general idea of right-censoring in these situations as
you describe and Stan should be able to fit such models.
I can make a bunch of specific suggestions about how you can
code Stan to be more robust.

The normal density and cdf are built into Stan, as is
the truncation you'd need for censored observations.  So you
shouldn't be defining norm_pdf and norm_cdf.  Also, you want
to work on the log scale, not on the linear scale.  For
example, rather than summing a normal_pdf, you want to
log_sum_exp built-in normal_lpdf.   It's much more arithmetically
stable.

That mu function can be dangerous because it's discontinuous
at the point x = v.  I'm not sure why you think you need that
1e200 return, which is enormous and won't have a derivative.
We also have stable versions of log(exp(x) - exp(v)) built in

  log_diff_exp(x, v) = log(exp(x) - exp(v))

and it'll be more stable than applying exp directly.

Your p_w function also has discontinuities.  Stan assumes that
the log density you define is continuously differentiable.

You can't declare a parameter

  real<lower=0> sigma;

and then use

  log(sigma) ~ normal(0, 1);

because the log transform requires a Jacobian.  Instead,
you should be using

  sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);

which builds in the Jacobian.

I also see you have some densities on non-unit scales:

  b0 ~ normal(70, 35);
  b1 ~ normal(-10, 5);
  mu_v ~ normal(log(200), log(0.2^2 + 1));

This can make it hard for Stan to do adaptation as it has
to find the scale.  One thing you can do to make this sample
better is to declare b0_raw and use

  b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

and set

  b0 = b0_raw * 35 + 70;

That puts the actual parameter being sampled, b0_raw,
on the unit scale.

You never want to do log(1 - u) for any u;  use the
built in log1m(u), which is more stable.  But really don't want
to take the log of p_w, you want to define p_w on the
log scale directly using log_sum_exp.

- Bob

>
> The model describes specimen lifetime as function of stress level. There is thought to be a fatigue limit which is stochastic variable that defines whether the component will have finite lifetime or not. Ryan states: "When collecting fatigue data, it is possible to observe a Žfinite value of W exactly or to observe an interval that contains W. But V is not observable. Thus, for purposes of estimating \theta via methods involving a likelihood, it is necessary to obtain the marginal distribution of W. This distribution has both a continuous and a discrete component.". And because of this there is integration performed on the joint distribution to get the marginal distribution of the log(lifetime) w.
>
> Right-censorship is needed because in practice one can't wait forever for the specimen to break. These interrupted tests, called run-outs, form the discrete component of the marginal distribution of W.

messages.subject: Multinomial model for large samples
messages.subject_clean: Multinomial model for large samples
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

Imagine I have N (discrete) observations from n individuals. Each observation X_i is a vector {X_1i, X_2i, ..., X_k}, where sum(X_i) = n. The problem I have is: N is in the millions, and since we can only have n*(n +1)/2 different values for X, this means we'll have many "repeated" observations, i.e, each X_j (j  =1, 2, n*(n +1)/2) will appear f_j times, sum(f_j) = N. So far, I've been downsampling the data proportional to f_j, but I'd like to use all of the data.

How can I include the frequencies in the multinomial likelihood in stan? If I were doing this outside of stan I'd just sum the log of each frequency f_j to the (multinomial) log-likelihood of X_j. Is there a way of incrementing l_p to achieve this?

Thanks in advance,

Luiz

The problem I have is: N is in the millions, and since we can only have n*(n +1)/2 different values for X, this means we'll have many "repeated" observations, i.e, each X_j (j  =1, 2, n*(n +1)/2) will appear f_j times, sum(f_j) = N. So far, I've been downsampling the data proportional to f_j, but I'd like to use all of the data.
>

In this case, you can do

for (j in 1:J) target += f_j * multinomial_lpmf(...);

Since the duplicative observations are actually observed, this is okay, as opposed to the situation where the f_j are estimates of how many people in the population are in stratum j.

Ben

messages.subject: rstanarm 2.12.1 released
messages.subject_clean: rstanarm 2.12.1 released
messages.body_plain:
The rstanarm package for version 2.12.1 was released this week and is now mirrored on CRAN. You can install it simply by executing in R

install.packages("rstanarm", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org/", dependencies = TRUE)

Little changed, although one serious bug was fixed: posterior_predict() would do the wrong thing following models estimated by stan_lmer or stan_glmer if the labels of the grouping factors contained spaces in them. Specifically, posterior_predict() would marginalize over those grouping factors rather than conditioning on them. This bug is likely about 6 months old, so if you have recently generated predictions from such a model with rstanarm, you should reestimate it using rstanarm 2.12.1.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Parser warning from example Multivariate Probit
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, September 17, 2016 at 5:21:34 PM UTC-4, Patrick Sadil wrote:
> Okay. So, is it accurate to summarise this as, the parser threw a warning at the sampling statement because it was being asked to perform operations on the target for a variable that was not declared in the parameters block?

Yes, although not just any operation but rather one that increments the posterior kernel in log units.

> Could I safely avoid the warning by instead transforming my data outside of stan? So, rather passing an N by D array, y, of 0s and 1s, I would instead give stan an N by D matrix of reals such that each 0 is replaced by a call to
>
> > runif(n=1, min = -1, max = 0)
>
> and each 1 is replaced by
>
> > runif(n = 1, min = 0, max = 1)?
>
> Then, the sampling statement could just be:
>
>     y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(beta_x, L_Omega);

That would avoid the parser warning and have the side effect of estimating a completely different model that is neither a multivariate probit model nor a model where y depends on x.

It would be better to estimate the multivariate probit model and either increment the target keyword by the logarithm of the absolute value of the derivative of the transformation from z to its parent variable(s) or recognize that this derivative is a constant (indeed 1.0), in which case you would be incrementing the target keyword by a constant (indeed 0.0) which has no effect on what values are proposed for the parameters of what proposals are accepted. Better still would be to understand the principles behind a change-of-variables including the circumstances when essentially nothing is changed.

Ben

First, y ~ foo(theta) statements don't fill in y.  y has
to be defined before they're called and it just increments
the log desnity.

Second, you can't move parameter transforms into the preprocessor
because they depend on parameters at every step.  The transformed
parameters block is this:

transformed parameters {
  vector[D] z[N];
  for (n in 1:N_pos)

    z[n_pos[n], d_pos[n]] <- z_pos[n];

  for (n in 1:N_neg)

    z[n_neg[n], d_neg[n]] <- z_neg[n];
}

And it's just defining all of z in terms of z_pos and z_neg.
So there's nothing non-linear there, so the

The sampling statement in question is just

 z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(beta_x, L_Omega);

So that's OK.

- Bob

messages.subject: Running ADVI in parallel (RStan)
messages.subject_clean: Running ADVI in parallel (RStan)
messages.body_plain:
I noticed from previous posts and personal experience that the ADVI (variational bayes) function can sometimes get stuck on local optima, so that it makes sense to try multiple runs with different random initializations, ideally in parallel. I have a few suggestions for updates to Stan (specifically, RStan which is what I use) that would facilitate this:

1. Allow a parameter analogous to "chains" that will allow multiple ADVI instances to run in parallel.
2. Expose the final value of the ELBO in the stanfit object result for each ADVI run (not just printing). Then if one ran multiple VB procedures, he/she could choose the best one based on comparing ELBO values. Note this is not model comparison but just a way of getting closer to the global optimum for a single model.
3. Allow "silent mode" to prevent so much output being printed. In parallel it would become jumbled.

The way I am currently doing parallel ADVI is:
1. Wrap calls to vb() with parallel::mclapply() to parallelize
2. Redirect STDOUT for each ADVI instance to a string using capture.output()
3. Parse the strings to get the final ELBO values and use to choose the stanfit object based on highest ELBO among the parallel instances

I can post this as an issue to github but wanted to get some feedback here first.

Hi Joseph,

The syntax you're using is wrong. If you've defined a function:
  foo_lpdf(real y, real bar);

then to use it you either say:
  target += foo_lpdf(y | bar);

or
  y ~ foo(bar);

Those two lines above will do the same thing when it's a user defined function. The bottom one is just shorthand for the one above.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Running ADVI in parallel (RStan)
messages.subject_clean: Running ADVI in parallel (RStan)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Will,

We've had discussions about diagnostics involving multiple ADVI runs but, as far as I know, there hasn't been too much progress made on that yet. But I do think it's a good idea to allow running in parallel, so you could definitely open an issue on github about that.

Jonah

On Sunday, September 18, 2016 at 9:56:52 PM UTC-4, Will Townes wrote:
> I noticed from previous posts and personal experience that the ADVI (variational bayes) function can sometimes get stuck on local optima, so that it makes sense to try multiple runs with different random initializations, ideally in parallel. I have a few suggestions for updates to Stan (specifically, RStan which is what I use) that would facilitate this:
>
> 1. Allow a parameter analogous to "chains" that will allow multiple ADVI instances to run in parallel.
> 2. Expose the final value of the ELBO in the stanfit object result for each ADVI run (not just printing). Then if one ran multiple VB procedures, he/she could choose the best one based on comparing ELBO values. Note this is not model comparison but just a way of getting closer to the global optimum for a single model.
> 3. Allow "silent mode" to prevent so much output being printed. In parallel it would become jumbled.
>
> The way I am currently doing parallel ADVI is:
> 1. Wrap calls to vb() with parallel::mclapply() to parallelize
> 2. Redirect STDOUT for each ADVI instance to a string using capture.output()
> 3. Parse the strings to get the final ELBO values and use to choose the stanfit object based on highest ELBO among the parallel instances
>
> I can post this as an issue to github but wanted to get some feedback here first.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

it's the first time I write to this list and that is because I am still trying to understand if learning R and Stan could be worth the effort (I am new to both the main R language and, obviously, Stan) for what I am willing to try.

My idea is to try to fit a compartmental model for dynamic PET kinetic analysis (that is a system of 2 differential equation whose solution is then convoluted with the blood input function, check HERE  <http://www.turkupetcentre.net/petanalysis/model_compartmental_fitting.html>for a reference ) using a bayesian approach. I should have from literature a set of prior distributions to try out (and then hopefully extend of change) but I am not sure if Stan is suitable for such a task or not.

If it could be, then the following question would be "how" to do it, but I think and like to proceed one step at a time ...

I really hope you can open my eyes on the R world.

Kind regards,

Michele

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Modeling and fitting a compartmental model to emission tomography (PET) data
messages.body_plain:
Stan lets you fit models that involve parametric diff eqs.
The manual explains how and there's a case study for
soil carbon models here:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html

It was the first case study, so it's way at the bottom.

There is also a lot of tutorial material one level up under
"DOCS".

- Bob

> On Sep 19, 2016, at 1:24 PM, Michele Scipioni <scipioni...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Stan users,
>
> it's the first time I write to this list and that is because I am still trying to understand if learning R and Stan could be worth the effort (I am new to both the main R language and, obviously, Stan) for what I am willing to try.
>
> My idea is to try to fit a compartmental model for dynamic PET kinetic analysis (that is a system of 2 differential equation whose solution is then convoluted with the blood input function, check HERE for a reference ) using a bayesian approach. I should have from literature a set of prior distributions to try out (and then hopefully extend of change) but I am not sure if Stan is suitable for such a task or not.
>
> If it could be, then the following question would be "how" to do it, but I think and like to proceed one step at a time ...
>
> I really hope you can open my eyes on the R world.
>
> Kind regards,
>
> Michele
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Vectorizing with point-wise exponentiation
messages.body_plain:
Here is my actual file, which I've tried to improve given Daniel's suggestions. This doesn't seem to speed things up too much. The goal of this model is to fit two time-varying peaks (each with their own independent parameters) to a surface.

I'm wondering if there's still any way to further optimize this code. Given that the base of the exponents are dynamic and dependent on the previous time step, I don't think they can be easily pre-computed. Also, since the ^ operator is not vectorized I can't see how to easily vectorize this problem.

Any thoughts? I truly appreciate all of your help!

-M

> >
> > parameters{
> > real a[T];
> > real b[T];
> > ...

> >
> > In this case, the parameters are dependent on the fit at the previous time point. Would that make creating a transformed data parameter not possible?

>  290:            koi_rps_true[n] ~ radius_lpdf(lookup_tbl[n], nrow_lkup_tbl, x_lo, x_hi, x_linstep, x_this);

> Joe

> // This function does linear interpolation in a lookup table for log radius pdf
> // The lookup_tbl has to be provided as data.
>
>     real radius_lpdf(real[] lookup_tbl,
>                                 int nrow_lkup_tbl,
>                                 real x_lo,
>                                 real x_hi,

>         }
>         if( x_this < x_lo ) {

> On Wednesday, September 14, 2016 at 1:35:34 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If you define your functions with suffix _lpdf (real outcome)
> or _lpmf (discrete outcome), then you can use sampling notation.
> See the manual chapter on user-defined functions for details
> and examples.
>
> The reason we don't have the real to int conversion built in is
> that it breaks derivatives so you have to be very careful
> that the result of whatever you do is still continuously
> differentiable or Stan's HMC will have a hard time
> sampling through the discontinuity.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Sep 14, 2016, at 2:20 PM, Daniel Rosenbloom <daniel.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm not sure... I've never given it a try. I've always just used increment_log_prob (or now, the new target+=).
> >
> > I am glad that someone else can make use of our rather absurd typecasting-by-binary-search trick!
> >
> > On Wed, Sep 14, 2016 at 1:32 PM, Joseph Catanzarite <jcat...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you for taking the trouble to answer my question, Daniel!
> >
> > Question: once I build the function (say I call it error_distribution),
> >
> > can I then treat it as one of Stan's canned distribution functions and sample from it via a statement such as
> >
> > y ~ error_distribution
> >
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Joe

> > On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 7:16:09 PM UTC-7, Daniel Rosenbloom wrote:
> > Hi Joseph,
> >
> > So it ain't pretty, but here's what we had to do. First, you need to build a function that typecasts floats to ints, since doing so is not native to the Stan language. This function does so quickly, by binary search:
> >
> >     int as_integer_bsearch(real i_this, int size_max) {
> >         // Outputs int(floor(i_this)), assuming that i_this is non-negative
> >         int right_bound;
> >         int left_bound;
> >         int mid;
> >
> >         right_bound <- size_max;
> >         left_bound  <- 0;
> >         mid <- (right_bound + left_bound)/ 2; // int division intentional
> >
> >         // special case
> >         if(i_this == right_bound) {
> >             return right_bound;
> >         }
> >         if(i_this == left_bound) {
> >             return left_bound;
> >         }
> >
> >         while(mid != left_bound && mid != right_bound) {
> >             if( i_this < mid ) {
> >                 right_bound <- mid;
> >             }
> >             else {
> >                 left_bound <- mid;
> >             }
> >             mid <- (right_bound + left_bound)/ 2;
> >         }
> >         return mid;
> >     }
> >
> >
> > Then here is the function that does the interpolation. The lookup_tbl has to be provided as data. For our particular problem, we had one regime where linear interpolation made the most sense, and another for logarithmic. Note that we are also coding in the left and right tail behaviors for the function (log-pdf of the Landau distribution):
> >
> >
> >     real landau_logp(real[] lookup_tbl,
> >                                 int nrow_lkup_tbl,
> >                                 real x_lo,
> >                                 real x_hi,
> >                                 real x_linstep,
> >                                 real x_breakpt,
> >                                 int idx_breakpt,
> >                                 real x_log10step,
> >                                 real x_this) {
> >         // Outputs Landau logpdf, using linear interpolation (to left of breakpoint), log interpolation
> >         // (to right of breakpoint), or tail behavior.
> >         // lookup_tbl: Provided as data
> >         // nrow_lkup_tbl: # rows in lookup_tbl
> >         // x_lo, x_hi: Outside these bounds, use analytic formulas for tail behavior
> >         // x_breakpt: Below this value, lookup table is given in linear steps; above it is logarithmic
> >         // idx_breakpt: Index of the breakpoint in the table
> >         // x_linstep: Linear step size
> >         // x_log10step: Log10 step size
> >         // x_this: The value to compute
> >
> >         real log10_x_this;
> >         real x_a; // x-value to left of x_this in table
> >         int idx_a; // index of x_a in table
> >         real f_a; // log-prob of x_a
> >         real f_b; // log-prob of x_b (value to right of x_this in table)
> >         real perc; // Used in interpolation
> >
> >         if( x_this < -365) {
> >             return negative_infinity(); // at -365, log-prob is -5e306
> >         }
> >         if( x_this < x_lo ) {
> >             return -exp( pow(-x_this,1.20591) / 1.741504 ); // left tail behavior, determined numerically
> >         }
> >         if (x_this > x_hi) {
> >             return  -2 * log(x_this); // right tail behavior
> >         }
> >
> >         if(x_this > x_breakpt) {
> >             // Logarithmic interpolation (i.e., linear interpolation on log(x))
> >             log10_x_this <- log10(x_this);
> >             idx_a <- idx_breakpt + as_integer_bsearch((log10_x_this - log10(x_breakpt))/x_log10step, nrow_lkup_tbl);
> >             x_a <- x_breakpt * pow(10, x_log10step * (idx_a - idx_breakpt));
> >             perc <- (log10_x_this - log10(x_a)) / x_log10step;
> >         } else {
> >             // Linear interpolation
> >             idx_a <- 1 + as_integer_bsearch( (x_this - x_lo)/x_linstep, nrow_lkup_tbl);
> >             x_a   <- x_lo + x_linstep * (idx_a - 1);
> >             perc <- (x_this - x_a)/x_linstep;
> >         }
> >
> >         f_a <- lookup_tbl[idx_a];
> >         f_b <- lookup_tbl[idx_a+1];
> >
> >         return f_a  + (f_b - f_a) * perc;
> >     }
> >
> >
> > Hope this helps!
> >
> > Best,
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 8:51:29 PM UTC-4, Joseph Catanzarite wrote:
> > We have estimated posterior distributions of measurement errors for each observation in our data set.
> >
> > The posterior distributions are relatively smooth.
> >
> > When fitting our observations to a model, is there a way in Stan to sample from a lookup table containing these posteriors, in order to marginalize over measurement errors ?
> >
> > Thanks!

messages.subject: Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
messages.subject_clean: Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am running a large vector autoregression model with a t distribution on the coefficients to help variable selection.

If I understand correctly, the centered parameterisation and non-centered parameterisation give different modes (because the integral of the density function is the same between equivalent points but not the density function itself).

Sampling is quite slow due to the large size of the model, so I thought I would give optimisation a try. (Meanfield ADVI does not converge in a reasonable number of iterations and full rank ADVI doesn't work at all).

With the non-centered parameterisation, which I use for sampling, the outputs are nothing like with sampling, including predictive performance. When I use the centered parameterisation, the model parameters are much closer to the sampling outputs, and the predictive performance of the model is much more similar.

Is this expected behaviour?

Quite interesting...

Julian

> > >     int as_integer_bsearch(real i_this, int size_max) {
> > >         // Outputs int(floor(i_this)), assuming that i_this is non-negative
> > >         int right_bound;
> > >         int left_bound;
> > >         int mid;
> > >

> > >         }
> > >         if(i_this == left_bound) {
> > >             return left_bound;
> > >         }
> > >
> > >         while(mid != left_bound && mid != right_bound) {
> > >             if( i_this < mid ) {
> > >                 right_bound <- mid;
> > >             }
> > >             else {
> > >                 left_bound <- mid;
> > >             }

> > >         return mid;
> > >     }

> > > Then here is the function that does the interpolation. The lookup_tbl has to be provided as data. For our particular problem, we had one regime where linear interpolation made the most sense, and another for logarithmic. Note that we are also coding in the left and right tail behaviors for the function (log-pdf of the Landau distribution):
> > >
> > >
> > >     real landau_logp(real[] lookup_tbl,
> > >                                 int nrow_lkup_tbl,
> > >                                 real x_lo,
> > >                                 real x_hi,

> > >                                 int idx_breakpt,
> > >                                 real x_log10step,

> > >         // nrow_lkup_tbl: # rows in lookup_tbl
> > >         // x_lo, x_hi: Outside these bounds, use analytic formulas for tail behavior
> > >         // x_breakpt: Below this value, lookup table is given in linear steps; above it is logarithmic
> > >         // idx_breakpt: Index of the breakpoint in the table
> > >         // x_linstep: Linear step size
> > >         // x_log10step: Log10 step size
> > >         // x_this: The value to compute
> > >
> > >         real log10_x_this;
> > >         real x_a; // x-value to left of x_this in table
> > >         int idx_a; // index of x_a in table
> > >         real f_a; // log-prob of x_a
> > >         real f_b; // log-prob of x_b (value to right of x_this in table)
> > >         real perc; // Used in interpolation

> > >         if (x_this > x_hi) {

> > >         }
> > >
> > >         if(x_this > x_breakpt) {
> > >             // Logarithmic interpolation (i.e., linear interpolation on log(x))
> > >             log10_x_this <- log10(x_this);

> > >             x_a <- x_breakpt * pow(10, x_log10step * (idx_a - idx_breakpt));
> > >             perc <- (log10_x_this - log10(x_a)) / x_log10step;
> > >         } else {
> > >             // Linear interpolation
> > >             idx_a <- 1 + as_integer_bsearch( (x_this - x_lo)/x_linstep, nrow_lkup_tbl);

> > >             perc <- (x_this - x_a)/x_linstep;

> > >         f_a <- lookup_tbl[idx_a];
> > >         f_b <- lookup_tbl[idx_a+1];

> > >     }

On Tuesday, September 20, 2016 at 9:12:38 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Optimization drops any Jacobians due to constraints.

Why? I'm confused as I thought NUTS and optimization would use the same target?

> I wrote up a little case study:

That case study gives an impression that Stan would make a difference between likelihood and prior, although in other discussions it has been emphasized that inference algorithms see only the target (e,g, energy).
You could improve the case study by making it more clear when the Jacobian due to constraint is automatically added, when it is not automatically added (and when it is dropped?).

Aki

>
>   http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
>
> But it's hard to say more without the code and example data.
>
> And by nothing like, I take it you're comparing posterior modes
> to posterior means?  Those aren't necessarily going to be anywhere
> near each other (I have another case study explaining this in
> the works).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Sep 19, 2016, at 6:32 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello!
> >
> > I am running a large vector autoregression model with a t distribution on the coefficients to help variable selection.
> >
> > If I understand correctly, the centered parameterisation and non-centered parameterisation give different modes (because the integral of the density function is the same between equivalent points but not the density function itself).
> >
> > Sampling is quite slow due to the large size of the model, so I thought I would give optimisation a try. (Meanfield ADVI does not converge in a reasonable number of iterations and full rank ADVI doesn't work at all).
> >
> > With the non-centered parameterisation, which I use for sampling, the outputs are nothing like with sampling, including predictive performance. When I use the centered parameterisation, the model parameters are much closer to the sampling outputs, and the predictive performance of the model is much more similar.
> >
> > Is this expected behaviour?
> >
> > Quite interesting...
> >
> > Julian

# data processing
getwd()
setwd("C:/Users/n01066737/Desktop/Angela")
getwd()
crashdata<-read.csv(file.choose(), header = T)
crashdata
summary(crashdata)
names(crashdata)
str(crashdata)

### converting factor variables to as.factors
crashdata$time_indicator<-as.factor(crashdata$time_indicator)
crashdata$treatment<-as.factor(crashdata$treatment)
crashdata$median_type<-as.factor(crashdata$median_type)
crashdata$landuse<-as.factor(crashdata$landuse)
crashdata$speed<-as.factor(crashdata$speed)

### checking the structure after converting the factor variables

str(crashdata)

### loading the rstan package

library(rstan)

### creating dummy variables for factor variables

cat_time<-model.matrix(~crashdata$time_indicator, data=crashdata)
cat_treatment<-model.matrix(~crashdata$treatment, data=crashdata)
cat_median_type<-model.matrix(~crashdata$median_type, data=crashdata)
cat_landuse<-model.matrix(~crashdata$landuse, data=crashdata)
cat_speed<-model.matrix(~crashdata$speed, data=crashdata)

### specifying the poisson-gamma mixture model

negbin<-"
data{
int<lower=0> N;                           # rows of data
vector[N] cat_time;                       # predictor variable
vector[N] cat_treatment;                  # predictor variable
vector[N] cat_median_type;                # predictor variable
vector[N] cat_landuse;                    # predictor variable
vector[N] cat_speed;                      # predictor variable
vector[N] ln_maj_aadt;                    # predictor variable
vector[N] ln_min_aadt;                    # predictor variable
vector[N] no_lanes_maj;                   # predictor variable
vector[N] no_lanes_min;                   # predictor variable
vector[N] no_lanes_min;                   # predictor variable
vector[N] median_width;                   # predictor variable
int<lower=0> total_crashes[N];            # response variable
}

parameters {
real<lower=0> phi;      # negative binomial dispersion parameter
real beta0;             # intercept
real beta1;
real beta2;
real beta3;
real beta4;
real beta5;
real beta6;
real beta7;
real beta8;
real beta9;
real beta10;
}

model {
### priors
phi ~    cauchy(0.001,0.001);
beta0 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta1 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta2 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta3 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta4 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta5 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta6 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta7 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta8 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta9 ~  normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
beta10 ~ normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
# data model
total_crashes~ neg_binomial_2_log(beta0 + beta1*cat_time + beta2*cat_treatment + beta3*cat_median_type + beta4*cat_landuse + beta5*cat_speed + beta6*ln_maj_aadt + beta7*ln_min_aadt + beta8*no_lanes_maj + beta9*no_lanes_min +beta10*median_width, phi);
}
"
write(negbin, file="negbin-glm.stan")
sm<-stan_model("negbin-glm.stan")
set.seed(1000)
N<- 849
phi<-0.7349047
beta0<--3.150702
beta1<-0.0479721
beta2<-0.3503469
beta3<-0.0028539
beta4<--0.1059735
beta5<-0.6936886
beta6<-0.2642703
beta7<-0.121047
beta8<-0.0255357
beta9<-0.1235194
beta10<--0.0093531
expected_crashes<-sampling(sm, data=list(N=N, crashes=crashdata$total_crashes, cat_time=crashdata$time_indicator -mean((crashdata$time_indicator)), cat_treatment=crashdata$treatment-mean((crashdata$treatment)), cat_median_type=crashdata$median-type-mean((crashdata$median-type)), cat_landuse=crashdata$landuse-mean((crashdata$landuse)), cat_speed=crashdata$speed-mean((crashdata$speed)), ln_maj_aadt=crashdata$ln_aadt_maj-mean((crashdata$ln_aadt_maj)), ln_min_aadt=crashdata$ln_min_aadt-mean((crashdata$ln_min_aadt)), no_lanes_maj=crashdata$no_lanes_maj-mean((crashdata$no_lanes_maj)), no_lanes_min=crashdata$no_lanes_min-mean((crashdata$no_lanes_min)), median_width=crashdata$median_width-mean((crashdata$median_width))), pars=c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "beta3", "beta4", "beta5", "beta6", "beta7", "beta8", "beta9", "beta10", "phi"), iter=50000, warmup=20000, chains=1)
expected_crashes
# plot the output
rstan::traceplot(expected_crashes, inc_warmup=FALSE)
library(rstanarm)
library(shinystan)
launch_shinystan(expected_crashes)

On Friday, September 16, 2016 at 5:36:56 PM UTC+1, Mehdi Hosseini wrote:

> Hi there,
>
> I am working on an ordinal regression problem.
>

I don't understand the pmf you're trying to define or how ordinal
models relate to the negative binomial.  Specifically what the bit
after what looks like the negative binomial hurdle.

It sounds like what you might
have is a measurement error model, where someone says six months,
but the true value is somewhere between 3 months and 9 months with
some model of variation in the population.

If you get errors during initialization, it's from evaluating
the transformed parameters or model blocks.  Any value of
parameters meeting declared constraints should have finite log density.
It's almost always a problem with illegal data, wrong sizes, or parameters
which are constrained but not declared with the proper constraints.

We don't recommend those gamma(0.01, 0.01) priors.  Can you use
something more informative?

Otherwise, the efficiency of these models often comes down to
parameterization.

- Bob

I'd suggest starting with a simpler example and working up.
Or you can try to use print statements in the existing program
to see where things go wrong if you're not getting a specific
line number out.  Test with simulated data on the simpler thing
to make sure it works.

Usually sampling fails due to specific exceptions being
thrown in numerical methods that expect inputs in certain ranges
or will overflow and underflow.

Putting variables on very different scales, as in this:

  phi ~    cauchy(0.001,0.001);

can be problematic.  Ideally for speed and stability,
parameters posteriors will be roughly normal(0, 1)---otherwise,
we have to rescale during adaptation.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Missing data imputation in Stan (or RStan)
messages.body_plain:
There are two popular approaches that involve Bayesian methods:

* (multiple) imputation:  build a model to predict the missing
data, sample missing values from posterior to form an imputed
data set, then fit the actual model with full data (given plus
imputed);  perhaps do this for more than one imputation,
then combine the results.

* joint model: build a model of the data and the outcomes and
fit it all at once.

The joint model gives you a coherent full Bayesian framework.
That's what's described in the manual.

The multiple imputation approach is often easier and less
computationally intensive.  And it can be based on ad hoc models
rather than coherent joint models (for instance, you can impute
each predictor separately).  And you're right---no descriptions of
how to do multiple imputation in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
messages.body_plain:
Because sampling targets a conditional measure and optimization targets a conditional density.  They are fundamentally different objects and transform in different ways.  In particular, a MAP is not defined for a measure but rather a density in a specific parameterization, which is why we don't want to include Jacobians that change this density when we do temporary transformations behind the scenes.

Finally, I would recommend you use vector beta instead of setting coefficient one by one. You could use
data{
    int<lower = 0> N;                               # rows of data
    int<lower = 0> P;                               # colums of design matrix
    matrix[N, P] X;                                  # design matrix

    int<lower=0> total_crashes[N];         # response variable
}

parameters {
real<lower=0> phi;      # negative binomial dispersion parameter

vector[P] Beta;
}

model {
### priors
phi ~    cauchy(0, 0.1);
for (i in 1:P) {
  Beta[i] ~ normal(0.0, 1.0E4);
}
# data model
total_crashes~ neg_binomial_2_log(X*Beta, phi);
}

Best,

Lu Zhang

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thank you for your comments on this.

I modified the code as you suggested but the traces are still not mixing well. I used the exception mu=1e200, x<v to represent a big number as the lifetime should go to infinity and I thought it'd help the numerical integration. I have now removed this exception and, instead, handle these cases in the numerical integrations. I rewrote the p_w and p_W as lp_w and lp_W respectively, as you suggested. In the log-likelihood I used log1m_exp(lp_W) for the right-censored observations.

Any further ideas why the model refuses to converge?

Regards,
Joona

perjantai 16. syyskuuta 2016 2.15.40 UTC+3 Bob Carpenter kirjoitti:
> I don't know the specific model, but I'm familiar with
> the general idea of right-censoring in these situations as
> you describe and Stan should be able to fit such models.
> I can make a bunch of specific suggestions about how you can
> code Stan to be more robust.
>
> The normal density and cdf are built into Stan, as is
> the truncation you'd need for censored observations.  So you
> shouldn't be defining norm_pdf and norm_cdf.  Also, you want
> to work on the log scale, not on the linear scale.  For
> example, rather than summing a normal_pdf, you want to
> log_sum_exp built-in normal_lpdf.   It's much more arithmetically
> stable.
>
> That mu function can be dangerous because it's discontinuous
> at the point x = v.  I'm not sure why you think you need that
> 1e200 return, which is enormous and won't have a derivative.
> We also have stable versions of log(exp(x) - exp(v)) built in
>
>
>   log_diff_exp(x, v) = log(exp(x) - exp(v))
>
> and it'll be more stable than applying exp directly.
>
> Your p_w function also has discontinuities.  Stan assumes that
> the log density you define is continuously differentiable.
>
> You can't declare a parameter
>
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>
> and then use
>
>   log(sigma) ~ normal(0, 1);
>
> because the log transform requires a Jacobian.  Instead,
> you should be using
>
>   sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
>
> which builds in the Jacobian.
>
> I also see you have some densities on non-unit scales:
>
>   b0 ~ normal(70, 35);
>   b1 ~ normal(-10, 5);
>   mu_v ~ normal(log(200), log(0.2^2 + 1));
>
> This can make it hard for Stan to do adaptation as it has
> to find the scale.  One thing you can do to make this sample
> better is to declare b0_raw and use
>
>   b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>
> and set
>
>   b0 = b0_raw * 35 + 70;
>
> That puts the actual parameter being sampled, b0_raw,
> on the unit scale.
>
> You never want to do log(1 - u) for any u;  use the
> built in log1m(u), which is more stable.  But really don't want
> to take the log of p_w, you want to define p_w on the
> log scale directly using log_sum_exp.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Sep 15, 2016, at 2:13 AM, joona....@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > I'm trying to reproduce Random Fatigue-Limit model (Pascual & Meeker 1999, Ryan 2003 doi: 10.1198/1061860032012) using pystan. I get the model (attached .py code) to run without errors but the traces (attached picture) look like it didn't converge.
> >
> > The model describes specimen lifetime as function of stress level. There is thought to be a fatigue limit which is stochastic variable that defines whether the component will have finite lifetime or not. The joint distribution of (log(lifetime) w, fatigue limit) ~ N(b0 + b1*log(stress - fatigue_limit), sigma), and log(fatigue_limit) = v ~ N(mu_v, sigma_v). Ryan states: "When collecting fatigue data, it is possible to observe a Žfinite value of W exactly or to observe an interval that contains W. But V is not observable. Thus, for purposes of estimating \theta via methods involving a likelihood, it is necessary to obtain the marginal distribution of W. This distribution has both a continuous and a discrete component.". And because of this there is integration performed on the joint distribution to get the marginal distribution of the log(lifetime) w.
> >
> > Right-censorship is needed because in practice one can't wait forever for the specimen to break. These interrupted tests, called run-outs, form the discrete component of the marginal distribution of W.
> >
> > Is this model possible to be modeled in stan? My code (137 lines, including test-data) is attached. I have used the functions block to describe the puzzle pieces for the custom likelihood and numerical (trapezoidal) integration of the marginal distribution.
> >
> > Thank you!
> > Joona

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,
let me explain the problem with further details.
Let's say there are a set of predictors, e.g. age and gender, and a response variable y which is censored and accepts one of the values from {never, once a year, once a month, once a week, etc}. There is also a latent variable y* with a hurdle negative binomial distribution that underlies the censored variable y using a set of cut-points θ as below

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-OnO2cRWr3II/V-JkGYbcbiI/AAAAAAAAAxQ/OLObL8EvjSMScKlaUEae0H6mXlkwlRYYgCLcB/s1600/d22a7fae381e77057095b4c990a31e9737f81c60.png>

The predictors as well as the censored variable are our observable. The latent variable, expressed by its mean and dispersion parameters, and the outpoints are our unknowns. We try to relate the predictors to the response variable via the latent variable and the cut-points. The following figure (copyright(c), 2014 by John Kruschke and Elsevier) resembles our problem. The only difference is the distribution of the latent variable which in our case is hurdle negative binomial.

As I said before, I have a maximum likelihood solution, where the cut-points are fixed and assumed to be known, following the paper of James S. McGinley et.al <http://et.al>, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25857717. However, in our case, the cut-points are based on a set of censored answers to a survey question. Someone says once a month, but the true answer is somewhere between twice a month and once every two months.
I am hoping to use stan to estimate the cut-points along with the latent variable's parameters using Bayesian inference.

On Tuesday, September 20, 2016 at 5:53:41 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't understand the pmf you're trying to define or how ordinal
> models relate to the negative binomial.  Specifically what the bit
> after what looks like the negative binomial hurdle.
>
> It sounds like what you might
> have is a measurement error model, where someone says six months,
> but the true value is somewhere between 3 months and 9 months with
> some model of variation in the population.
>
> If you get errors during initialization, it's from evaluating
> the transformed parameters or model blocks.  Any value of
> parameters meeting declared constraints should have finite log density.
> It's almost always a problem with illegal data, wrong sizes, or parameters
> which are constrained but not declared with the proper constraints.
>
> We don't recommend those gamma(0.01, 0.01) priors.  Can you use
> something more informative?
>
> Otherwise, the efficiency of these models often comes down to
> parameterization.
>
> - Bob

Hi,

If I understood correctly, this is what I did:
transformed parameters {
    real b0;
    real b1;
    real mu_v;
    b0 = b0_raw*35 + 75;
    b1 = b1_raw*5 - 10;
    mu_v = sqrt(log(0.2^2+1))*mu_v_raw + log(200);
    }
model {
    sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
    b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    b1_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    mu_v_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma_v ~ lognormal(0, 1);
    target += L(c, w, x, b0, b1, mu_v, sigma_v, sigma, N);
}

It first resulted in this kind of error:
"""
Rejecting initial value:
  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity.
  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value.

Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
"""
I added some prints to find out that my log-likelihood was giving nan's. This was fixed when I started using negative_infinity() in the numerical integration for the cases where log(0) was expected.

The code, promisingly, took longer time to run. Chain #2 was finished in 291 seconds (Total), Chain #1 took 2151 seconds, Chain #3 4182 seconds and Chain #0 4517 seconds. When I look at the traces it looks like one of the chains looks promising whereas others have remained constant value. I noticed that the chains were threaded to run on different cpus.

Any further tips on getting this to run and/or improve robustness? Would it be possible to utilize greater amount of cpus in parallel environments like computational cluster (parallelize the for-loops of the numerical integration)? Perhaps if I get this to work I should look at the ADVI for performance.

Regards,
Joona

keskiviikko 21. syyskuuta 2016 9.55.44 UTC+3 Andrew Gelman kirjoitti:
> Hi, I haven't looked at the detials but I'd suggest putting parameters on unit scale so you should not be having parameters such as 1e200 or even log(200) or log(75).  Put everything on unit scale and then you can use weakly informative priors such as normal(0,1) and you might get some stability.
> A
> > On Sep 21, 2016, at 2:52 AM, joona....@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > Thank you for your comments on this.
> >
> > I modified the code as you suggested but the traces are still not mixing well. I used the exception mu=1e200, x<v to represent a big number as the lifetime should go to infinity and I thought it'd help the numerical integration. I have now removed this exception and, instead, handle these cases in the numerical integrations. I rewrote the p_w and p_W as lp_w and lp_W respectively, as you suggested. In the log-likelihood I used log1m_exp(lp_W) for the right-censored observations.
> >
> > Any further ideas why the model refuses to converge?
> >
> > Regards,
> > Joona
> >
> > perjantai 16. syyskuuta 2016 2.15.40 UTC+3 Bob Carpenter kirjoitti:
> > > I don't know the specific model, but I'm familiar with
> > > the general idea of right-censoring in these situations as
> > > you describe and Stan should be able to fit such models.
> > > I can make a bunch of specific suggestions about how you can
> > > code Stan to be more robust.
> > >
> > > The normal density and cdf are built into Stan, as is
> > > the truncation you'd need for censored observations.  So you
> > > shouldn't be defining norm_pdf and norm_cdf.  Also, you want
> > > to work on the log scale, not on the linear scale.  For
> > > example, rather than summing a normal_pdf, you want to
> > > log_sum_exp built-in normal_lpdf.   It's much more arithmetically
> > > stable.
> > >
> > > That mu function can be dangerous because it's discontinuous
> > > at the point x = v.  I'm not sure why you think you need that
> > > 1e200 return, which is enormous and won't have a derivative.
> > > We also have stable versions of log(exp(x) - exp(v)) built in
> > >
> > >
> > >   log_diff_exp(x, v) = log(exp(x) - exp(v))
> > >
> > > and it'll be more stable than applying exp directly.
> > >
> > > Your p_w function also has discontinuities.  Stan assumes that
> > > the log density you define is continuously differentiable.
> > >
> > > You can't declare a parameter
> > >
> > >   real<lower=0> sigma;
> > >
> > > and then use
> > >
> > >   log(sigma) ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >
> > > because the log transform requires a Jacobian.  Instead,
> > > you should be using
> > >
> > >   sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
> > >
> > > which builds in the Jacobian.
> > >
> > > I also see you have some densities on non-unit scales:
> > >
> > >   b0 ~ normal(70, 35);
> > >   b1 ~ normal(-10, 5);
> > >   mu_v ~ normal(log(200), log(0.2^2 + 1));
> > >
> > > This can make it hard for Stan to do adaptation as it has
> > > to find the scale.  One thing you can do to make this sample
> > > better is to declare b0_raw and use
> > >
> > >   b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >
> > > and set
> > >
> > >   b0 = b0_raw * 35 + 70;
> > >
> > > That puts the actual parameter being sampled, b0_raw,
> > > on the unit scale.
> > >
> > > You never want to do log(1 - u) for any u;  use the
> > > built in log1m(u), which is more stable.  But really don't want
> > > to take the log of p_w, you want to define p_w on the
> > > log scale directly using log_sum_exp.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Sep 15, 2016, at 2:13 AM, joona....@gmail.com wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > I'm trying to reproduce Random Fatigue-Limit model (Pascual & Meeker 1999, Ryan 2003 doi: 10.1198/1061860032012) using pystan. I get the model (attached .py code) to run without errors but the traces (attached picture) look like it didn't converge.
> > > >
> > > > The model describes specimen lifetime as function of stress level. There is thought to be a fatigue limit which is stochastic variable that defines whether the component will have finite lifetime or not. The joint distribution of (log(lifetime) w, fatigue limit) ~ N(b0 + b1*log(stress - fatigue_limit), sigma), and log(fatigue_limit) = v ~ N(mu_v, sigma_v). Ryan states: "When collecting fatigue data, it is possible to observe a Žfinite value of W exactly or to observe an interval that contains W. But V is not observable. Thus, for purposes of estimating \theta via methods involving a likelihood, it is necessary to obtain the marginal distribution of W. This distribution has both a continuous and a discrete component.". And because of this there is integration performed on the joint distribution to get the marginal distribution of the log(lifetime) w.
> > > >
> > > > Right-censorship is needed because in practice one can't wait forever for the specimen to break. These interrupted tests, called run-outs, form the discrete component of the marginal distribution of W.
> > > >
> > > > Is this model possible to be modeled in stan? My code (137 lines, including test-data) is attached. I have used the functions block to describe the puzzle pieces for the custom likelihood and numerical (trapezoidal) integration of the marginal distribution.
> > > >
> > > > Thank you!
> > > > Joona

On Wednesday, September 21, 2016 at 5:34:02 AM UTC-4, Dung Tran wrote:
> it gives an error: integer parameters or transformed parameters are not allowed. But I cannot specify real numbers because of the model: adl[i] ~ ordered_logistic(mu, cutpoints), i.e., the response here adl, has to be integer.

Well, HMC cannot have integer unknowns because integers are not differentiable. For missingness in an outcome only, you can introduce a latent utility variable that is constrained to be between the appropriate, albeit unknown, cutpoints when the outcome is observed and is unconstrained when the outcome is missing. However, this approach is quite difficult and may not sample particularly well.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Users!

I am trying to implement an ordered probit model in Stan that is described by John Kruschke (Doing Bayesian Data Analysis, Chapter 23 and briefly here <http://doingbayesiandataanalysis.blogspot.co.uk/2014/11/ordinal-probit-regression-transforming.html>) and written in JAGS (see code attached). The model runs well in JAGS for non-hierarchical models, but crawls for hierarchical problems with larger data sets (e.g. cumulative threshold mixed models incorporating heterogeneous variances/location-scale models, see here  <http://download.springer.com/static/pdf/470/art%253A10.1186%252F1297-9686-28-3-249.pdf?originUrl=http%3A%2F%2Fgsejournal.biomedcentral.com%2Farticle%2F10.1186%2F1297-9686-28-3-249&token2=exp=1474476681~acl=%2Fstatic%2Fpdf%2F470%2Fart%25253A10.1186%25252F1297-9686-28-3-249.pdf*~hmac=bb30b66d59e8257ff4f0093d5e8fe7688d365bf5b01017aba41e644d60e24830>or here <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2847414/>).

Diverging from the typical ordered probit model using the unit cumulative normal distribution, and the one presented in section 6.7 of the Stan Manual, Kruschke's model fixes the first and last thresholds/cut-points to constants so that the location and scale of the cumulative normal distribution can be estimated. To do this, a vector of thresholds are supplied in the data list ('thresh' in the model code attached), with the fixed thresholds denoted with constants and the remaining thresholds as NA/missing.

I have attempted this approach in Stan (see attachment for Stan and JAGS code), but Stan throws an error when missing data is supplied in the threshold vector. Thanks for pointing out the error in our manual.  It'll
be fixed for the next release:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2051#issuecomment-248715502

to summarize, you need to redeclare beta as a matrix:

parameters {
  matrix[J, K] beta;

and then use the sampling statement:

  y ~ normal(rows_dot_product(x, beta[jj]), sigma);

beta[jj] will be an N x K matrix, and x is an N x K matrix
and the rows-dot-product operation means you take each
of the N rows and dot-product their K-vectors to get a scalar,
so the result is an N-vector.

- Bob

Thanks.

We strongly recommend not including Stan programs in R
programs as strings because you lose line numbers in messages, and
you either lose transpose (') or quotes for print (").  I'd also
recommend following our layout style (follows Google C++ style),
but that's up to you;  the non-standard layouts are harder for us
to follow and they almost all use too much vertical space for
the number of lines of code.

Also, you probably meant "book" instead of "bppk" in the comment.

We'd also suggest putting priors directly on scale (sigma)
rather than squared scale (your sigma2).  See the manual chapter
on regression for recommendations.

You can make mu a local variable inside the model, or even replace
mu with B * theta in the normal sampling statement, which will cut
down on the output.

We're happy to accept working case studies with some text explanation
of what's going on.  I particularly like replications of work that's
appeared elsewhere, becuase we can check we're getting the right answer.

messages.body_plain:
We don't have any parallelization built in.  You'd have to
access the C++ level and work there with a parallel interface
and be very very careful to synchronize anything that touches
autodiff.

If the sampler is getting stuck, running more chains or making
them faster won't help---the problem needs an alternative
parameterization.  Getting stuck is almost always due to their
being a highly curved volume of the posterior where Stan's
adapted step size is too large.

- Bob

>> perjantai 16. syyskuuta 2016 2.15.40 UTC+3 Bob Carpenter kirjoitti:
>> I don't know the specific model, but I'm familiar with
>> the general idea of right-censoring in these situations as
>> you describe and Stan should be able to fit such models.
>> I can make a bunch of specific suggestions about how you can
>> code Stan to be more robust.
>>
>> The normal density and cdf are built into Stan, as is
>> the truncation you'd need for censored observations.  So you
>> shouldn't be defining norm_pdf and norm_cdf.  Also, you want
>> to work on the log scale, not on the linear scale.  For
>> example, rather than summing a normal_pdf, you want to
>> log_sum_exp built-in normal_lpdf.   It's much more arithmetically
>> stable.
>>
>> That mu function can be dangerous because it's discontinuous
>> at the point x = v.  I'm not sure why you think you need that
>> 1e200 return, which is enormous and won't have a derivative.
>> We also have stable versions of log(exp(x) - exp(v)) built in
>>
>>
>>   log_diff_exp(x, v) = log(exp(x) - exp(v))
>>
>> and it'll be more stable than applying exp directly.
>>
>> Your p_w function also has discontinuities.  Stan assumes that
>> the log density you define is continuously differentiable.
>>
>> You can't declare a parameter
>>
>>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>>
>> and then use
>>
>>   log(sigma) ~ normal(0, 1);
>>
>> because the log transform requires a Jacobian.  Instead,
>> you should be using
>>
>>   sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
>>
>> which builds in the Jacobian.
>>
>> I also see you have some densities on non-unit scales:
>>
>>   b0 ~ normal(70, 35);
>>   b1 ~ normal(-10, 5);
>>   mu_v ~ normal(log(200), log(0.2^2 + 1));
>>
>> This can make it hard for Stan to do adaptation as it has
>> to find the scale.  One thing you can do to make this sample
>> better is to declare b0_raw and use
>>
>>   b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>>
>> and set
>>
>>   b0 = b0_raw * 35 + 70;
>>
>> That puts the actual parameter being sampled, b0_raw,
>> on the unit scale.
>>
>> You never want to do log(1 - u) for any u;  use the
>> built in log1m(u), which is more stable.  But really don't want
>> to take the log of p_w, you want to define p_w on the
>> log scale directly using log_sum_exp.
>>
>> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Are you all set or was there a further question?  If
you want to estimate true values given censoring, you
need to either integrate out the possible true values or
declare a parameter with appropriate constraints and sample.

- Bob

> On Sep 21, 2016, at 6:41 AM, Mehdi Hosseini <mehd...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
> let me explain the problem with further details.
> Let's say there are a set of predictors, e.g. age and gender, and a response variable y which is censored and accepts one of the values from {never, once a year, once a month, once a week, etc}. There is also a latent variable y* with a hurdle negative binomial distribution that underlies the censored variable y using a set of cut-points θ as below
>
>

> The predictors as well as the censored variable are our observable. The latent variable, expressed by its mean and dispersion parameters, and the outpoints are our unknowns. We try to relate the predictors to the response variable via the latent variable and the cut-points. The following figure (copyright(c), 2014 by John Kruschke and Elsevier) resembles our problem. The only difference is the distribution of the latent variable which in our case is hurdle negative binomial.
>
>

> As I said before, I have a maximum likelihood solution, where the cut-points are fixed and assumed to be known, following the paper of James S. McGinley et.al <http://et.al>, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25857717. However, in our case, the cut-points are based on a set of censored answers to a survey question. Someone says once a month, but the true answer is somewhere between twice a month and once every two months.
> I am hoping to use stan to estimate the cut-points along with the latent variable's parameters using Bayesian inference.
>
>
> On Tuesday, September 20, 2016 at 5:53:41 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't understand the pmf you're trying to define or how ordinal
> models relate to the negative binomial.  Specifically what the bit
> after what looks like the negative binomial hurdle.
>
> It sounds like what you might
> have is a measurement error model, where someone says six months,
> but the true value is somewhere between 3 months and 9 months with
> some model of variation in the population.
>
> If you get errors during initialization, it's from evaluating
> the transformed parameters or model blocks.  Any value of
> parameters meeting declared constraints should have finite log density.
> It's almost always a problem with illegal data, wrong sizes, or parameters
> which are constrained but not declared with the proper constraints.
>
> We don't recommend those gamma(0.01, 0.01) priors.  Can you use
> something more informative?
>
> Otherwise, the efficiency of these models often comes down to
> parameterization.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lawrence

The number and place of knots is solved by using Penalty in B-Spline. When we use Penalty in B-Spline, we can choose a large number of knots (about 10 to 20 is recommended) to ensure the desired flexibility. In fact, the penalty control the variance of estimated parameters. If change "num_knots= 20" in attached file (for instance 15 , 30), you will see the results do not change much.

Comparing GPR and Penalized B-Spline is a good idea. I will do it as soon as possible and inform you. If you have the Stan model of GPR, please send me it.

- Bistoon
