Hi Tran,

Thanks. The reason I am interested in fixing the first and last thresholds is that, as explained by John Krusckhe (see the original post), is that the mean and sd can be estimated from the data and interpreted on the latent scale. So, rather than estimating different intercepts (1 less than the number of categories) from the data, as is most common in statistical packages, we have one intercept that is the average of the latent scale. I find this much more interpretable, and would like to know if it can be implemented in Stan similar to JAGS.

I should mention that one user (Oscar Giles) I spoke to off the forum has implemented the Kruschke-style model by algebraically manipulating the Stan manual model to satisfy the different constraints of fixed first and last thresholds (using the functions Kruschke has written about on his blog; see the original post for the link).

I read the manual for the reparameterization and looked through the section 22.6 funnel example to find out the kind of normalization that Andrew already suggested.

I tried re-introducing the exception for the cases where -log(0) is expected to the mu-function now using the positive_infinity() to perhaps help further avoiding nan's.

This time I had two chains mixing (trace_v4.png). I also plotted the correlations of the parameters (correlations_v4.png) and from these two chains that were mixing I tried plotting the predictive fit (fit_v4.png).

In the correlations plot it seems like the two chains are distinct as (mu_v, sigma_v) clusters are separated.

In the model the fatigue limit (_v) parameters should be the cause of all trouble as they produce the discontinuity in the prediction. messages.body_plain:
Usually when a chain gets stuck it's because you haven't
explored enough of the posterior during warmup and wound up
with a too-high stepsize.  HMC assumes the posterior is
continuously differentiable everywhere; jumps can pose
problems for the sampler being able to move.

You can try increasing adapt_delta (target acceptance
rate) and lowering stepsize (initial step size for adaptation).
Both can help with mixing, but if the problem is pathological,
you either need to rethink the model or reparameterize.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If the question is how to create a vector with fixed first
and last position, you can do that with transformed parameters
in Stan a number of different ways.  One would be to use
a scaled simplex:

data {
  real L;
  real<lower = L> U;
  int<lower = 3> K;  // number of cutpoints
  ...

transformed data {
  real<lower = 0> diff;
  diff = U - L;
  ...

parameters {
  simplex[K - 1] cuts_raw;
  ...

transformed parameters {
  ordered[K] cuts;

  cuts[1] = L;
  cuts[2:K] = L + diff * cumulative_sum(cuts_raw);

- Bob

> On Sep 22, 2016, at 6:57 AM, Conor Goold <cg1...@bristol.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> Hi Tran,
>
> Thanks. The reason I am interested in fixing the first and last thresholds is that, as explained by John Krusckhe (see the original post), is that the mean and sd can be estimated from the data and interpreted on the latent scale. So, rather than estimating different intercepts (1 less than the number of categories) from the data, as is most common in statistical packages, we have one intercept that is the average of the latent scale. I find this much more interpretable, and would like to know if it can be implemented in Stan similar to JAGS.
>
> I should mention that one user (Oscar Giles) I spoke to off the forum has implemented the Kruschke-style model by algebraically manipulating the Stan manual model to satisfy the different constraints of fixed first and last thresholds (using the functions Kruschke has written about on his blog; see the original post for the link).
>
> On Thursday, 22 September 2016 11:00:31 UTC+1, Dung Tran wrote:
> Hi Conor,
>
> I am also running ordinal variable in Stan. As in JAGS, I always allow the cutpoints (thresholds) are unknown and will be estimated from the data. To do that, I think, we should remove the intercept from 'mu'. It means you should remove the 'alpha' from mu[i] <- alpha + beta * x[i]. Actually the number of cutpoints is equal to the number of categories - 1. Then using 'cate-1' cutpoints, then we do not to fix anything. That is what I am doing.
>
> Best,
> Tran.
>

messages.subject: Parallel chains in RStan
messages.subject_clean: Parallel chains in RStan
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

I'm running different sets of data on the same model in different chains in parallel,
this can for example be very useful if you are doing some sort of cross validation on your model.

One way of doing this is for example :
s1 <- stan_model(model_code = hcode) # compile the model
library(parallel)
sflist <-
  mclapply(1:36, mc.cores = 36,
           function(i) sampling(object = s1, data = foo_data[[i]], chains = 1,
                                chain_id = i, iter = 1000, warmup = 350,seed = seed))

But if you do it with the mclapply from the parallel package, you can't see the progress bars in Rstudio.
So in the newest version of Stan it is actually possible to run chains in parallel(without the parallel package), but I can't figure out if I can input a list of different data sets to run on in parallel(foo_data[[i]]), without the parallel package.

So can I do this with only the sampling function? And if not, can you show me how you did get the output to be printed in the console of Rstudio so I can implement this?

Best regards,
Jökull Snæbjarnarson

We try to relate the predictors to the response variable via the latent variable and the cut-points. The following figure (copyright(c), 2014 by John Kruschke and Elsevier) resembles our problem. The only difference is the distribution of the latent variable which in our case is hurdle negative binomial.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > As I said before, I have a maximum likelihood solution, where the cut-points are fixed and assumed to be known, following the paper of James S. McGinley et.al <http://et.al>, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25857717. However, in our case, the cut-points are based on a set of censored answers to a survey question. Someone says once a month, but the true answer is somewhere between twice a month and once every two months.
> > > > > I am hoping to use stan to estimate the cut-points along with the latent variable's parameters using Bayesian inference.

> > > > > after what looks like the negative binomial hurdle.

> > > > > some model of variation in the population.
> > > > >
> > > > > If you get errors during initialization, it's from evaluating
> > > > > the transformed parameters or model blocks.  Any value of
> > > > > parameters meeting declared constraints should have finite log density.
> > > > > It's almost always a problem with illegal data, wrong sizes, or parameters

> > > > >

messages.subject: Using init values with ADVI (vb) or BFGS (optimizing) to compute a regularization path
messages.subject_clean: Using init values with ADVI (vb) or BFGS (optimizing) to compute a regularization path
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan experts,

I have a model that includes what might be normally described as a random effects component. That is, there is a batch of coefficients that are modeled (in this case, with t-distribution), which induces some shrinkage or regularization of those coefficients.

I'm interested in using the exact same model, but where I just set the scale parameters for that distribution, rather than learning them from the data. And, in fact, I want to fit variations on the model for a whole set of possible values of those scale parameters. You can think of this as wanting to fit an entire regularization path where we are treating those scale parameters as tuning parameters. These would then be tuned using a held out sample / cross-validation as part of a larger procedure.

Is this something others have used Stan for? It seems like I could use the init parameter to vb/optimizing to use the results from some prior point in the path to initialize the next run.

However, looking at how the ELBO convergence diagnostic works, I wonder if this will end up resulting in much longer runs than needed in order for convergence to be detected, since tol_rel_obj is defined with respect to the change in ELBO from the start, correct? Maybe BFGS would work better.

Thanks for any pointers on this topic. I know what I'm doing isn't very Bayesian, but seemed like a nice way to do regularization with an arbitrary model.

Best,
Dean

Dean Eckles
Assistant Professor
MIT Sloan School of Management

On Fri, Sep 23, 2016 at 12:53 AM, Dean Eckles <eck...@mit.edu> wrote:
> Is this something others have used Stan for? It seems like I could use the init parameter to vb/optimizing to use the results from some prior point in the path to initialize the next run.

Yes. For this type of model, I'd highly suggest thinking about the model and building it up very carefully. After that, run NUTS. I would not trust the vb/optimizing estimates because that's not what you're looking for.

> However, looking at how the ELBO convergence diagnostic works, I wonder if this will end up resulting in much longer runs than needed in order for convergence to be detected, since tol_rel_obj is defined with respect to the change in ELBO from the start, correct? Maybe BFGS would work better.

Eh. The problem you described should be fit with full Bayes. If you specify it correctly, the full Bayes model in Stan will do a good enough job and quickly enough.

>
> Thanks for any pointers on this topic. I know what I'm doing isn't very Bayesian, but seemed like a nice way to do regularization with an arbitrary model.

That's fine. If that's what you want to do, the language is flexible enough to specify that particular model. If you understand the properties of the model implemented and the inference algorithms, we encourage it.

Daniel

Hi Daniel,

Sure!  I'm lucky to find that I keep a copy of all the error during the debugging.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using init values with ADVI (vb) or BFGS (optimizing) to compute a regularization path
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using init values with ADVI (vb) or BFGS (optimizing) to compute a regularization path
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dean.  Believe it or not, your idea is very close to something I've been interested in for awhile, using Stan to fit models with preset values of key hyperparameters, then doing some sort of approximate integration and model averaging.   Most of the others in the Stan team hate this idea but I think it has a lot of promise.  So maybe we can talk about this one together and either prove 'em all wrong or, more likely, go down in flames!
Andrew

P.S.  There's also been some talk about instituting a conjugate gradient optimizer in Stan.

> On Sep 22, 2016, at 6:53 PM, Dean Eckles <eck...@mit.edu> wrote:
>

> Hi Stan experts,
>
> I have a model that includes what might be normally described as a random effects component. That is, there is a batch of coefficients that are modeled (in this case, with t-distribution), which induces some shrinkage or regularization of those coefficients.
>
> I'm interested in using the exact same model, but where I just set the scale parameters for that distribution, rather than learning them from the data. And, in fact, I want to fit variations on the model for a whole set of possible values of those scale parameters. You can think of this as wanting to fit an entire regularization path where we are treating those scale parameters as tuning parameters. These would then be tuned using a held out sample / cross-validation as part of a larger procedure.
>
> Is this something others have used Stan for? It seems like I could use the init parameter to vb/optimizing to use the results from some prior point in the path to initialize the next run.
>
> However, looking at how the ELBO convergence diagnostic works, I wonder if this will end up resulting in much longer runs than needed in order for convergence to be detected, since tol_rel_obj is defined with respect to the change in ELBO from the start, correct? Maybe BFGS would work better.
>
> Thanks for any pointers on this topic. I know what I'm doing isn't very Bayesian, but seemed like a nice way to do regularization with an arbitrary model.
>
> Best,
> Dean
>
> Dean Eckles
> Assistant Professor
> MIT Sloan School of Management
>

BFGS does sound like what you’re looking for at the moment. This would also be most closely related to how others calculate parameter estimates along a regularization path.

The convergence diagnostics for MCMC and VI will be more conservative than necessary for this type of calculation, so it would be relatively slow (if that’s a concern on your model+dataset). There’s also a practical issue, which is that with the current ADVI interface, you can only initialize the mean parameters of the normal approximation. The standard deviation parameters will always be learnt from scratch.

Dustin

Thanks for these replies, Daniel and Andrew. I appreciate the guidance about worrying about whether to trust the variational results. (Maybe I should see how well they agree with NUTS in my cases. I did that, but pretty informally.)

Two pieces of additional background that might clarify my choice not to use NUTS:
1. While fitting a single model doesn't take terribly long, I also want to use this as part of a simulation study, so I intend on running this (that is, the whole regularization path) many thousands of times. And NUTS is pretty slow by comparison (hey, I know it is actually fast by other comparisons!). And I really only need the point estimate right now.
2. The likelihood in this model doesn't correspond to my loss function. I'm doing causal inference and have another cross-validation procedure I'm using to try to make some bias–variance tradeoffs with respect to the relevant loss function.

Andrew, glad to hear you're interested. Using a Bayesian framework like Stan can make is easy to implement lots of arbitrary models, some parts of which I might want to pick via some non-Bayesian data-driven method. ML folks are always noting the nice Bayesian interpretations of their regularization paths, maybe we can note the nice regularization paths generated by tuning a hyperparameter in our otherwise fully Bayesian models. Happy to chat more when I'm next at Columbia if not before then.

Best,
Dean

messages.subject: Scale-free parameters
messages.subject_clean: Scale-free parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

Just some off-line communication between Camelia, Andrew, Mike and myself that probably belongs on Stan-Users.

Camelia sent through an interesting question on scale-free parameters:

Original message (Camelia):

Hi Jim, hope all is well and you're enjoying fall in NY!

I think I have come across an untamed part of stan, and was wondering if you had any insights.

I'm trying to understand the idea of using 'scale-free' parameters. Gelman says "Aim to keep all parameters scale-free. [A way to do this is to] scale by some conventional value, for example if a parameter has a "typical" value of 4.5, you could work with log(theta/4.5) ". Full post here: http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/189970/in-bayesian-linear-regression-why-do-we-assume-parameter-prior-has-zero-mean

My questions are

- Does this apply to transformed parameters?

- If a parameter has a typical value of 4.5, why can we not instead set a weak prior centered at 4.5 ? (assuming 4.5 makes sense)

- In the context of the problem I'm working on, I need to infer the parameters of a Beta(a, b) distribution. Here is a snippet below. lambda[i] is typically around 10, which leads to a large value for b, which is what I want. According to Gelman, I should be "working with" lambda[i]/10 though. The exponent term makes me a bit nervous; the prior on this is, I think, overly sensitive, and I sometimes see bi-modalities in lambda_r.

transformed parameters {
// signal distribution parameters
phi[i] <- inv_logit(phi_r[r[i]] + phi_d[d[i]]);
lambda[i] <- 1 + exp(lambda_r[r[i]] + lambda_d[d[i]]);

// transformed signal distribution parameters
a <- lambda[i] * phi[i];
b <- lambda[i] * (1 - phi[i]);

// implied search and hit rates
search_rate[i] <- beta_ccdf(t_i[i], a, b);
hit_rate[i] <- beta_conditional_mean(t_i[i], a, b);
}

I haven't been able to find much in the way of explanation of "scale-free" parameters online. If you have any insights / any this makes sense, would be super helpful!
c.

My response:

Hey Camelia -

I've included Andrew and Mike in the email, who can probably provide a more thoughtful response. Also, I'd encourage you to post interesting questions like this on Stan-users.

I've always understood the quest for scale-free priors as some transformation we want to make to the data or parameters so that a) the geometry of the posterior (params, not transformed params) is easy for HMC to navigate b) the scale of your data don't upset the quality of the model fit. If we make transformations to the data, it's important not to implicitly be informing your prior with data (which is probably the case if you convert your data to z-scores--this is irrelevant to your particular problem, but I found it interesting when I learned it).

This might be helpful:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/scale-free|sort:relevance/stan-users/FjWL2290A5w/X0_tjLFbBgAJ <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/scale-free%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/FjWL2290A5w/X0_tjLFbBgAJ>

Cheers,
Jim

Andrew:

Hi, scale-free is about computation but it's also about interpretability and it's also about being able to do a better job with priors, especially weakly informative priors.  The idea is that scale free parameters should typically (tho not necessarily) in the (0, 1) range in absolute value, suggesting that things like N(0,1) could be weakly informative priors.  So I'm not a fan of a prior centered at 4.5.  The answer would have to depend on context, but I think maybe you'd \want some multiplicative factor here?
A

P.S. As Jim says, stan-users is the best place for such a discussion!

And Mike:

To echo the other comments:

It’s not really “scale free” but rather “scale unified”.  As you noted a nice
way to think about this is in terms of units.  Once you’ve identified the
appropriate units of your problem then you can redefine your system
of units so that all of the expected effects are all around 1 in those units.

This has nice computational benefits — if your effects vary on the order of
10^{6} in one direction and 10^{-6} in the other, then it will take 10^{12}
steps to explore everything, but if everything is order 1 then it will take
order 1 steps to jump to a new point.

But the real benefit is that it facilities building good priors.  We like to
use “weakly” informative priors where we don’t know if an effect
exists but if it does we have some idea of it’s scale (a recent
example that has come up lately is in physiological models — however
complicated the body is, blood can’t floor faster than a certain amount,
so the effects of any drug can’t change blood flow by more than that
amount).  Ultimately these manifest as priors of the form

x ~ normal(0, x_scale);

or

x ~ cauchy(0, x_scale);

Now if all of the scales are order 1, then all of your priors will look
the same and you have much less bookkeeping to do.

Adding a mean to the prior introduces more information, turning the
weakly informative prior into something much more informative.  Now
if that is information that you actually believe then go for it, but always
verify that the fit was good and the prior mean wasn’t in tension with
the rest of the model.

messages.body_plain:
The procedure Dean is describing is standard operating procedure in machine
learning.   For example, it's what you see in the Hastie,
Tibshirani and Friedman book and their papers on elastic net.  It
avoids the "problem" of putting priors on parameters. I find the parameter
plots vs. regularization strength they produce very enlightening.  It's usually
done with straight-up penalized maximum likelihood, which you'd get
with L-BFGS in Stan.  With optimization, there's probably an advantage to starting
each optimization at the previous optimum for speed---at least
that's what Hastie et al. report.  I'd always suspected that a lot of the motivation
for doing things this way was that the software in play wouldn't generalize
to hierarchical priors (no optimum, which is why you need max marginal
likelihood, aka "empirical Bayes").  For example, if you want to throw Vowpal
Wabbit at a ton of data or many of the logistic regression optimization packages
out there.

Like Avi, I'm not sure what Dean meant about warnings---the R wrappers
for L-BFGS have worked well for me when I've tried them.

I'll add a warning that this makes sense only when the coefficients for
which you are generating priors are on the same scale.  If you have effects
on the order of 1e6 and others on the order of 1e-6, you can't motivate
a one-size-fits-all prior or regularization.  So it might help to at least
standardize the predictors.

- Bob

Believe it or not, your idea is very close to something I've been interested in for awhile, using Stan to fit models with preset values of key hyperparameters, then doing some sort of approximate integration and model averaging.   Most of the others in the Stan team hate this idea but I think it has a lot of promise.  So maybe we can talk about this one together and either prove 'em all wrong or, more likely, go down in flames!

messages.subject: Latent mixture with known parameters in one case?
messages.subject_clean: Latent mixture with known parameters in one case?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Let's say I have a time series whose growth is either 0 or positive. Some values of the time series are
missing and so I want to use a state-space representation.

The state model is:

x(t) = x(t-1) with probability theta

x(t) = x(t-1) + r(t) with probability 1- theta

and the "growth bump" r(t) is always non-negative

r(t) ~ normal_{+}(0, sigma)

Another way of putting it is that r(t) is 0 with probability theta, and takes the above distribution with probability
1- theta. There's then a measurement model:

observation(t) ~ normal(x(t), sd_measurement_error)

The question is how to implement the structure? At the moment, I'm hacking it, by simply stating that rather than
being precisely 0 in the first case, r(t) is small.

model {
   // priors for theta and sigma

    target += log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal_lpdf(r[t] | 0, 0.01), // r[t] very small rather than precisely 0
                                          log(1-theta) + normal_lpdf(r[t] | 0, sigma);
}

Is there a better way of doing this?

messages.subject: Failure to run a multivariate count model
messages.subject_clean: Failure to run a multivariate count model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan-users
I want to update a model with multivariate count data (common in biodiversity modelling). I use a scaled inverse Wishart to express the covariance for the multivariate normal distribution of logged intensities. Since my data is counts, I would like to use a Poisson process at the last step to derive the likelihood.
My problem is that adding this last step does not work. I can run the model using logged counts as data on the multivariate normal directly, but as soon as I add the observation process (the Poisson distribution on data) the sampler get NaN values on the multivariate normal and a lot of other errors. This is frustrating since the model without the Poisson step works.

I have tried adding initials with no success.

I attach an artificial generated data and code with the two alternative models.

It would be much appreciated if anyone could hint what is wrong : )
.
~Ullrika

Not yet.  This keeps coming up.  We hope to get to this soon
after the big refactor of commands lands, but we're not sure
when that'll be.

For now, just keep doubling *both* warmup and sampling stages
until you get convergence and high enough effective sample
size.  You almost always want longer warmup if you haven't
gotten high enough n_eff or convergence.  The only time
you want to do what you suggest is when you know warmup
has converged across chains and you have almost but not
quite high enough n_eff for some purpose.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Latent mixture with known parameters in one case?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Latent mixture with known parameters in one case?
messages.body_plain:
Agree with Michael that you want to think generatively.  What
you really have is a discrete parameter:

  z(t) ~ bernoulli(theta);

which will be 1 if x(t) != x(t-1) [equivalently r(t) != 0]
and 0 otherwise.

Marginalizing out the z(t) is exponential in the number
of time steps because there are 2^T paths for t in 1:T.

I don't see how you can fit the model in less than exponential
time in the number of time steps in Stan.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Problems with tiny stepsizes and (lower precision) Differential Equation models?
messages.body_plain:
I take it you mean Stan's step sizes are small in the Hamiltonian
simulation, not that the step sizes in the BDF integrator are small (both
are doing stepwise solutions of a system of diff eqs).

Yes, it's a possible problem if you initialize somewhere that's
poorly conditioned.  Tighter priors and more reasonable inits
will help.  One thing to watch out for is interval-constrained
parameters.  They initialize in the middle of the range, but people
like to do uniform(0, 1e4) for parameters and don't realize they'll
get 5e3 as the center of initialization.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Failure to run a multivariate count model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Failure to run a multivariate count model
messages.body_plain:
We recommend using a scaled LKJ prior for covariance, because
it's easier to reason about as a prior (unless you have prior
data, in which case inverse Wishart is conjugate).  We also
recommend using the much more efficient and stable
Cholesky-factor parameterization, which LKJ supports.  That may
solve the problem if the NaN are coming from numerical instability.
Otherwise, you'll need to track down what the parameters are that
are getting generated for the Poisson (or poisson_log, which takes
the log mean/variance as a parameter rather than the mean/variance).

Also, the data may not be consistent with a Poisson process.  We
tend to use overdispersed models, but those are even trickier to fit.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using init values with ADVI (vb) or BFGS (optimizing) to compute a regularization path
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using init values with ADVI (vb) or BFGS (optimizing) to compute a regularization path
messages.body_plain:
A brief follow-up on this topic.

I now recall why I was using VB rather than BFGS: BFGS seemed to be quite variable from run-to-run in its results, and often inconsistent with the MCMC and VB results. So that's why I was using VB even when seemingly just using BFGS would make sense. My guess is that the penalized likelihood is just really flat and perhaps not convex.

One concrete remaining issue is how tolerance is specified for VB:

> However, looking at how the ELBO convergence diagnostic works, I wonder if this will end up resulting in much longer runs than needed in order for convergence to be detected, since tol_rel_obj is defined with respect to the change in ELBO from the start, correct?

That is, it would be nice to be be able to specify other ways to detect convergence in VB. At least if I'm understanding this correctly that if I provide very helpful initialization, VB may run for much longer than really needed. I don't see any open issues on Github about this yet — maybe that is worth opening?

Best,
Dean

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problems with tiny stepsizes and (lower precision) Differential Equation models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Problems with tiny stepsizes and (lower precision) Differential Equation models?
messages.body_plain:
You’re decreasing the precision to really low levels (the default
in the original implementation was 1e-8) which causes really
inaccurate solves that immediately obstruct the validity of the
Metropolis correction.  In other words, the transitions are
corrupted by noise and you end up getting stuck in the tails
instead of moving towards the typical set.  The adaptation
tries to compensate the only way it knows how, by decreasing
the step size, but because the inaccuracies are not due to
HMC integrator error this doesn’t do anything and you get stuck
in a loop where the step size goes to really small values.

Lesson: nothing good happens when you try to make things
faster by sacrificing accuracy.  Unless you have extreme
simplifications (i.e. everything is Gaussian), high-dimensional
problems are too fragile and the only hope you have is to do
things correctly.

If that means that your model runs too slowly then you have
to limit the scope of your model to something that will run in
the required time.

messages.subject: Re: Editing stanfit graphs
messages.subject_clean: Editing stanfit graphs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tobias, there are two options that come to mind. (1) edit the ggplot object returned by traceplot() or (2) modify the parameter names in the stanfit object and then create the traceplot. I'll use the "eight_schools" Stan demo as an example.

stanfit <- stan_demo("eight_schools")
trace <- traceplot(stanfit)

1) The labels you want to change are taken from the "parameter" factor variable in the "data" slot of the object. To see what they currently are use

print(levels(trace$data$parameter))

and to change them you can use the replacement form of the levels() function:

levels(trace$data$parameter)[1] <- "new name" # change only the first

levels(trace$data$parameter) <- new_names # change all names, if new_names is character vector of correct length

plot(trace) # check the modified plot

2) To change the names in the stanfit object you can use the names method for stanfit objects. You can see what they currently are with

print(names(stanfit))

 "mu"       "theta[1]" "theta[2]" "theta[3]" "theta[4]" "theta[5]"
 "theta[6]" "theta[7]" "theta[8]" "tau"      "lp__"

and then you can replace as many of them as you want

names(stanfit)[1] <- "not_mu_anymore"
print(names(stanfit))

 "not_mu_anymore" "theta[1]"       "theta[2]"       "theta[3]"
 "theta[4]"       "theta[5]"       "theta[6]"       "theta[7]"
 "theta[8]"       "tau"            "lp__"

Then when you create the traceplot it should use the new names.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: Is there a way to speed up estimation in Stan if by linearizing functions?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a way to speed up estimation in Stan if by linearizing functions?
messages.body_plain:
I have the following nonlinear system involving a fixed variable X, and two random variables Y and Z:

E(Y)  = f(w1 * X)
E(Z|Y) = f(w2 * Y)

where f(u) = u / (1 + u)

I assume both Y and Z Gamma distributed:

Y ~ Gamma(alphaY, alphaY / E(Y))
Z ~ Gamma(alphaZ, alphaZ / E(Y|Z))

I can fit this in Stan without problems.

However, if I linearize the equation Y = f(w1* X)  I get  Y^-1 = (1/w1) + (1/w1)(1/X), then estimate (1/w1) using Gamma GLM, for example using bayesglm() from the arm package, the estimation is much faster.  Of course I know bayesglm isn't designed for hierarchical modeling.

Actually, my full model has some parts that are linearizable like this and parts that are not.  My question is, is there a way I can make use this linearizability in my model to speed it up and make the workflow more reproducible?  Perhaps using Hamiltonian MCMC for the nonlinear steps and the arm package's augmented EM for the linearizable steps.

Perhaps a more general Bayesian question, suppose you had a hierarchical model where some steps of the hierarchy have a structure that were easy to work with if they were stand-alone, such as having a conjugate prior.  Can you take advantage of that simplicity? Or is it MCMC for one, MCMC for all?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, September 27, 2016 at 11:48:21 AM UTC-4, Robert Ness wrote:
> However, if I linearize the equation Y = f(w1* X)  I get  Y^-1 = (1/w1) + (1/w1)(1/X), then estimate (1/w1) using Gamma GLM, for example using bayesglm() from the arm package, the estimation is much faster.  Of course I know bayesglm isn't designed for hierarchical modeling.

The stan_glmer() function in the rstanarm package is designed for hierarchical modeling and uses Stan rather than a hacked IRLS. Make sure to set QR = TRUE if you don't have an informative prior on the betas.

> Actually, my full model has some parts that are linearizable like this and parts that are not.  My question is, is there a way I can make use this linearizability in my model to speed it up and make the workflow more reproducible?  Perhaps using Hamiltonian MCMC for the nonlinear steps and the arm package's augmented EM for the linearizable steps.

That does not sound like a good idea so fortunately it is not possible.

> Perhaps a more general Bayesian question, suppose you had a hierarchical model where some steps of the hierarchy have a structure that were easy to work with if they were stand-alone, such as having a conjugate prior.  Can you take advantage of that simplicity? Or is it MCMC for one, MCMC for all?

HMC in Stan proposes all the parameters jointly. I suppose you could update a subset of them holder the complementary subset fixed, but that would be suboptimal. The reason why HMC works better than Gibbs sampling is because it does not condition on parameters and you get less dependence in the draws. The reason why NUTS works better than one-step HMC is because NUTS is greedy and tries to get across the relevant part of the parameter space each iteration. You don't get that with other traditional MCMC algorithms.

Ben

Hi Michael, Bob,

Thanks for the excellent feedback. Based on this feedback, I changed 2 things to test if it works better;
  1) I increased precision of bdf_integrate, but allowed it to do fewer iterations (1,000 iterations, both precision are 1e-7.)
  2) I decreased the adapt_window (the slow adaptation interval), and left the initial and final adaptation intervals higher.

The result is that it allows the model to finish the 200 warmup iterations about a hundred times faster than the original (hours instead of days). The values it arrives look good, and the confidence intervals are (comparatively) small.

The next question I have is how to check if this is converging well, especially if there is anything you'd suggest in particular given my approach;
The Rhat values are all in (0.97,1.02), it's not exceeding the max treedepth anywhere, and the pairs plot looks great. I'm running multiple chains - I ran 2 in the run on my laptop for this data, and I ran 8 on the server that's ~halfway done.

What else should I be trying or checking? (Or is this a horrible approach, and why?)

Thanks so much,
David

On Monday, September 26, 2016 at 3:56:39 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> You’re decreasing the precision to really low levels (the default
> in the original implementation was 1e-8) which causes really
> inaccurate solves that immediately obstruct the validity of the
> Metropolis correction.  In other words, the transitions are
> corrupted by noise and you end up getting stuck in the tails
> instead of moving towards the typical set.  The adaptation
> tries to compensate the only way it knows how, by decreasing
> the step size, but because the inaccuracies are not due to
> HMC integrator error this doesn’t do anything and you get stuck
> in a loop where the step size goes to really small values.
>
> Lesson: nothing good happens when you try to make things
> faster by sacrificing accuracy.  Unless you have extreme
> simplifications (i.e. everything is Gaussian), high-dimensional
> problems are too fragile and the only hope you have is to do
> things correctly.
>
> If that means that your model runs too slowly then you have
> to limit the scope of your model to something that will run in
> the required time.
>

hi dean,

if i recall correctly i wrote up a little heuristic procedure that determines an appropriate "running window" for tracking convergence. `tol_rel_obj` is then defined with respect to averaged ELBO values within that window.

my experience has been, at least for the default values of `tol_rel_obj`, that ADVI stops prematurely rather than running longer than necessary. but that might just be due to the types of models i've played around with.

all this said: there's definitely room for improvement in assessing convergence for VI; how to best do this is arguably an open research area.

cheers
alp

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the pointers Avi, that's very helpful.

In general it would be great if Aki and co-authors would consider including guidance along these lines in their final loo paper.

On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 4:58:17 PM UTC+2, Avraham Adler wrote:
> On Tuesday, September 13, 2016 at 8:36:23 AM UTC-4, Tom Wallis wrote:
> > Hi Daniel,
> >
> > Sorry for the late reply.
> >
> > I'm afraid I didn't state much more than what is written at the bottom of p. 20 of Aki et al's paper (v5):
> >
> > "Comparing the models on PSIS-LOO reveals an estimated difference in elpd of 10.2 (with a standard error of 5.1) in favor of Model A. "
> >
> >
> > So in my application I basically state that one model is preferred according to the LOO elpd estimate. Given that I'm comparing one model with and one model without an interaction term, and there's a pretty obvious interaction just from plotting the data, I think the model comparison results for my application are uncontroversial.
> >
> >
> > More generally though, I think it would be of great practical value if Aki and co-authors could include an example of converting elpd to a more intuitive scale for some given application (as stated in Aki's second reply, above).
>
> If you've multiplied by -2 and are on the deviance scale, you can probably use Burnham & Anderson's (2002, §2.6) AIC rules of thumb as does Spieghalter et al.(2002, §9.2.4) for DIC, as they are all estimates of the expected log pointwisepredictive density penalized for bias, I believe. Take the difference between any model's WAIC or elpd-loo on deviance scale from the model with the minimal value. B&A's heuristics are:
>
> Difference between 0 - 2: Substantial evidence for second model as well
> Difference between 4 - 7: Considerably less evidence for second model with respect to first
> Difference greater than 10: Essentially no evidence for second model
>
> Remember it is the difference that is important, the absolute magnitude is more a function of the number of data points than anything else.
>
>
> Avi
>
>
> References:
> Burnham, K. P. & Anderson, D. R., Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach, Springer Science+Business Media, Inc., 2002
> Spiegelhalter, D. J.; Best, N. G.; Carlin, B. P. & Van Der Linde, A., Bayesian measures of model complexity and fit, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), Blackwell Publishers, 2002, 64, 583-639 http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9868.00353/abstract;jsessionid=22CC7D20205F4D694F6F506D70B60834.f01t02

Hi!

Plans are to refactor the ODE system with the aim to make specification of the analytic Jacobian possible for the stiff and the non-stiff solver at the very same time. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ADVI - current statistical thinking
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] ADVI - current statistical thinking
messages.body_plain:
> On Sep 28, 2016, at 8:14 AM, 'Peadar Coyle' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all,
> I'm one of the PyMC3 contributors - I ran into Michael Betancourt yesterday at an event in London.
>
> He told me 'ADVI doesn't really work'.

It's well known because of the direction of KL-divergence being
optimized that

* variational inference underestimates posterior variance.

But we don't really know how much (or at least I don't).

Rayleigh and Andrew wrote an evaluation package for ADVI a bunch of
models we have prebuilt for Stan and have the right answers
through Stan's (and often JAGS's) MCMC.  I don't know if
he made the R repo for this public.

They're evaluating how often the posterior mean for
a parameter falls within one posterior standard deviation
of the posterior mean.  I don't know if it evaluates posterior
variance estimates.

The tests are for ADVI, not just for normal variational approximations.
Specifically, ADVI can fail for two reasons: it fails to find the
correct parameters to minimize the KL divergence (there are adaptation
and tuning parameters for the optimization) or the normal approximation
is inappropriate.  The former is likely to improve over time as
the ADVI defaults improve.

I'm also not sure the proportion of models for which ADVI gets
every parameter to within one posterior s.d., fails to get
at least one parameter within one posterior s.d., or just
fails to converge.  And it varies between the mean
field (independent normal approximation per parameter)
and full rank (multivariate normal approximation).

Word on the street is that

* it works better with more data so that the posterior
  is more approximately normal (independent or multivariate)

* the prior parameters in a hierarchical model may
 be off and the lower-level coefficients still roughly
 correct

* it can often perform very well predictively even when
  some params are off by more than one posterior s.d. (the
  previous hierarchical model case would be an example)

I hope the ADVI devs can clarify!

Until we have some better understanding of the nature of
the multivariate normal approximation, it's hard to know when
we can trust the parameter estimates from ADVI.  On the other
hand, if we focus on predictions or other event probabilities,
and we have an independent means of calibration (like held out data),
then we can evaluate those independently and ADVI is going to be able
to fit models at scales we won't even be able to test with MCMC.
This latter property is why we're excited about making it work and
undertanding where it will work.

- Bob

log(0) is -infinity, not NaN.  It might raise a pole error in
some implementations, but won't raise a domain error.
See:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/log/

Stan follows the standard's behavior for built-in functions.

But what can happen is that downstream, you might try to
add positive infinity to negative infinity, which gives you NaN.
Or divide.

- Bob

Bob, it was L-BFGS. Though I experimented with larger values of history_size with little effect. But perhaps I should try BFGS just to be sure.

This was a hierarchical model to start with (for fully Bayesian inference), but then I am fixing the scale at a series of values. That's how I am creating the regularization path.

But this is also a measurement error model. The model has the form:
> Y ~ normal(alpha + X_true * beta, sigma);
> for (i in 1:N) {
>     X_true[i] ~ student_t(nu_x, mu_x, sigma_x);
>   X[i] ~ multi_normal(X_true[i], tau);
> }
> beta ~ normal(0, sigma_beta);
With nu_x, sigma_x, tau, and sigma_beta all fixed as "data" (in addition to Y and X). tau is really known and then some subset of the others can be used to form a regularization path / grid.

So maybe this ends up being mode-less some how, but that wasn't an obvious case of the hierarchical model mode-lessness to me.

Best,
Dean

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is estimation in an SDE possible?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is estimation in an SDE possible?
messages.body_plain:
The problem with SDEs is that, unlike ODEs, they are not deterministic
so you can’t “solve” them in the same way that you can an ODE.  Instead
you have to marginalize over all possible SDE solutions, or paths, to get
a valid answer.  In theory this requires dealing with an infinite dimensional
space which is not feasible in Stan, but there are many approximations.
For example, you can discretize time and hence the path, treating it
similarly to a hidden Markov model or an autoregressive time series.
This is similar to what Dominic mentions in the slides, and is how INLA
approximates SDEs, too.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ulrika,

I think the problems stems from the fact that you declare lambda in your model block. If you move the declaration to the parameter block, I think your model with poisson will work. I never grok why exactly but parameters with a distribution need to go into the parameters block. In the model block, you can declare parameters that are deterministically related to other parameters.

For what it's worth. The results as is look fine with chains = 4, iter = 200 and you can also use cores = 4 (or whatever is applicable) to run the chains in parallel. I still encountered quite some numerical issues with the positive definiteness of LDLT_factor. You might want to look into the LKJ prior and the Cholesky decomposition which are much more stan and numerical friendly. Section 6.14 in the 2.12 Stan User's guide might be helpful for that.

Stijn

Your intuition is right. Even if you initialize at the global optima, ADVI will continue to wander around as the convergence diagnostic is not tripped yet. Moreover, while it’s wandering, ADVI can depart from the global optima due to the variance of its stochastic gradients. (This is also a problem that appears in a benchmark test that Bob mentioned here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/ZNBMJgNAWmo).)

Dustin

>
> > [I guess my concern was that if I provide quite good initialization (because it is from a prior run with a barely different penalty), my interpretation of this convergence detection was that it would still want a large relative improvement from that starting point, which might take a long time to find. But it sounds like that is a misunderstanding of how the convergence detection works.]
>
> Your intuition is right. Even if you initialize at the global optima, ADVI will continue to wander around as the convergence diagnostic is not tripped yet. Moreover, while it’s wandering, ADVI can depart from the global optima due to the variance of its stochastic gradients. (This is also a problem that appears in a benchmark test that Bob mentioned here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/ZNBMJgNAWmo).)
>
> Dustin

> >
> > [I guess my concern was that if I provide quite good initialization (because it is from a prior run with a barely different penalty), my interpretation of this convergence detection was that it would still want a large relative improvement from that starting point, which might take a long time to find. > > > if i recall correctly i wrote up a little heuristic procedure that determines an appropriate "running window" for tracking convergence. `tol_rel_obj` is then defined with respect to averaged ELBO values within that window.
> > >
> > > my experience has been, at least for the default values of `tol_rel_obj`, that ADVI stops prematurely rather than running longer than necessary. but that might just be due to the types of models i've played around with.

> > > >
> > > > One concrete remaining issue is how tolerance is specified for VB:
> > > > > However, looking at how the ELBO convergence diagnostic works, I wonder if this will end up resulting in much longer runs than needed in order for convergence to be detected, since tol_rel_obj is defined with respect to the change in ELBO from the start, correct?

> > > >
> > > > Best,

> > > > >
> > > > > But I wonder whether even if you could use a hierarchical prior, would it really be better? Maybe if the model is correctly specified and your "real" loss function is the likelihood. Maybe not otherwise.
> > > > >

> > > > > > The procedure Dean is describing is standard operating procedure in machine

messages.body_snippet:
Dear all,

I have a rather simple problem for which I nevertheless do not seem to be able to find the answer (note that the following is not my actual problem, but a simpler data set illustrating the

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.body_plain:
The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.

The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
evaluation set to test real-world calibration.

Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:

  vector[N] y;
  vector[K] mu;
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;

  y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);

  mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

  sigma[k] ~ ...;

You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.

- Bob

Given that the goal is a meta-analytic assessment across groups, I want to weight each individual equally and not the groups. I figure I need to somehow weight the individual group effect by some function of the group size, but I am not able to do this properly.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

My apologies for an initially general inquiry, but does anyone have suggestions for how to effectively estimate models in RStan in a simulation context?

There have been several questions posted to a local listserv by students who report that only one or two models can be estimated before the system crashes as a result of running out of memory. It isn't clear what is being stored rather than overwritten when using RStan that results in such high memory usage.

Would a potential fix be to include a line or two of code, possibly to delete the model and then re-initialize the model within the loop?

Thank you very much,
Shauna

Hello Daniel,

Thanks so much for your reply. Looks like I had that bug in the first code sample I posted, but stan was recovering from it (I didn't have priors on lambda[1] ... lambda[k-1], and only a prior on lambda[k] --- but stan didn't seem to really mind those missing priors). When I added the "transform parameters" block (in the second code sample I posted) I seem to have blasted that bug everywhere :).

When I fixed the bug you pointed out, the "transform parameters" block works fine. I've now implemented a mixture of multivariate Gaussians in rstan with a prior on the covariance matrix of each mixture component given by HLH, where H is a diagonal matrix with exponentially distributed entries, and L is a uniform distribution on correlation matrices. I feel like this is a good prior, because L can capture arbitrary correlation structure, and then H can scale the extent to which that structure affects each coordinate of the data, with some robustness added through the L1 penalty induced by the exponential prior on H.

In case anyone is interested, I've wrapped inference based on this model into an R S3 object with a predict method, which can impute sporadically missing values in a test set using the conditional distribution induced by the samples produced by stan. The training and target data is rescaled internally into a range for which the prior makes sense, so not much preprocessing or parameter tweaking needs to be done, aside from chosing k (k is the number of mixture components, it is not a for loop index).

Usage is like this:

> fit = mgfit(x)
> pred = predict(fit, y)

Here, x is an nxd matrix with no NAs, and y is an mxd matrix with any pattern of NAs. pred will be mxd and it will have the predictions for NA values of y, found by averaging the predictions (conditional multivariate Gaussian means) over all collected MCMC iterations and all components (weighted by posterior component assignment probabilities).

I'm calling this v0.1 because there may still be bugs in my for loop indices :) and I haven't tested corner cases. Here's an example on the iris dataset, showing better than chance performance:

> # load dataset
> x = iris[, 1:4]
>
> # split into test set and train set
> x = x[sample(length(x))]
> n = dim(x)[1]
> d = dim(x)[2]
> n.train = floor(n/2)
> x.train = x[1:n.train, ]
> x.validate = x[-(1:n.train), ]
> x.test = x.validate
> n.test = dim(x.test)[1]
>
> # hold out 1/2 entries sporadically in test set
> for (j in 1:d) {
>   x.test[sample(n.test, floor(n.test/2)), j] = NA
> }
>
> x.validate[!is.na <http://is.na>(x.test)] = NA
>
> # fit mixture of Gaussians
> fit = mgfit(x.train)
>
> # predict into test set
> x.pred = predict(fit, x.test)
>
> # print RMSEs of model, compared to baseline
> cat('RMSEs:\n')
> cat('VARIABLE MODEL BASE\n')
> for (j in 1:d) {
>   mask = is.na <http://is.na>(x.test[, j])
>   model = x.pred[mask, j]
>   truth = x.validate[mask, j]
>   base = mean(x.train[, j])
>   model.rmse = sqrt(mean(truth - model)^2)
>   base.rmse = sqrt(mean(truth - base)^2)
>   cat(sprintf("%s %.4f %.4f\n", colnames(x)[j], model.rmse, base.rmse))
> }

The output is:

> ...
> RMSEs:
> VARIABLE MODEL BASE
> Sepal.Length 0.2311 1.0938
> Petal.Length 1.1687 2.5691
> Petal.Width 0.8141 1.2664
> Sepal.Width 0.1416 0.2485

Not bad! Here's the code for mgfit and predict.mg <http://predict.mg> (mg.r):

> # mgfit/predict v0.1: model and predict variables using a mixture of Gaussians
> # Copyright (c) 2016, Lloyd T. Elliott
> # All rights reserved.
>
> # Redistribution and use in source and binary forms, with or without
> # modification, are permitted provided that the following conditions are met:
>
> # 1. Redistributions of source code must retain the above copyright notice, this
> # list of conditions and the following disclaimer.
>
> # 2. Redistributions in binary form must reproduce the above copyright notice,
> # this list of conditions and the following disclaimer in the documentation
> # and/or other materials provided with the distribution.
>
> # THIS SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED BY THE COPYRIGHT HOLDERS AND CONTRIBUTORS "AS IS"
> # AND ANY EXPRESS OR IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, THE
> # IMPLIED WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY AND FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE ARE
> # DISCLAIMED. IN NO EVENT SHALL THE COPYRIGHT HOLDER OR CONTRIBUTORS BE LIABLE
> # FOR ANY DIRECT, INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL, EXEMPLARY, OR CONSEQUENTIAL
> # DAMAGES (INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, PROCUREMENT OF SUBSTITUTE GOODS OR
> # SERVICES; LOSS OF USE, DATA, OR PROFITS; OR BUSINESS INTERRUPTION) HOWEVER
> # CAUSED AND ON ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, WHETHER IN CONTRACT, STRICT LIABILITY,
> # OR TORT (INCLUDING NEGLIGENCE OR OTHERWISE) ARISING IN ANY WAY OUT OF THE USE
> # OF THIS SOFTWARE, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGE.
>
> # fit a model
> mgfit = function(x, # dataset
>     k = 7, # number of components to use in mixture
>     seed = NULL, # random seed for stan (NULL = generate random seed)
>     quiet = TRUE, # suppress all output (currently unimplemented)
>     iter = 1000, # number of iterations
>     thin = 10, # amount of thinning (collected = iter/thin)
>     burnin = .75 # proportion of initial iterations to throw away as burnin
>     ) {
>
>   if (is.null(seed)) {
>     seed = sample(.Machine$integer.max, 1)

>   }
>
>   model = "// Multivariate mixture of Gaussians
>     data {
>       int<lower=2> n;
>       int<lower=2> k;
>       int<lower=2> d;
>       row_vector[d] x[n];
>     }
>
>     parameters {
>       simplex[k] rho;
>       row_vector[d] mu[k];
>       corr_matrix[d] lambda[k];

>       vector<lower=0>[d] h[k];

>     }
>
>     transformed parameters {
>       cov_matrix[d] omega[k];
>       for (j in 1:k) {

>         vector[d] al;
>         for (i in 1:d) {
>           al[i] = 1.0/h[j][i];
>         }
>         omega[j] = diag_matrix(al) * inverse(lambda[j]) * diag_matrix(al);

>       }
>     }
>
>     model {
>       rho ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0, k));
>       for (j in 1:k) {
>         mu[j] ~ normal(0, 1);

>         lambda[j] ~ lkj_corr(1);
>         h[j] ~ exponential(1);

>       }
>
>       for (i in 1:n) {
>         real p[k];
>         for (j in 1:k) {
>           row_vector[d] z;
>           z = x[i] - mu[j];

>           p[j] = log(rho[j]) + multi_normal_prec_lpdf(x[i] | mu[j], omega[j]);
>         }
>
>         target += log_sum_exp(p);
>       }
>     }"
>
>   library(rstan)
>   n = dim(x)[1]
>   d = dim(x)[2]
>
>   # scale training set
>   means = colMeans(x)
>   stds = apply(x, 2, sd)
>   x = t(apply(x, 1, function(v) { return((v - means)/stds) }))
>   pars = c("rho", "mu", "lambda", "omega", "h")
>   identities = list()
>   ones = list()

>   for (j in 1:k) {

>     identities[[j]] = diag(rep(1, d))
>     ones[[j]] = rep(1, d)
>   }
>
>   init = list(list(rho = rep(1/k, k),

>     mu = matrix(0, nrow = k, ncol = d),

>     lambda = identities,
>     omega = identities,
>     h = ones))

>
>   data = list(x = x, n = n, d = d, k = k)

>   samples = stan(model_code = model,
>     data = data,
>     pars = pars,

>     chains = 1,
>     iter = iter,
>     thin = thin,
>     seed = seed,
>     init = init)
>
>   result = structure(list(k = k,
>     d = d,
>     samples = samples,
>     means = means,
>     stds = stds,
>     count = iter/thin,
>     burnin = burnin), class = "mg")
>
>   return(result)
> }

> # helper functions
> mvnpdf = function(x, mu, logdet, omega) {
>   v = matrix(x - mu)
>   return(-logdet/2 - (t(v) %*% omega %*% v)/2)
> }
>
> logsumexp = function(x) {
>   m = max(x)
>   return(log(sum(exp(x - m))) + m)
> }

> # perform predictions based on model
> predict.mg <http://predict.mg> = function(mg, x) {
>
>   # scale test set
>   x = t(apply(x, 1, function(v) { return((v - mg$means)/mg$stds) }))
>   k = mg$k
>   d = mg$d
>   n = dim(x)[1]
>   z = matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = d)
>   count = mg$count
>   burnin = mg$burnin
>   samples = fit$samples@sim$samples[[1]]
>   denom = 0
>   for (iter in ceiling(count * burnin):count) {
>     denom = denom + 1
>
>     # extract sample from stan's trace
>     rho = rep(NA, k)
>     mus = list()
>     lambdas = list()

>     for (j in 1:k) {

>       token = sprintf("rho[%d]", j)
>       rho[j] = unlist(samples[token])[iter]
>       mu = matrix(NA, nrow = d, ncol = 1)
>       for (i in 1:d) {
>         token = sprintf("mu[%d,%d]", j, i)
>         mu[i, 1] = unlist(samples[token])[iter]
>       }
>
>       omega = matrix(NA, nrow = d, ncol = d)
>       for (i1 in 1:d) {
>         for (i2 in 1:d) {
>           token = sprintf("omega[%d,%d,%d]", j, i1, i2)
>           omega[i1, i2] = unlist(samples[token])[iter]
>         }
>       }
>
>       mus[[j]] = mu
>       lambdas[[j]] = solve(omega)
>     }
>
>     transforms = list()

>     for (i in 1:n) {
>

>       # find the missingness pattern
>       pattern = is.na <http://is.na>(x[i, ])
>       x1 = matrix(x[i, pattern])
>       x2 = matrix(x[i, !pattern])
>       if (sum(pattern) == d) {
>
>         # fully observed row: nothing to predict
>         next
>       }
>
>       if (sum(pattern) == 0) {
>
>         # completely missing row: predict the mean
>         next
>       }
>
>       p = rep(0, k)

>       for (j in 1:k) {

>         key = sprintf("%s%d", paste(sprintf("%d", pattern), collapse = ""), j)
>         if (is.null(transforms[[key]])) {
>
>           # we haven't seen this pattern: calculate the conditionals
>           lambda22 = lambdas[[j]][!pattern, !pattern]
>           omega22 = solve(lambda22)
>           if (is.matrix(lambda22)) {
>             logdet22 = unlist(determinant(lambda22, logarithm = TRUE))[[1]]
>           } else {
>             logdet22 = log(lambda22)
>           }
>
>           lambda12 = lambdas[[j]][pattern, !pattern]
>           transform = lambda12 %*% solve(lambda22)
>           info = list(omega22 = omega22,
>             logdet22 = logdet22,
>             transform = transform)
>
>           transforms[[key]] = info
>         } else {
>
>           # we've already seen this pattern: retreive the conditionals
>           info = transforms[[key]]
>           omega22 = info$omega22
>           logdet22 = info$logdet22
>         }
>
>         # compute posterior component assignment
>         mu2 = mus[[j]][!pattern, 1]
>         p[j] = log(rho[j]) + mvnpdf(x2, mu2, logdet22, omega22)
>       }
>
>       # normalize posterior component assignments
>       p = exp(p - logsumexp(p))

>       for (j in 1:k) {
>

>         # average the conditional predictions
>         key = sprintf("%s%d", paste(sprintf("%d", pattern), collapse = ""), j)
>         transform = transforms[[key]]$transform
>         mu1 = matrix(mus[[j]][pattern, 1])
>         mu2 = matrix(mus[[j]][!pattern, 1])
>         inc = p[j] * (mu1 + transform %*% (x2 - mu2))
>         z[i, pattern] = z[i, pattern] + inc
>       }
>     }
>   }
>
>   z = z/denom
>
>   # transform the predictions back to the original space
>   z = t(apply(z, 1, function(v) { return(v * mg$stds + mg$means) }))
>
>   # remove observed values from predictions
>   z[!is.na <http://is.na>(x)] = NA
>   return(z)
> }

That seems to work for rstan version 2.12.1 and R version 3.3.1.

But I've found that my call to stan is pretty slow. Does the following block introduce inefficiency in stan?

> vector[d] al;
> for (i in 1:d) {
>   al[i] = 1.0/h[j][i];
> }

I know that sometimes software like stan can be sped up if for loops are rolled into a single function call. Is that true for stan? I tried "al = 1.0/h[j];" but that gave me an error. I'm not having much luck profiling this code.

L

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the response. Unfortunately, this does not seem to solve the problem. Or I am incorrectly implementing this idea.

Also, in my real example (which was too long to write an easily understandable mail), the data is actually not normally distributed but follows a multinomial distribution and I have multiple random effects and parameters. The random effects are each parameterized as multivariate non-centered parametrizations with mean 0 which leads to the situation that the individual predictions are something like:

mu[j]      = mu_mu[2] + deltahat[j,1] + delta2hat[group[j],3] + ...; // and then some more transformations with mu along the way...

Consequently, please allow me to stay with this somewhat convoluted parameterization for the present example, to which I added independent sigmas per group as per your advise:

data {
  int<lower=1> nsubj;
  int<lower=1> ngroup;
  int<lower=1> group[nsubj];
  real y[nsubj];
  // real esize[nsubj]; // some function of group size probably helps
}
parameters {
  real mu_mu;
  vector[ngroup] deltahat;
  real<lower=0> sigma_i;

  real<lower=0> sigma[ngroup];

}
transformed parameters {
  real mu[nsubj];  // individual parameters

  for (j in 1:nsubj) {
    // add displacement to group level parameters:
    mu[j] = mu_mu + deltahat[group[j]]; // esize[j]*deltahat[group[j]] does not work...
  }
}
model {
  deltahat ~ normal(0, sigma_i);
  for (j in 1:nsubj) {

    y[j] ~ normal(mu[j], sigma[group[j]]);
  }
}

When doing so, the estimated mean is still near to the group mean, but not to the individual means:

# estimated mean
get_posterior_mean(f1, pars = "mu_mu")[,5]

# [1] 0.8881976

# weighted mean:
mean(aggregate(y~group, d, mean)$y)
# [1] 0.8834377

# unweighted mean:
mean(d$y)
# [1] 0.8590205

Likewise, when fitting this data to a set of very contrived simulated data, in which group size and group mean are perfectly correlated (but the variance is constant), we again only obtain the mean of the groups (which makes a lot of sense, give the model):

#### simulated data:
group_means <- 1:9
group_sizes <- seq(10, 90, by = 10)
y <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(group_sizes), function(x) rnorm(group_sizes[x], mean = group_means[x])))
groups <- rep(seq_along(group_means), times = group_sizes)

Results in:
get_posterior_mean(f_sim, pars = "mu_mu")[,5]
# [1] 5.063131
mean(group_means)
# [1] 5
mean(y)
# [1] 6.263281

To me it is difficult to see, how adding independent variances here should help in weighting the overall effect. In principle they could all be identical.

Thanks,
Henrik

PS: I have also followed your example and used a different parameterization, but this leads to the same results (although a lot faster):

data {
  int<lower=1> nsubj;
  int<lower=1> ngroup;
  int<lower=1> group[nsubj];
  real y[nsubj];
}

parameters {
  real mu_mu;
  vector[ngroup] mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma_mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma[ngroup];
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

  for (j in 1:nsubj) {

    y[j] ~ normal(mu[group[j]], sigma[group[j]]);
  }
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}

Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 15:40:38 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
> That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.
>
> The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
> Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
> some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
> look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
> have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
> evaluation set to test real-world calibration.
>
> Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
> are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
> g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:
>
>   vector[N] y;
>   vector[K] mu;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);
>
>   mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
>   sigma[k] ~ ...;
>
> You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
This is more of a modeling question, so I hope I can post it here.

I have data on injured people, and I'd like to see how a particular treatment improves their clotting ability (a scalar) from time A to time B. Different injuries are different though, some involve different parts of the body, and some are worse than others. I have categorical variables such as injury type which a-priori I do not believe affect clotting ability. I also have injury severity scores on a scale from 1 to 5 for 6 different parts of the body e.g. head, abdomen, chest, etc. My first naive solution is model the treatment effect separately (but hierarchically) for every possible combination of injury score crossed with injury type. For example patients in a motorcycle crash with a head injury score of 4, abdomen injury score of 5, and chest injury score of 4 would have their own treatment effect mu_{M,4,5,5}. I would then put, say a normal prior over those mu's.

The problem here is I believe this violates the exchangability of the mu's. A-priori I expect the higher rated injuries to not respond as well to the treatment. On the other hand, while it's clear mu_{M,4,5,5} is worse off than mu_{M,1,2,2}, it's up for debate whether mu_{M,5,4,4} is worse off i.e. there sort of is, but there sort of isn't an order here.

I'm sure people have encountered this problem before, but I didn't know what to search for. Any tips or references would be greatly appreciated.

Stijn's right---the loops are fast in Stan, and setting yhat
and then calling y ~ bernoulli(yhat) will be faster, though
it's not going to be that much faster because there aren't
any shared computations to exploit in this case---it just
eliminates some virtual function calls in the derivative
calculations.

When we get inv_logit vectorized (hopefully in the next release),
this will be a one-liner:

  y ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii] + (1 - gamma[ii]) * inv_logit(alpha[ii] .* (theta[jj] - beta[ii]));

assuming all of gamma, alpha, theta, and beta are declared as vector
types (not real arrays).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Your log density is evaluating to log(0) or -infinity.
Stan programs need to return finite log densities.   So
you need to debug your program and figure out why your
model doesn't have support at the initialization values.

This isn't related to the bug you link.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You may have been running for so many iterations that
it wouldn't fit into memory when you were done.

Always start small and build out until you get R-hat near
1 and n_eff > 100 for all parameters (and lp__).  The 2000
iteration default is probably too high.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.body_plain:
Here's how to test that things are working properly.

Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
Repeat.

If that works, your model's coded properly.

When you have

  y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)

you don't expect mu_mu to be the mean of the y.  Instead,
normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu) are trying to capture the variation
in the mu[k] across groups.

The reason to have the variance components is that you don't expect
each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the
mu will play into the variability of the mu_mu estimate.

- Bob

> On Sep 29, 2016, at 10:45 AM, Henrik Singmann <sing...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the response. Unfortunately, this does not seem to solve the problem. Or I am incorrectly implementing this idea.
>
> Also, in my real example (which was too long to write an easily understandable mail), the data is actually not normally distributed but follows a multinomial distribution and I have multiple random effects and parameters. The random effects are each parameterized as multivariate non-centered parametrizations with mean 0 which leads to the situation that the individual predictions are something like:
>
> mu[j]      = mu_mu[2] + deltahat[j,1] + delta2hat[group[j],3] + ...; // and then some more transformations with mu along the way...
>
> Consequently, please allow me to stay with this somewhat convoluted parameterization for the present example, to which I added independent sigmas per group as per your advise:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=1> nsubj;
>   int<lower=1> ngroup;
>   int<lower=1> group[nsubj];
>   real y[nsubj];
>   // real esize[nsubj]; // some function of group size probably helps
> }
> parameters {
>   real mu_mu;
>   vector[ngroup] deltahat;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_i;
>   real<lower=0> sigma[ngroup];
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   real mu[nsubj];  // individual parameters
>
>   for (j in 1:nsubj) {
>     // add displacement to group level parameters:
>     mu[j] = mu_mu + deltahat[group[j]]; // esize[j]*deltahat[group[j]] does not work...
>   }
> }
> model {
>   deltahat ~ normal(0, sigma_i);
>   for (j in 1:nsubj) {
>     y[j] ~ normal(mu[j], sigma[group[j]]);
>   }
> }
>
> When doing so, the estimated mean is still near to the group mean, but not to the individual means:
>
> # estimated mean
> get_posterior_mean(f1, pars = "mu_mu")[,5]
> # [1] 0.8881976
>
> # weighted mean:
> mean(aggregate(y~group, d, mean)$y)
> # [1] 0.8834377
>
> # unweighted mean:
> mean(d$y)
> # [1] 0.8590205
>
>
> Likewise, when fitting this data to a set of very contrived simulated data, in which group size and group mean are perfectly correlated (but the variance is constant), we again only obtain the mean of the groups (which makes a lot of sense, give the model):
>
> #### simulated data:
> group_means <- 1:9
> group_sizes <- seq(10, 90, by = 10)
> y <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(group_sizes), function(x) rnorm(group_sizes[x], mean = group_means[x])))
> groups <- rep(seq_along(group_means), times = group_sizes)
>
> Results in:
> get_posterior_mean(f_sim, pars = "mu_mu")[,5]
> # [1] 5.063131
> mean(group_means)
> # [1] 5
> mean(y)
> # [1] 6.263281
>
> To me it is difficult to see, how adding independent variances here should help in weighting the overall effect. In principle they could all be identical.
>
> Thanks,
> Henrik
>
> PS: I have also followed your example and used a different parameterization, but this leads to the same results (although a lot faster):
> data {
>   int<lower=1> nsubj;
>   int<lower=1> ngroup;
>   int<lower=1> group[nsubj];
>   real y[nsubj];
> }
> parameters {
>   real mu_mu;
>   vector[ngroup] mu;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_mu;
>   real<lower=0> sigma[ngroup];
> }
> model {
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>   for (j in 1:nsubj) {
>     y[j] ~ normal(mu[group[j]], sigma[group[j]]);
>   }
>   sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
> }
>
>
>
> Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 15:40:38 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
> That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.
>
> The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
> Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
> some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
> look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
> have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
> evaluation set to test real-world calibration.
>
> Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
> are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
> g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:
>
>   vector[N] y;
>   vector[K] mu;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);
>
>   mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
>   sigma[k] ~ ...;
>
> You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Efficient way to compute distance in rstan
messages.body_plain:
I think that's actually squared distance, not distance.  If
you just want distance, you can use the built-in hypot(x, y)
function.  Otherwise, there's not going to be a more efficient
way to do this.  I'd suggest using square(x - y) instead of
(x - y)^2, but that's a minor savings given that I think our
pow(x-y, 2) checks for a 2 and reduces to square() call.

- Bob
