messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sharing.

The biggest speedup would come from using a Cholesky factor
data type to parameterize a correlation matrix.  See the manual
chapter on regression for an example.  And this is going to
be really slow:

 omega[j] = diag_matrix(al) * inverse(lambda[j]) * diag_matrix(al);

First, we have quad_form_diag() function that'd make it much more
efficient than filling diagonal matrices, but you don't want to do
that, either.

Then use multi_normal_cholesky with the scaled cholesky factor, and you
won't need to use the precision form, and won't have to do inverses yourself.

- Bob

> On Sep 29, 2016, at 10:17 AM, Lloyd Elliott <lloyd.elli...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello Daniel,
>

> Thanks so much for your reply. Looks like I had that bug in the first code sample I posted, but stan was recovering from it (I didn't have priors on lambda[1] ... lambda[k-1], and only a prior on lambda[k] --- but stan didn't seem to really mind those missing priors). When I added the "transform parameters" block I seem to have blasted that bug everywhere :).

>
> When I fixed the bug you pointed out, the "transform parameters" block works fine. I've now implemented a mixture of multivariate Gaussians in rstan with a prior on the covariance matrix of each mixture component given by HLH, where H is a diagonal matrix with exponentially distributed entries, and L is a uniform distribution on correlation matrices. I feel like this is a good prior, because L can capture arbitrary correlation structure, and then H can scale the extent to which that structure affects each coordinate of the data, with some robustness added through the L1 penalty induced by the exponential prior on H.
>
> In case anyone is interested, I've wrapped inference based on this model into an R S3 object with a predict method, which can impute sporadically missing values in a test set using the conditional distribution induced by the samples produced by stan. The training and target data is rescaled internally into a range for which the prior makes sense, so not much preprocessing or parameter tweaking needs to be done, aside from chosing k (k is the number of mixture components, it is not a for loop index).
>
> Usage is like this:
>
> fit = mgfit(x)
> pred = predict(fit, y)
>

> Here, x is an nxd matrix with no NAs, and y is an mxd matrix with any pattern of NAs. pred will be mxd and it will have the predictions for non-NA values of y, found by averaging the predictions (conditional multivariate Gaussian means) over all collected MCMC iterations and all components (weighted by posterior component assignment probabilities).

>
> I'm calling this v0.1 because there may still be bugs in my for loop indices :) and I haven't tested corner cases. Here's an example on the iris dataset, showing better than chance performance:
>
> # load dataset
> x = iris[, 1:4]
>
> # split into test set and train set
> x = x[sample(length(x))]
> n = dim(x)[1]
> d = dim(x)[2]
> n.train = floor(n/2)
> x.train = x[1:n.train, ]
> x.validate = x[-(1:n.train), ]
> x.test = x.validate
> n.test = dim(x.test)[1]
>
> # hold out 1/2 entries sporadically in test set
> for (j in 1:d) {
>   x.test[sample(n.test, floor(n.test/2)), j] = NA
> }
>
> x.validate[!is.na <http://is.na>(x.test)] = NA
>
> # fit mixture of Gaussians
> fit = mgfit(x.train)
>
> # predict into test set
> x.pred = predict(fit, x.test)
>
> # print RMSEs of model, compared to baseline
> cat('RMSEs:\n')
> cat('VARIABLE MODEL BASE\n')
> for (j in 1:d) {
>   mask = is.na <http://is.na>(x.test[, j])
>   model = x.pred[mask, j]
>   truth = x.validate[mask, j]
>   base = mean(x.train[, j])
>   model.rmse = sqrt(mean(truth - model)^2)
>   base.rmse = sqrt(mean(truth - base)^2)
>   cat(sprintf("%s %.4f %.4f\n", colnames(x)[j], model.rmse, base.rmse))
> }
>
> The output is:
>
> ...
> RMSEs:
> VARIABLE MODEL BASE
> Sepal.Length 0.2311 1.0938
> Petal.Length 1.1687 2.5691
> Petal.Width 0.8141 1.2664
> Sepal.Width 0.1416 0.2485
>
> Not bad! Here's the code for mgfit and predict.mg <http://predict.mg> (mg.r):
>
> # mgfit/predict v0.1: model and predict variables using a mixture of Gaussians
> # Copyright (c) 2016, Lloyd T. Elliott
> # All rights reserved.
>
> # Redistribution and use in source and binary forms, with or without
> # modification, are permitted provided that the following conditions are met:
>
> # 1. Redistributions of source code must retain the above copyright notice, this
> # list of conditions and the following disclaimer.
>
> # 2. Redistributions in binary form must reproduce the above copyright notice,
> # this list of conditions and the following disclaimer in the documentation
> # and/or other materials provided with the distribution.
>
> # THIS SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED BY THE COPYRIGHT HOLDERS AND CONTRIBUTORS "AS IS"
> # AND ANY EXPRESS OR IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, THE
> # IMPLIED WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY AND FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE ARE
> # DISCLAIMED. IN NO EVENT SHALL THE COPYRIGHT HOLDER OR CONTRIBUTORS BE LIABLE
> # FOR ANY DIRECT, INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL, EXEMPLARY, OR CONSEQUENTIAL
> # DAMAGES (INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, PROCUREMENT OF SUBSTITUTE GOODS OR
> # SERVICES; LOSS OF USE, DATA, OR PROFITS; OR BUSINESS INTERRUPTION) HOWEVER
> # CAUSED AND ON ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, WHETHER IN CONTRACT, STRICT LIABILITY,
> # OR TORT (INCLUDING NEGLIGENCE OR OTHERWISE) ARISING IN ANY WAY OUT OF THE USE
> # OF THIS SOFTWARE, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGE.
>
> # fit a model
> mgfit = function(x, # dataset
>     k = 7, # number of components to use in mixture
>     seed = NULL, # random seed for stan (NULL = generate random seed)
>     quiet = TRUE, # suppress all output (currently unimplemented)
>     iter = 1000, # number of iterations
>     thin = 10, # amount of thinning (collected = iter/thin)
>     burnin = .75 # proportion of initial iterations to throw away as burnin
>     ) {
>
>   if (is.null(seed)) {
>     seed = sample(.Machine$integer.max, 1)
>   }
>
>   model = "// Multivariate mixture of Gaussians
>     data {
>       int<lower=2> n;
>       int<lower=2> k;
>       int<lower=2> d;
>       row_vector[d] x[n];
>     }
>
>     parameters {
>       simplex[k] rho;
>       row_vector[d] mu[k];
>       corr_matrix[d] lambda[k];
>       vector<lower=0>[d] h[k];
>     }
>
>     transformed parameters {
>       cov_matrix[d] omega[k];
>       for (j in 1:k) {
>         vector[d] al;
>         for (i in 1:d) {
>           al[i] = 1.0/h[j][i];
>         }
>         omega[j] = diag_matrix(al) * inverse(lambda[j]) * diag_matrix(al);
>       }
>     }
>
>     model {
>       rho ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0, k));
>       for (j in 1:k) {
>         mu[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
>         lambda[j] ~ lkj_corr(1);
>         h[j] ~ exponential(1);
>       }
>
>       for (i in 1:n) {
>         real p[k];
>         for (j in 1:k) {
>           row_vector[d] z;
>           z = x[i] - mu[j];
>           p[j] = log(rho[j]) + multi_normal_prec_lpdf(x[i] | mu[j], omega[j]);
>         }
>
>         target += log_sum_exp(p);
>       }
>     }"
>
>   library(rstan)
>   n = dim(x)[1]
>   d = dim(x)[2]
>
>   # scale training set
>   means = colMeans(x)
>   stds = apply(x, 2, sd)
>   x = t(apply(x, 1, function(v) { return((v - means)/stds) }))
>   pars = c("rho", "mu", "lambda", "omega", "h")
>   identities = list()
>   ones = list()
>   for (j in 1:k) {
>     identities[[j]] = diag(rep(1, d))
>     ones[[j]] = rep(1, d)
>   }
>
>   init = list(list(rho = rep(1/k, k),
>     mu = matrix(0, nrow = k, ncol = d),
>     lambda = identities,
>     omega = identities,
>     h = ones))
>
>   data = list(x = x, n = n, d = d, k = k)
>   samples = stan(model_code = model,
>     data = data,
>     pars = pars,
>     chains = 1,
>     iter = iter,
>     thin = thin,
>     seed = seed,
>     init = init)
>
>   result = structure(list(k = k,
>     d = d,
>     samples = samples,
>     means = means,
>     stds = stds,
>     count = iter/thin,
>     burnin = burnin), class = "mg")
>
>   return(result)
> }
>
> # helper functions
> mvnpdf = function(x, mu, logdet, omega) {
>   v = matrix(x - mu)
>   return(-logdet/2 - (t(v) %*% omega %*% v)/2)
> }
>
> logsumexp = function(x) {
>   m = max(x)
>   return(log(sum(exp(x - m))) + m)
> }
>
> # perform predictions based on model
> predict.mg <http://predict.mg> = function(mg, x) {
>
>   # scale test set
>   x = t(apply(x, 1, function(v) { return((v - mg$means)/mg$stds) }))
>   k = mg$k
>   d = mg$d
>   n = dim(x)[1]
>   z = matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = d)
>   count = mg$count
>   burnin = mg$burnin
>   samples = fit$samples@sim$samples[[1]]
>   denom = 0
>   for (iter in ceiling(count * burnin):count) {
>     denom = denom + 1
>
>     # extract sample from stan's trace
>     rho = rep(NA, k)
>     mus = list()
>     lambdas = list()
>     for (j in 1:k) {
>       token = sprintf("rho[%d]", j)
>       rho[j] = unlist(samples[token])[iter]
>       mu = matrix(NA, nrow = d, ncol = 1)
>       for (i in 1:d) {
>         token = sprintf("mu[%d,%d]", j, i)
>         mu[i, 1] = unlist(samples[token])[iter]
>       }
>
>       omega = matrix(NA, nrow = d, ncol = d)
>       for (i1 in 1:d) {
>         for (i2 in 1:d) {
>           token = sprintf("omega[%d,%d,%d]", j, i1, i2)
>           omega[i1, i2] = unlist(samples[token])[iter]
>         }
>       }
>
>       mus[[j]] = mu
>       lambdas[[j]] = solve(omega)
>     }
>
>     transforms = list()
>     for (i in 1:n) {
>
>       # find the missingness pattern
>       pattern = is.na <http://is.na>(x[i, ])
>       x1 = matrix(x[i, pattern])
>       x2 = matrix(x[i, !pattern])
>       if (sum(pattern) == d) {
>
>         # fully observed row: nothing to predict
>         next
>       }
>
>       if (sum(pattern) == 0) {
>
>         # completely missing row: predict the mean
>         next
>       }
>
>       p = rep(0, k)
>       for (j in 1:k) {
>         key = sprintf("%s%d", paste(sprintf("%d", pattern), collapse = ""), j)
>         if (is.null(transforms[[key]])) {
>
>           # we haven't seen this pattern: calculate the conditionals
>           lambda22 = lambdas[[j]][!pattern, !pattern]
>           omega22 = solve(lambda22)
>           if (is.matrix(lambda22)) {
>             logdet22 = unlist(determinant(lambda22, logarithm = TRUE))[[1]]
>           } else {
>             logdet22 = log(lambda22)
>           }
>
>           lambda12 = lambdas[[j]][pattern, !pattern]
>           transform = lambda12 %*% solve(lambda22)
>           info = list(omega22 = omega22,
>             logdet22 = logdet22,
>             transform = transform)
>
>           transforms[[key]] = info
>         } else {
>
>           # we've already seen this pattern: retreive the conditionals
>           info = transforms[[key]]
>           omega22 = info$omega22
>           logdet22 = info$logdet22
>         }
>
>         # compute posterior component assignment
>         mu2 = mus[[j]][!pattern, 1]
>         p[j] = log(rho[j]) + mvnpdf(x2, mu2, logdet22, omega22)
>       }
>
>       # normalize posterior component assignments
>       p = exp(p - logsumexp(p))
>       for (j in 1:k) {
>
>         # average the conditional predictions
>         key = sprintf("%s%d", paste(sprintf("%d", pattern), collapse = ""), j)
>         transform = transforms[[key]]$transform
>         mu1 = matrix(mus[[j]][pattern, 1])
>         mu2 = matrix(mus[[j]][!pattern, 1])
>         inc = p[j] * (mu1 + transform %*% (x2 - mu2))
>         z[i, pattern] = z[i, pattern] + inc
>       }
>     }
>   }
>
>   z = z/denom
>
>   # transform the predictions back to the original space
>   z = t(apply(z, 1, function(v) { return(v * mg$stds + mg$means) }))
>
>   # remove observed values from predictions
>   z[!is.na <http://is.na>(x)] = NA
>   return(z)
> }
>
> That seems to work for rstan version 2.12.1 and R version 3.3.1.
>
> But I've found that my call to stan is pretty slow. Does the following block introduce inefficiency in stan?
>
> vector[d] al;
> for (i in 1:d) {
>   al[i] = 1.0/h[j][i];
> }
>
> I know that sometimes software like stan can be sped up if for loops are rolled into a single function call. Is that true for stan? I tried "al = 1.0/h[j];" but that gave me an error. I'm not having much luck profiling this code.
>
> L

messages.body_plain:
There are multiple kinds of convergence here.  The previous discussion
was about whether the optimizer is considered to have converged.  Then
Andrew raised the question of whether when you run this all multiple times,
each run produces the same answer, which helps diagnose whether you've converged
to the wrong answer if the runs don't agree.  I don't think there are any
Markov chains involved here.  We can just inspect the posterior normal approximations
in multiple runs---we don't have to draw a sample from each normal approximation
and use R-hat.

- Bob

> On Sep 28, 2016, at 9:26 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi, I think the key to the convergence diagnostic will be using multiple chains.
> A

>> Source for the convergence diagnostic can be found here:
>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/variational/advi.hpp#L401
>>
>> > [I guess my concern was that if I provide quite good initialization (because it is from a prior run with a barely different penalty), my interpretation of this convergence detection was that it would still want a large relative improvement from that starting point, which might take a long time to find. But it sounds like that is a misunderstanding of how the convergence detection works.]
>>
>> Your intuition is right. Even if you initialize at the global optima, ADVI will continue to wander around as the convergence diagnostic is not tripped yet. Moreover, while it’s wandering, ADVI can depart from the global optima due to the variance of its stochastic gradients. (This is also a problem that appears in a benchmark test that Bob mentioned here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/ZNBMJgNAWmo).)
>>
>> Dustin

messages.subject: Sampling from inverted beta/dirichlet
messages.subject_clean: Sampling from inverted beta/dirichlet
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I'm fitting a fairly weird model (one that I've posted here in the past) that contains mixtures.

Because I want to favor categorization, I prefer sampling mixture weights (per case) from, e.g., a beta or dirichlet where the parameters are < 1. That puts more probability over 0s and 1s, and helps 'encourage' assignment to one cluster over others.

However, I noticed today that when using beta(.2,.2) as a prior, for example, that sampling was *slow* (like, 45 minutes later, and only hitting 10%, slow), and I assume that it's because so MUCH probability is over 0 and 1, and the geometry of that is awful to sample from (the negative log of that would be like an inverted U, constrained at 0 and 1).

Because of that, is it preferred to instead parameterize as log-odds and sample from a wide logistic?

That is, is it preferred to use:
vector[N] pi_logit;
pi_logit ~ logistic(pi_logit_mean, 5); pi_logit_mean ~ logistic(0,5);

as opposed to:
vector[N] pi;
pi ~ dbeta(alpha*scale,beta*scale); alpha = (pi_mean); beta = 1 - pi_mean; scale = .2; pi_mean ~ uniform(0,1)

I assume the logistic is easier to sample from, geometrically, than a beta/dirichlet that is highly pointed near bounded areas (0 and 1). Am I correct in thinking about this?

Use softmax regression to estimate logits of groups, then place a MVN(logits[n], 5*1.6*Identity) prior on that as an approximation to a dirichlet.

That is, rather than using: pi[n,1:K] ~ dirichlet(somePredicted/Hierarchical parameters), I could use pi_logit[n,1:K] ~ multinormal(somePredicted/Hierarchical parameters, scaling to adjust multinormal akin to using N(0,1.6) as logistic approx).

I'll play with this tomorrow.

messages.body_plain:
I understand that stan samples from the joint posterior.

I'm simply stating that my priors are purposefully placing greater probability toward constrained areas to encourage clustering (encouraging probability values of 0 and 1), which likely causes the posterior to be difficult to sample from, as the -log of that creates an extremely steep "hill" of sorts. To avoid that, I can reparameterize in terms of logits (which aren't constrained), and use a prior that is fairly wide so that larger logit values are more probable.
Extending that to a multigroup case is the difficulty. beta -> dirichlet, as logit -> ?; I'm thinking I could use a MVN approximation to a 'multivariate logistic' distribution of sorts.

messages.body_plain:
the weights are used as a plug-in device to create a noisy approximation for the population likelihood estimated from an informative sample (where the inclusion probabilities for units in the population are correlated with the response variable of interest).   the weights are normalized to sum to the number of (asymptotic) observations in order that the posterior uncertainty is correct.  so the weighting serves to re-balance information in the sample to approximate the balance in the population (and does not represent the number of units in the population).  while there are other fully bayesian approaches, there is a good reason i choose to use this weighted plug-in approach.  the weights can be regressed on the response to reduce their variability if that is problem in estimation.  the approach generally works well in gibbs sampling, though perhaps there would be additional issues in HMC regarding the stability of the sampler geometry.

anyway, thanks for providing me a link to the function.  i see the computation of -log1p(exp(theta)) portion of logp and its gradient, but can't find the n*theta piece, so i don't see a direct way of multiplying by the weights.   i'm guessing that if i write a weighted bernoulli_logit_lpmf() as a user function  that operates on each observation, it will be computationally too slow.  if you have any thoughts here, I'd appreciate having them.

messages.body_plain:
so there are two distributions that govern the observed sample under a complex sampling design:  1. the population generating distribution; 2. the known sampling design distribution.   the attached paper shows that the plug-in (weighted - based on first order inclusion probabilities) pseudo posterior estimator is frequentist consistent with respect to this joint distribution.

https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ejs/1468847267

even if observations are conditionally independent under the population generating distribution, they are typically not under the sampling design distribution (for samples taken from the population).  if the observations were independent, the amount of posterior information would be the sample size, n.   the theory in the above paper defines a class of sampling designs that guarantee consistency.  the pairwise dependence is required to asymptotically attenuate to 0 for designs in this class - so, asymptotically, the number of observations reflects the posterior uncertainty.   of course, we don't work in asymptopia and an area of active research is approximating the amount of information in the sample where dependence is induced by the sampling design distribution.

all to say, the virtue in the plug-in approach is that it is fully general and offers asymptotically correct inference under any population generating model based solely on observed quantities - the sample observations and weights - with no requirement to know (to parameterize) the sampling design.

i am familiar with the your approach of using weights to form post-strata.  very clever, but it requires an "information sufficiency" argument - that is, the sample reflects all the information in the population, if in different balance - to avoid imputing the non-sampled units (for consistent estimation).  the paper is not explicit in this point, but it is a requirement.  i hope to use it and, perhaps, further generalize it, but it is a less general approach than the plug-in estimator.  lastly, something not discussed in our preference for fully bayes is whether the data are able to offer any comment on a model for the weights, since the former (data) are acquired under the population generating model and the latter (weights) are acquired under the sampling design distribution.

anyway, if you have any other comments regarding how to implement a weighted likelihood approach that would efficiently sample, i'd appreciate having them.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I understand your point and appreciate the recommendations about testing ones model. But it does not really answer my actual question, so please apologize that I come back to it.

The parameter I want to estimate is not the (unweighted) mean of the groups, but the mean of the participants (i.e., a weighted group mean). Imagine this like a meta-analysis on the individual level data. And in a meta-analysis it is common to weight the effect by the sample sizes of the individual studies.

So if my parameterization does not allow me to estimate the value I am actually interested in (i.e., mu_mu captures the variations across groups), my question is:  How can I parameterize a model that estimates a hyper-parameter corresponding to the weighted group mean (i.e., groups weighted by their sample size) while including a random effect of group (i.e., adequately accounting for the fact that individuals within my groups might be more similar to the other group members than members of other groups) and possibly other random effects (which are not part of the simple example)?

Cheers,
Henrik

Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 23:22:26 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> Here's how to test that things are working properly.
>
> Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
> 50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
> Repeat.
>
> If that works, your model's coded properly.
>
> When you have
>
>   y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)
>
> you don't expect mu_mu to be the mean of the y.  Instead,
> normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu) are trying to capture the variation
> in the mu[k] across groups.
>
> The reason to have the variance components is that you don't expect
> each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the
> mu will play into the variability of the mu_mu estimate.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Sep 29, 2016, at 10:45 AM, Henrik Singmann <sing...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Thanks for the response. Unfortunately, this does not seem to solve the problem. Or I am incorrectly implementing this idea.
> >
> > Also, in my real example (which was too long to write an easily understandable mail), the data is actually not normally distributed but follows a multinomial distribution and I have multiple random effects and parameters. The random effects are each parameterized as multivariate non-centered parametrizations with mean 0 which leads to the situation that the individual predictions are something like:

> I wish I could post a reproducible example, but it happens to me quite regularly that I make changes to my rstan model code and then go to compile, but it happens very quickly and the model is unchanged. I then need to close and reopen rstudio to be able to compile the model. Is there anything I can check or change in this regard?

We're going to need an example.  The stan_model() function checks for that, so it must not be getting called.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
If it matters then you could get the wrong estimates (bias). But wrong is not binary. The degree of wrongness matters, so in some cases you could get estimates that are close enough and in others the estimates could be misleading. It's really case by case.

Hopefully more people will chime in. If not, I recommend posting an update in a new thread (with a different heading).

On Friday, September 30, 2016, Arya Pourzanjani <pour...@gmail.com> wrote:
> What are the downsides to ignoring non-exchangeability of these coefficients? In this case it just seems like I'd be using a prior that is more uninformative than it should be, which means wider posteriors. Is there anything else that could happen that I'm overlooking would make my inferences misleading?
>
> On Thu, Sep 29, 2016 at 7:58 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I got mixed up and that was a response to a different question sorry. For yours, the first thing to do is what you suggested is not quite right. That is, fit a model that ignores the partial ordering you suspect, because that's always easier and you'll have something to compare to and build on.
> >
> > In your case what that amounts to doing is ignoring prior information about correlations between a predictor and the treatment effect, if I understand correctly. So to account for that information you could model that correlation in the prior.
> >
> > Hope that gets you started,
> >
> > Jonah
